children.title: Affine Hulls
children.top_down_role: Smallest affine spaces containing point configurations.

assumptions_latex: A base point \(s_0\in S\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}(S)=s_0+\operatorname{span}(S-s_0)\).

notation.meaning: Affine hull of a point set.
Difference set relative to the base point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent affine-combination and translated-linear-span representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its affine hull is \[\operatorname{aff}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i s_i:k\in\mathbb{N},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\in\mathbb{R},\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Equivalently, for any fixed \(s_0\in S\), \[\operatorname{aff}(S)=s_0+\operatorname{span}\{s-s_0:s\in S\}.\] This set is independent of the chosen base point and is the unique smallest affine subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine hull is the set of affine combinations of points, equivalently a base point plus the span of all relative differences.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Hulls

children.title: Affine Dimension
children.top_down_role: Dimensional structure relative to an affine hull.

assumptions_latex: A base point \(s_0\in S\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim_{\mathrm{aff}}(S)=\dim\operatorname{span}(S-s_0)\).

notation.meaning: Affine dimension of the point set.
Linear span of differences from a base point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine dimension of a nonempty Euclidean point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine dimension of a nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the dimension of its affine hull. For any base point \(s_0\in S\), it is given by \[\dim_{\mathrm{aff}}(S):=\dim\bigl(\operatorname{aff}(S)\bigr)=\dim\operatorname{span}\{s-s_0:s\in S\}.\] The value does not depend on \(s_0\). Equivalently, \(\dim_{\mathrm{aff}}(S)=d\) when the largest affinely independent subset of \(S\) has \(d+1\) points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine dimension is the dimension of the span of point differences, or one less than the largest affinely independent subset size.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Dimension

children.title: Discrete Point Configurations
children.top_down_role: Finite point families underlying combinatorial convex hulls.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) determines the polytope \(P=\operatorname{conv}(A)\).

notation.meaning: Finite indexed or unindexed point configuration.
Convex hull generated by the configuration.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Euclidean point configurations used as generators of combinatorial polytopes.

source_refs.locator: Section 3.5. Convex Hulls and Polytopes p. 69

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite discrete point configuration in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty finite set \(A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), or an indexed family when repeated labels must be retained. Its associated convex polytope is \[P=\operatorname{conv}(A)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i a_i:\lambda_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Its affine rank is \(1+\dim_{\mathrm{aff}}(A)\). Points of \(A\) need not all be vertices of \(P\); some may lie in the convex hull of the others.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete point configuration is a finite collection of Euclidean points; its convex hull is a polytope, though not every listed point must be a vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Point Configurations

source_witnesses.locator: Section 3.5. Convex Hulls and Polytopes p. 69

children.title: Conic Recession Calculus
children.top_down_role: Conic representations of directions, unboundedness, and homogeneous systems.

children.title: Polyhedral Cones
children.top_down_role: Finitely described conic structures in polyhedral geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polyhedral cone admits both finite inequality and finite generator representations.

notation.meaning: Matrix defining a homogeneous inequality representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogeneous halfspace and ray representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedral cone if there exists a finite matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) such that \[C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le 0\}.\] Equivalently, there exist finitely many vectors \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[C=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i r_i:\lambda_i\ge 0\right\}.\] Thus a polyhedral cone is convex, closed, contains the origin, and is closed under addition and multiplication by nonnegative scalars.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral cone is equivalently the solution set of finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities or the nonnegative span of finitely many rays.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Cones

children.title: Recession Directions
children.top_down_role: Directional structure governing unbounded polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\) is a recession direction exactly when \(x+td\in P\) for every \(x\in P\) and \(t\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global recession directions of nonempty convex sets and linear inequality systems.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Algorithmic Aspects of Convex Sets: Formulation of the Problems p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a recession direction if \[x+td\in P\qquad\text{for every }x\in P\text{ and every }t\ge 0.\] The set of all recession directions is the recession cone \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\). If \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron, then \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\le0\}.\] In particular, \(P\) is bounded exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction can be followed indefinitely from every feasible point; for a polyhedron, these directions satisfy the associated homogeneous inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession Directions

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Algorithmic Aspects of Convex Sets: Formulation of the Problems p. 46

children.title: Homogenized Representations
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous conic encodings of affine polyhedral systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(P)=\{(y,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:Ay\le tb,\ t\ge0\}\), and its slice at \(t=0\) is \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\times\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Homogenization cone of the polyhedron P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed homogenization of a nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the nonempty polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), define its closed homogenization by \(H(P)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(x,1):x\in P\}\). Then \[H(P)=\{(y,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:Ay\le tb,\ t\ge0\}.\] For every \(t>0\), \((y,t)\in H(P)\) exactly when \(y/t\in P\), while \((y,0)\in H(P)\) exactly when \(y\in\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:Ad\le0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenization embeds a polyhedron as the positive-height slices of a cone, whose zero-height slice records all recession directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Homogenized Representations

children.title: Pointedness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conic regimes distinguished by the presence or absence of lines.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is line-free if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\) is pointed, equivalently if and only if \(P\) has a vertex.

notation.meaning: Lineality space of a cone C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness and lineality criteria for polyhedral recession cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is pointed precisely when \(C\cap(-C)=\{0\}\). For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), the following conditions are equivalent: \(P\) contains no affine line; its recession cone \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\) is pointed; and \(P\) has at least one vertex. If \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), its lineality directions form \(\{d:Ad=0\}\), so pointedness is equivalent to \(Ad=0\) implying \(d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is line-free exactly when its recession cone is pointed; for nonempty polyhedra, this is also exactly the regime in which vertices exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness Regimes

children.title: Polar-Blocker Duality Family
children.top_down_role: Dual geometric constructions used for packing and covering systems.

children.title: Polar Constructions
children.top_down_role: Geometric dual constructions for convex sets and cones.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((C^\circ)^\circ=C\).

notation.meaning: Polar of C with unit upper bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit polar and bipolar identity in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its polar is \[C^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\text{ for every }x\in C\}.\] If \(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains the origin, then the bipolar identity \((C^\circ)^\circ=C\) holds. More generally, for arbitrary \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), one has \((S^\circ)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S\cup\{0\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar collects vectors whose inner product with every point is at most one; taking the polar twice returns the closed convex hull with the origin.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar Constructions

children.title: Blocking Constructions
children.top_down_role: Dual descriptions associated with upward-closed covering structures.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is a nonempty closed convex set with \(P+\mathbb{R}_+^n=P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bl}(\operatorname{bl}(P))=P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blocking duality for closed convex upper-comprehensive sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\), define its blocker by \[\operatorname{bl}(P)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:y^Tx\ge1\text{ for every }x\in P\}.\] If \(P\) is nonempty, closed, convex, upper-comprehensive in the sense that \(P+\mathbb{R}_+^n=P\), and excludes the origin, then \(\operatorname{bl}(P)\) has the same properties and \(\operatorname{bl}(\operatorname{bl}(P))=P\). Thus membership in \(P\) is characterized by all blocker inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The blocker of an upper-comprehensive nonnegative convex set consists of nonnegative vectors pairing to at least one with every point, and blocking twice recovers the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Blocking Constructions

children.title: Antiblocking Constructions
children.top_down_role: Dual descriptions associated with downward-closed packing structures.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and downward-comprehensive.
There exists \(\bar x\in P\) with \(\bar x_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{abl}(P)\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and downward-comprehensive, and \(\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(P))=P\).

notation.meaning: A point of P with every coordinate strictly positive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antiblocking duality for compact downward-comprehensive convex sets containing a strictly positive point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\), define its antiblocker by \[\operatorname{abl}(P)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:y^Tx\le 1\text{ for every }x\in P\}.\] Suppose \(P\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and downward-comprehensive: whenever \(x\in P\) and \(0\le z\le x\), one has \(z\in P\). If there exists \(\bar x\in P\) with \(\bar x_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), then \(\operatorname{abl}(P)\) is also nonempty, compact, convex, and downward-comprehensive, and \(\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(P))=P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antiblocker uses upper inner-product bounds in the nonnegative orthant. For a compact downward-comprehensive convex set containing a strictly positive point, the antiblocker has the same structural properties, and applying the construction twice recovers the original set.
knowledge_statements.title: Antiblocking Constructions

children.title: Packing–Covering Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Structural links among blocking, antiblocking, packing, and covering viewpoints.

assumptions_latex: The packing problem has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le\mathbf{1},\ x\ge0\}=\min\{\mathbf{1}^Ty:A^Ty\ge c,\ y\ge0\}\).

notation.meaning: All-ones vector of the dimension determined by context.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear packing and covering pair with unit capacities and costs.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 10. Trees and arborescences: packing and covering p. 339

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times n}\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\). The packing program and its covering dual are \[\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le\mathbf{1},\ x\ge0\}\quad\text{and}\quad\min\{\mathbf{1}^Ty:A^Ty\ge c,\ y\ge0\}.\] If the packing optimum is finite, both programs attain optimal solutions and their optimal values are equal. Every feasible pair satisfies \(c^Tx\le\mathbf{1}^Ty\), making covering solutions upper certificates for packings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative linear packing problem has a covering dual; under finite optimality, both attain the same value, and every cover bounds every packing.
knowledge_statements.title: Packing–Covering Correspondences

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 10. Trees and arborescences: packing and covering p. 339

children.title: Polyhedral Description Geometry
children.top_down_role: Structural organization of finite linear inequality systems and their geometry.

children.title: Polyhedral Description-Generator Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Bounded and unbounded linear descriptions and their generating representations.

children.title: Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Possibly unbounded sets described by finite linear systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a polyhedron exactly when \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) for some finite matrix-vector pair \((A,b)\).

notation.meaning: A finite real matrix and right-hand-side vector.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional halfspace definition, allowing empty and unbounded polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a set representable as the intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces. Equivalently, there exist an integer \(m\ge0\), a matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and a vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}.\] Equalities are permitted through pairs of opposite inequalities; the definition allows \(P\) to be empty, lower-dimensional, or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is the solution set of finitely many linear inequalities, equivalently a finite intersection of closed affine halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedra

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite linear-inequality description of a subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron if there exist an \(m\times n\) matrix \(A\) and a vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge b\},\] where the inequality is componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is a subset of Euclidean space described by a finite system of linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge b\}\text{ is a polyhedron.}

source_evidence.locator: The geometry of linear programming / 2.1. Polyhedra and convex sets / Definition 2.1

source_refs.locator: The geometry of linear programming / 2.1. Polyhedra and convex sets / Definition 2.1

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedron

source_witnesses.locator: The geometry of linear programming / 2.1. Polyhedra and convex sets / Definition 2.1

children.title: Polytopes
children.top_down_role: Bounded polyhedral sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a polytope if and only if it is a bounded polyhedron, equivalently \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)\) for some finite \(V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: Convex hull of a set V.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition including the empty polytope by convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polytope in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the convex hull of a finite set: \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)=\left\{\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_vv:\lambda_v\ge0,\ \sum_{v\in V}\lambda_v=1\right\}\] for some finite \(V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). Equivalently, a set is a polytope exactly when it is a bounded polyhedron. Under the usual convention, \(\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\), so the empty set is also a polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope is the convex hull of finitely many points; equivalently, it is a bounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Polytopes

children.title: Inequality Representations
children.top_down_role: Linear constraint descriptions of polyhedral sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An inequality representation of \(P\) is any finite system \(Ax\le b\) whose feasible set equals \(P\).

notation.meaning: The halfspace defined by the i-th inequality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite halfspace descriptions, including redundant inequalities and implicit equalities.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inequality representation of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a finite system \(Ax\le b\) satisfying \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:a_i^Tx\le b_i\}.\] An inequality is valid for \(P\) when it holds for every \(x\in P\), and it is redundant in the displayed representation when deleting it leaves the represented set unchanged. Different systems may therefore represent the same polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality representation describes a polyhedron as the feasible set of finitely many linear inequalities; distinct and redundant systems can define the same set.
knowledge_statements.title: Inequality Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

children.title: Generator Representations
children.top_down_role: Point and ray descriptions of polyhedral sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a polyhedron if and only if \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\) for finite sets \(V,R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(V\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minkowski–Weyl point-and-ray representation for nonempty polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron if and only if finite sets \(V,R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(V\neq\varnothing\), exist such that \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R).\] Equivalently, every \(x\in P\) can be written as \(x=\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_vv+\sum_{r\in R}\mu_rr\), where \(\lambda_v\ge0\), \(\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_v=1\), and \(\mu_r\ge0\). The conical part generates all recession behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty polyhedron is a convex hull of finitely many points plus a cone generated by finitely many rays, and every such set is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.title: Generator Representations

children.title: Boundedness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural distinction between polytopes and unbounded polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:Ad\le0\}=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundedness criterion for nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), its recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+\lambda d\in P\text{ for all }x\in P,\ \lambda\ge0\}=\{d:Ad\le0\}.\] The polyhedron \(P\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}\). Hence any nonzero solution of \(Ad\le0\) is a directly checkable witness of unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is bounded exactly when its recession cone contains only zero; any nonzero recession direction certifies unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundedness Boundary

children.title: Polyhedral Face Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Global and local combinatorial organization of polyhedral faces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic facial notions for a nonempty polyhedron represented by linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\). If \(c\ne0\) and \(\delta=\max\{cx:x\in P\}<\infty\), then \(\{x:cx=\delta\}\) is a supporting hyperplane of \(P\). A face of \(P\) is either \(P\) itself or the intersection of \(P\) with a supporting hyperplane. A point \(x\) is a vertex of \(P\) when \(\{x\}\) is a face; it is also called a basic solution of \(Ax\le b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting hyperplane is a finite maximizing level set of a nonzero linear functional. A face is the whole polyhedron or its intersection with such a hyperplane. A singleton face is a vertex, also called a basic solution of the inequality system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:cx=\delta\}\text{ supports }P;\quad F=P\text{ or }F=P\cap\{x:cx=\delta\};\quad \{x\}\text{ a face}\Rightarrow x\text{ is a vertex/basic solution}.

source_evidence.locator: Linear Programming / 3.1. Polyhedra / Definition 3.3

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting Hyperplanes, Faces, and Vertices

children.title: Faces
children.top_down_role: Exposed substructures across all dimensions of a polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonempty face of \(P\) has the form \(F=\{x\in P:c^Tx=\delta\}\), where \(c^Tx\le\delta\) is valid for \(P\).

notation.meaning: A face exposed by a valid inequality.
Maximum of the exposing linear functional over P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed-face definition specialized to nonempty polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty subset \(F\subseteq P\) is a face of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) when some inequality \(c^Tx\le\delta\), valid for every \(x\in P\), satisfies \[F=\{x\in P:c^Tx=\delta\}.\] Equivalently, \(F\) is the set of maximizers of a linear functional over \(P\), with \(\delta=\max_{x\in P}c^Tx\). By convention, both \(P\) itself and the empty set are also faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is the subset where a valid linear inequality is tight, equivalently the maximizers of a linear functional; the whole polyhedron and empty set are included.
knowledge_statements.title: Faces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the common dimension of minimal faces and the bounded-polyhedron specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b\}\) be a polyhedron. Every minimal face of \(P\) has dimension \(n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\). The minimal faces of polytopes are vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every minimal face has dimension equal to the ambient dimension minus the rank of the constraint matrix. For a polytope, minimal faces are vertices.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b\}\text{ is a polyhedron}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall F\text{ minimal face of }P,\ \dim F=n-\operatorname{rank}(A);\qquad P\text{ a polytope}\implies F\text{ is a vertex}

source_evidence.locator: Linear Programming / 3.1. Polyhedra / Corollary 3.10

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension of Minimal Faces

children.title: Facets
children.top_down_role: Maximal proper faces relative to affine dimension.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron of dimension \(d\geq 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is a facet of }P\iff F\text{ is a face of }P\text{ and }\dim(F)=d-1\).

notation.meaning: dimension of the affine hull of \(P\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses dimension relative to the affine hull. When the empty set is included as a face, the maximal-proper-face characterization is restricted to nonempty faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron with \(d=\dim(P)\geq 1\). A subset \(F\subseteq P\) is a facet of \(P\) if and only if \(F\) is a face of \(P\) and has codimension one relative to \(P\), namely \(\dim(F)=d-1\). Equivalently, facets are the maximal proper nonempty faces of \(P\): \(F\neq\varnothing\), \(F\neq P\), and there is no face \(G\) satisfying \(F\subsetneq G\subsetneq P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A facet is a face whose dimension is one less than the polyhedron's dimension; equivalently, it is a maximal proper nonempty face.
knowledge_statements.title: Facets

children.title: Vertices
children.top_down_role: Zero-dimensional polyhedral faces.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a convex polyhedron and \(v\in P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\text{ is a vertex of }P\iff \{v\}\text{ is a face of }P\iff v\text{ is an extreme point of }P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies vertices with zero-dimensional faces and extreme points of a convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex polyhedron. A point \(v\in P\) is a vertex of \(P\) when the singleton \(\{v\}\) is a face of \(P\). Equivalently, \(v\) is an extreme point: whenever \(x,y\in P\), \(0<\lambda<1\), and \(v=\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\), one has \(x=y=v\). Thus a vertex is precisely a zero-dimensional nonempty face of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex is a zero-dimensional face, equivalently a point that is not a nontrivial convex combination of two points of the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertices

children.title: Face Lattices
children.top_down_role: Global containment organization of polyhedral faces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq)\) is a bounded lattice with \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\) and \(F\vee G=\bigcap\{H\in\mathcal{F}(P):F\cup G\subseteq H\}\).

notation.meaning: set of all faces of \(P\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\)
meet and join in the inclusion order

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the empty face and the whole polyhedron as the least and greatest lattice elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) contain every face of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\), ordered by inclusion. Then \((\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq)\) is a bounded lattice. For faces \(F,G\in\mathcal{F}(P)\), their meet is \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\), and their join is the smallest face containing both, given by \(F\vee G=\bigcap\{H\in\mathcal{F}(P):F\cup G\subseteq H\}\). The least element is \(\varnothing\), and the greatest element is \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The faces ordered by inclusion form a bounded lattice: intersection is meet, and the smallest face containing two faces is their join.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Lattices

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces of a Face Are Exactly the Contained Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral closure under taking faces and inheritance of the face-containment structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron and let \(F\) be a face of \(P\). Then \(F\) is a polyhedron. Moreover, for every \(F'\subseteq F\), \[F'\text{ is a face of }P\iff F'\text{ is a face of }F.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of a polyhedron is itself a polyhedron. A subset of that face is a face of the original polyhedron exactly when it is a face of the face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a polyhedron},\qquad \bigl(F'\text{ is a face of }P\bigr)\iff\bigl(F'\text{ is a face of }F\bigr).

source_evidence.locator: Linear Programming / 3.1. Polyhedra / Corollary 3.6

knowledge_statements.title: Faces of a Face Are Exactly the Contained Faces

children.title: Face Incidence Structure
children.top_down_role: Local incidence relationships among faces of different dimensions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is incident with }G\iff F\subseteq G\text{ or }G\subseteq F\), with cover incidence characterized by no intermediate face.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses incidence as comparability under face inclusion and distinguishes immediate incidence by the cover relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For faces \(F,G\in\mathcal{F}(P)\), the faces are incident when they are comparable in the face order, that is, when \(F\subseteq G\) or \(G\subseteq F\). If \(F\subsetneq G\), then \(F\) is immediately incident with \(G\) when no face \(H\in\mathcal{F}(P)\) satisfies \(F\subsetneq H\subsetneq G\). The incidence structure is therefore the inclusion poset of faces; its Hasse diagram records precisely these immediate incidences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two faces are incident when one contains the other. Immediate incidence means that no third face lies strictly between them in the inclusion order.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Incidence Structure

children.title: Minimal Polyhedral Description Criteria
children.top_down_role: Descriptional issues governing full dimension, implied constraints, and irredundancy.

children.title: Polyhedral Dimension
children.top_down_role: Affine dimensional structure of polyhedra and their descriptions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(P)=\dim(\operatorname{aff}(P))=\dim\operatorname{span}(P-P)\).

notation.meaning: set of pairwise differences of points of \(P\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines intrinsic dimension, independent of the dimension of the chosen ambient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its dimension is the dimension of its affine hull: \(\dim(P):=\dim(\operatorname{aff}(P))\). Equivalently, for any \(x_0\in P\), one has \(\dim(P)=\dim\operatorname{span}\{x-x_0:x\in P\}=\dim\operatorname{span}(P-P)\). The polyhedron is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) exactly when \(\dim(P)=n\), equivalently when \(\operatorname{aff}(P)=\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron's dimension is the dimension of its affine hull, equivalently the linear span of all differences between its points.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Dimension

children.title: Redundant Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraints implied by the remainder of a linear description.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for }i\in I\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\text{ is redundant}\iff P_{-k}\subseteq\{x:a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\}\iff P_{-k}=P\).

notation.meaning: polyhedron defined by the full inequality system

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundancy is defined relative to a particular finite inequality description, not solely to the represented polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\), and fix \(k\in I\). Define \(P_{-k}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\setminus\{k\}\}\). The inequality \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\) is redundant in this description exactly when deleting it does not enlarge the feasible set, equivalently when \(P_{-k}=P\), or when every \(x\in P_{-k}\) already satisfies \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is redundant when removing it leaves the represented feasible set unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Constraints

children.title: Irredundant Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Linear descriptions without removable constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for }i\in I\}\) is a finite inequality description.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\leq b\text{ is irredundant}\iff \forall k\in I\ \exists x^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ a_i^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}\leq b_i\ (i\neq k),\ a_k^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}>b_k\).

notation.meaning: witness that inequality \(k\) cannot be deleted

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes irredundancy by a deletion witness for every inequality in a finite system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite description \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\) is irredundant when none of its inequalities is redundant. Equivalently, for every \(k\in I\), there exists a deletion witness \(x^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}\leq b_i\) for every \(i\in I\setminus\{k\}\), while \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}>b_k\). Hence deleting any single inequality strictly enlarges the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality description is irredundant exactly when each inequality has a point satisfying all the others but violating that inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Irredundant Descriptions

children.title: Description Minimality Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural standards for comparing the economy of linear descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\) is a finite inequality description with \(a_i\neq 0\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\leq b\text{ is irredundant}\iff \forall i\in I,\ F_i=\{x\in P:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\text{ is a facet and distinct indices define distinct facets}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to full-dimensional polyhedra; lower-dimensional descriptions additionally require equations for the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and full-dimensional, and let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\), where \(I\) is finite and \(a_i\neq 0\) for every \(i\in I\). This description is irredundant exactly when every equality set \(F_i=\{x\in P:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\) is a facet of \(P\) and distinct indices define distinct facets. Consequently, after positive rescaling of inequalities is identified, a minimal inequality description contains exactly one supporting inequality for each facet of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional polyhedron, a description is minimal exactly when it contains one essential supporting inequality for each facet and no duplicates.
knowledge_statements.title: Description Minimality Criteria

children.title: Polyhedral Skeleton Geometry
children.top_down_role: Edge structure and graph-theoretic organization of polyhedra.

children.title: Vertex Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Local edge incidence among polyhedral vertices.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron and \(u,v\) are distinct vertices of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\text{ and }v\text{ are adjacent}\iff \operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\text{ is a one-dimensional face of }P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines adjacency through edges, the one-dimensional bounded faces of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) and \(v\) be distinct vertices of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). The vertices are adjacent when the segment \(\operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\), called an edge. Equivalently, there is a supporting hyperplane of \(P\) whose intersection with \(P\) is exactly \(\operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\). Vertex adjacency is symmetric and supplies the edge relation used in the one-skeleton of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct vertices are adjacent when the segment joining them is an edge, meaning a one-dimensional face of the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Adjacency

children.title: Polyhedral Skeletons
children.top_down_role: Graphs formed by polyhedral vertices and edges.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P)=(V(P),E(P))\), where \(\{u,v\}\in E(P)\iff \operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\text{ is a one-dimensional face of }P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the combinatorial one-skeleton, not the geometric union of embedded vertices and edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The one-skeleton of a polyhedron \(P\) is the undirected graph \(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P)=(V(P),E(P))\). Its node set \(V(P)\) is the set of vertices of \(P\), and \(\{u,v\}\in E(P)\) exactly when \(u\neq v\) and \(\operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\). Thus the abstract edges of the skeleton correspond bijectively to the bounded one-dimensional faces of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-skeleton is the graph whose nodes are polyhedral vertices and whose edges join precisely the adjacent vertex pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Skeletons

children.title: Graph Diameters
children.top_down_role: Global distance structure within polyhedral skeletons.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph with \(V\neq\varnothing\).
\(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path from \(u\) to \(v\).
\(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron whose one-skeleton is nonempty and connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{diam}(G)=\max_{u,v\in V}d_G(u,v)\); hence \(\operatorname{diam}(P)=\operatorname{diam}(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures unweighted shortest-path length in a finite abstract one-skeleton; it is not Euclidean diameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V\neq\varnothing\), let \(d_G(u,v)\) be the minimum number of edges in any path joining \(u\) and \(v\). The graph diameter is \(\operatorname{diam}(G):=\max\{d_G(u,v):u,v\in V\}\). For a polyhedron \(P\) whose one-skeleton is nonempty and connected, its combinatorial diameter is \(\operatorname{diam}(P):=\operatorname{diam}(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P))\), the largest minimum number of edge pivots needed to travel between two vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diameter of a finite connected graph is the greatest shortest-path distance between two nodes; a polyhedron's combinatorial diameter is the diameter of its nonempty connected one-skeleton.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Diameters

children.title: Skeleton Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Connectivity structure of the vertex-edge graph of a polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P))\geq d\), equivalently deletion of fewer than \(d\) vertices leaves the skeleton connected.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States Balinski's theorem for bounded polyhedra; the supplied inventory lacks a reliable exact theorem locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a \(d\)-dimensional polytope with \(d\geq 1\). Then its one-skeleton \(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P)\) is \(d\)-vertex-connected: for every set \(S\) of fewer than \(d\) vertices, the graph obtained from \(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P)\) by deleting \(S\) and all incident edges remains connected. Equivalently, the vertex connectivity satisfies \(\kappa(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P))\geq d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balinski's theorem says that the graph of a d-dimensional polytope remains connected after deletion of any fewer than d vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Skeleton Connectivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is the standard form of Balinski's theorem for a d-dimensional polytope, and theorem is the correct content kind. However, no source reference or inspectable theorem locator is supplied, so the nontrivial connectivity claim cannot pass source review.

children.title: Linear Programming Duality Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Dual representations and alternative systems underlying feasibility and optimality certificates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The finite-dimensional equivalence of polyhedral and finitely generated cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(K\) is polyhedral if and only if there exist finitely many vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone in finite-dimensional real space is polyhedral exactly when it is generated conically by finitely many vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is polyhedral}\iff\exists v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}

source_evidence.locator: Linear Programming / 3.4. Duality / Theorem 3.29

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski–Weyl theorem for cones

directory_assessment.rationale: The listed foundation hierarchy lacks a precise general container for polyhedral-cone representation theorems; structural adoption should await independent review.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual of an Inequality-Form Linear Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the dual pair for a maximization LP with unrestricted primal variables and inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linear program \(\max\{cx:Ax\le b\}\), the dual linear program is \(\min\{yb:yA=c,\ y\ge0\}\). The original program is called the primal linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of the maximization LP with Ax ≤ b is the minimization LP over nonnegative y satisfying yA = c; the original LP is called the primal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dual}\!\left(\max\{cx:Ax\le b\}\right)=\min\{yb:yA=c,\ y\ge0\}.

source_evidence.locator: Linear Programming / 3.4. Duality / Definition 3.18

knowledge_statements.title: Dual of an Inequality-Form Linear Program

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment of a finite linear-programming supremum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inequality-form linear programs over a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\neq\varnothing\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(\delta:=\sup\{c^\top x:x\in P\}<\infty\), then there exists \(z\in P\) such that \(c^\top z=\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a linear objective has a finite supremum over a nonempty polyhedron defined by finitely many linear inequalities, then the supremum is attained by a feasible point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear programs and their solution regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines inequality-form linear programming, feasible and optimal solutions, and the feasible-bounded, infeasible, and unbounded regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the linear program \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b\}\) seeks an \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) maximizing \(c^\top x\). A vector \(x\) is feasible if \(Ax\le b\), and it is optimal if it is feasible and attains the maximum. Writing \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), the program is infeasible when \(P=\varnothing\), and unbounded when \(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\,\exists x\in P\) such that \(c^\top x>\alpha\). If it is neither infeasible nor unbounded, it has an optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality-form linear program maximizes a linear objective over the vectors satisfying its linear inequalities. Such a vector is feasible, and a feasible vector attaining the maximum is optimal. The program is infeasible if its feasible set is empty and unbounded if feasible objective values exceed every real threshold. Otherwise, an optimal solution exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\varnothing\;\lor\;\bigl(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\,\exists x\in P:c^\top x>\alpha\bigr)\;\lor\;\bigl(\exists z\in P:c^\top z=\max_{x\in P}c^\top x\bigr).

notation.meaning: Primal constraint matrix, right-hand side, and objective vector.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional maximization form with nonnegative variables and upper-bound constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the canonical primal linear program is
\[
\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}.
\]
Its feasible region is \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\). The value is \(p^*=\sup_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\), with \(p^*=-\infty\) when \(P=\varnothing\) and \(p^*=+\infty\) when the objective is unbounded above on \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical primal LP maximizes a linear objective over nonnegative variables satisfying componentwise upper-bound constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Formulations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual of the canonical primal maximization form used throughout this shard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Associated with the primal program \(\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\) is the dual program
\[
\inf\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}.
\]
Its feasible region is \(D=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}\), and its value is \(d^*=\inf_{y\in D}b^{\mathsf T}y\), using the corresponding extended-real conventions for infeasibility and unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual minimizes a linear upper bound using nonnegative multipliers whose weighted constraint coefficients dominate the primal objective coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Standard-Form Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-corresponding reductions among equality, inequality, sign-restricted, and free-variable finite-dimensional LP forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A free variable \(x_j\in\mathbb{R}\) may be replaced by \(x_j=x_j^+-x_j^-\), where \(x_j^+,x_j^-\ge0\). An inequality \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) may be replaced by \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+s_i=b_i\), where \(s_i\ge0\); an inequality in the opposite direction may first be multiplied by \(-1\). An equality may be replaced by the two corresponding opposite inequalities. These transformations preserve feasibility and objective values under the natural correspondence of solutions. A minimization problem with objective \(f(x)\) may be represented as a maximization problem with objective \(-f(x)\); the feasible set is unchanged and the objective values are negated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free variables, inequalities, and equalities can be converted by variable splitting, slack variables, sign reversal, and paired inequalities while preserving corresponding objective values. Changing minimization to maximization negates, rather than preserves, objective values.
assumptions_latex: All variables and constraints are finite-dimensional and real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint and variable transformations preserve corresponding feasible objective values, while replacing minimization of \(f\) by maximization of \(-f\) negates those values.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative parts replacing a free variable.

children.title: Primal–Dual Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural pairing between primal and dual descriptions.

assumptions_latex: The primal is \(\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\).
The dual is \(\inf\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal constraints correspond to dual variables, primal variables correspond to dual constraints, and dualizing twice recovers the primal after canonical identification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row-column correspondence for the canonical primal-dual representation pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the canonical pair, each primal row \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) determines a nonnegative dual variable \(y_i\), while each nonnegative primal variable \(x_j\) determines the dual inequality \((A^{\mathsf T}y)_j\ge c_j\). Thus transposition exchanges rows and columns, maximization with upper-bound constraints becomes minimization with lower-bound constraints, and primal and dual slacks are \(b-Ax\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y-c\). Applying the same correspondence to the dual recovers the primal after canonical sign identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualization exchanges constraints and variables, transposes the coefficient matrix, reverses optimization direction and inequalities, and is involutive in canonical form.

children.title: Weak Duality

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak duality for the canonical finite-dimensional linear-programming pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(x\ge0\) and \(Ax\le b\), and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfies \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\), then \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\). Consequently, when both feasible regions are nonempty, their extended optimal values satisfy \(p^*\le d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every dual feasible value upper-bounds every primal feasible value, so the primal optimal value cannot exceed the dual optimal value when both feasible regions are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\), and hence \(p^*\le d^*\) whenever both feasible regions are nonempty.

children.title: Strong Duality
children.top_down_role: Value-equality regimes for primal-dual optimization pairs.

assumptions_latex: The primal and dual are the canonical finite-dimensional pair.
At least one member of the pair has a finite attained optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both programs attain optimal solutions and \(p^*=d^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attained finite-dimensional LP strong duality, excluding infeasible and unbounded cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the canonical primal-dual pair
\[
\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\},\qquad
\inf\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}.
\]
If either program has a finite optimal solution, then the other also has an optimal solution. There exist feasible \(x^*\) and \(y^*\) such that \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*=b^{\mathsf T}y^*\); equivalently, the finite optimal values satisfy \(p^*=d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When either member of a finite-dimensional primal-dual pair has a finite optimum, both attain optima with equal objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Duality

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-halfspace interpretation of feasible dual multipliers and supporting-hyperplane interpretation of zero-gap primal-dual pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\). Every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\) defines a valid containing halfspace \(P\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\}\). If \(x^*\in P\) and a dual-feasible \(y^*\) satisfy \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*=b^{\mathsf T}y^*\), then \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y^*\}\) is a supporting hyperplane of \(P\) at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-feasible multiplier defines a halfspace containing the primal polyhedron. Equality at a primal feasible point makes its boundary a supporting hyperplane there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\}\); equality at \(x^*\in P\) yields a supporting hyperplane at \(x^*\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A geometric duality criterion for boundedness above of a feasible maximization-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\). Then \(\max\{cx:Ax\le b\}\) is bounded above if and only if \(c\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\), where \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) are the rows of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible maximization LP, the objective is bounded above exactly when its objective vector lies in the cone generated by the constraint-matrix rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{cx:Ax\le b\}\text{ is bounded above}\iff c\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes objective vectors that make every point of a prescribed nonempty subset optimal.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\ge0\), \(Ax\le b\), \(y\ge0\), and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\). The feasible pair \((x,y)\) is primal-dual optimal if and only if
\[
y_i(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)=0\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m,
\]
and
\[
x_j((A^{\mathsf T}y)_j-c_j)=0\quad\text{for every }j=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Equivalently, every positive variable has a tight corresponding constraint and every positive multiplier has a tight primal constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal-dual pair is optimal exactly when each variable or multiplier is complementary to its corresponding nonnegative slack.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Slackness Conditions

children.title: Primal–Dual Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Paired feasible witnesses supporting optimality conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-duality-gap certificate for finite-dimensional canonical linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A primal-dual optimality certificate is a pair \((x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(x\ge0\), \(Ax\le b\), \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\). With \(v:=c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\), the certificate establishes that \(x\) and \(y\) are optimal and that \(p^*=d^*=v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual feasible points with equal objective values jointly certify their optimality and the common optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(v:=c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\), the pair \((x,y)\) certifies \(p^*=d^*=v\).

children.title: Degenerate Certificate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Certificate interpretation when multiple active structures or optimal solutions occur.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Certificate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pair-specific degeneracy through failure of strict complementarity in standard-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible primal-dual pair \((x,y)\), let \(s=c-A^Ty\geq0\). The pair is an optimality certificate when \(c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts=0\), equivalently when \(x_i s_i=0\) for every \(i\). Call this certificate pair-degenerate when \(D_0(x,y)=\{i:x_i=s_i=0\}\) is nonempty. Equivalently, it is pair-degenerate when it fails strict complementarity, which requires \(x_i+s_i>0\) for every \(i\). Pair-degeneracy does not by itself imply nonoptimality or nonuniqueness of the primal or dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal primal-dual certificate is pair-degenerate when some primal variable and its complementary dual slack are both zero, equivalently when that pair is not strictly complementary.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) are feasible for \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\leq c\}\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate is pair-degenerate exactly when \(D_0(x,y)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Indices simultaneously zero on both complementary sides.

children.title: Linear Programming Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundary regimes affecting duality, certificates, and algorithmic interpretation.

children.title: Infeasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feasibility failures viewed through dual witnesses and alternative systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\varnothing\iff \exists y\in\mathbb{Q}^m\text{ with }A^Ty\geq0\text{ and }b^Ty<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas infeasibility alternative for an equality-form rational linear system with nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \(Ax=b,\ x\geq0\), or \(A^Ty\geq0,\ b^Ty<0\). Consequently, infeasibility of \(P\) has a finite rational certificate \(y\) satisfying \(A^Ty\geq0\) and \(b^Ty<0\). Verification consists solely of exact matrix-vector multiplication and rational inequality tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard-form system is infeasible exactly when a rational Farkas vector has nonnegative transformed coefficients and a negative pairing with the right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Regimes

children.title: Unboundedness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective escape behavior and associated recession witnesses.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in P}c^Tx=-\infty\iff \exists d\geq0\text{ with }Ad=0\text{ and }c^Td<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal unboundedness for minimization over a nonempty standard-form rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear program \(\inf\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\) is unbounded below if and only if there exists a recession direction \(d\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(d\geq0\), and \(c^Td<0\). Given any \(x^0\in P\), the ray \(x^0+td\) is feasible for every \(t\geq0\), and its objective value is \(c^Tx^0+t c^Td\). Thus \((x^0,d)\) is an exactly verifiable unboundedness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible standard-form minimization problem is unbounded exactly when it has a feasible recession direction with strictly negative objective slope.
knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness Regimes

children.title: Degeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonunique active structures affecting certificates and geometric interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal basic-solution degeneracy in equality-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) contain \(r\) indices such that the columns of \(A_B\) are linearly independent. A basic feasible solution associated with \(B\) has \(x_j=0\) for \(j\notin B\), while \(x_B\) is the unique nonnegative vector satisfying \(A_Bx_B=b\). It is degenerate when at least one component of \(x_B\) is zero. Equivalently, a basic feasible solution \(x\) is degenerate exactly when \(|\{i:x_i>0\}|<r\). Degeneracy does not imply infeasibility or failure of optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic feasible solution is degenerate when at least one basic variable is zero, equivalently when fewer than the rank of the constraint matrix many variables are positive.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a basic feasible solution of \(Ax=b,\ x\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is degenerate}\iff |\{i:x_i>0\}|<r\).

notation.meaning: An index set of r linearly independent columns used as a basis.
The submatrix formed by the basis columns.

children.title: Duality Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Exceptional settings where standard duality conclusions need qualification.

assumptions_latex: The primal is \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), and the dual is \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\leq c\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-dimensional rational linear programming has no positive duality gap; failure regimes are exhausted by infeasibility and unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete status boundary for a finite-dimensional standard-form primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((P)\) and \((D)\) are both feasible, both attain finite optima and their optimal values are equal. If \((P)\) is feasible while \((D)\) is infeasible, then \((P)\) is unbounded below. If \((D)\) is feasible while \((P)\) is infeasible, then \((D)\) is unbounded above. Both programs may be infeasible. Weak duality excludes primal unboundedness when the dual is feasible and excludes dual unboundedness when the primal is feasible. Hence a positive finite duality gap is not a failure regime for this linear-programming model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional primal-dual LP pair, feasible problems have equal attained optima; all remaining failures reduce to the permitted infeasible or unbounded status combinations.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality Failure Boundaries

children.title: Rational Polyhedral Complexity Foundations
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic and representation-size foundations connecting polyhedral geometry to polynomial computation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unimodular invariance of Gomory–Chvátal closure and integer hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States preservation of polyhedrality and equivariance of the closure and integer hull under unimodular linear transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron, let \(U\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) be unimodular, and define \(f(P):=\{Ux:x\in P\}\). Then \(f(P)\) is a polyhedron. If \(P\) is rational, then \[(f(P))'=f(P')\qquad\text{and}\qquad (f(P))_I=f(P_I).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unimodular linear image of a polyhedron is polyhedral. For a rational polyhedron, both Gomory–Chvátal closure and integer hull commute with the unimodular transformation.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is rational for the closure and integer-hull identities}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(P)\text{ is a polyhedron};\qquad (f(P))'=f(P'),\quad (f(P))_I=f(P_I)\text{ when }P\text{ is rational}.

source_evidence.locator: Integer Programming / 5.5. Cutting Planes / Lemma 5.34

knowledge_statements.title: Unimodular invariance of Gomory–Chvátal closure and integer hull

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gomory–Chvátal truncation commutes with taking faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States compatibility of every truncation level with restriction to a face of a rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is a face of a rational polyhedron \(P\), then \[F'=P'\cap F.\] More generally, for every \(i\in\mathbb N\), \[F^{(i)}=P^{(i)}\cap F.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a face F of a rational polyhedron P, applying any number of Gomory–Chvátal truncations to F gives the intersection of F with the corresponding truncation of P.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a rational polyhedron}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'=P'\cap F,\qquad F^{(i)}=P^{(i)}\cap F\text{ for all }i\in\mathbb N.

source_evidence.locator: Integer Programming / 5.5. Cutting Planes / Lemma 5.33

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite convergence to the integer hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes finite Gomory–Chvátal rank for every rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every rational polyhedron \(P\), there exists \(t\in\mathbb N\) such that \[P^{(t)}=P_I.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every rational polyhedron reaches its integer hull after finitely many Gomory–Chvátal truncations.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a rational polyhedron}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists t\in\mathbb N\;\;P^{(t)}=P_I.

source_evidence.locator: Integer Programming / 5.5. Cutting Planes / Theorem 5.35

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gomory–Chvátal closure of a TDI system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the closure obtained by rounding the right-hand side of an integral TDI description and records rational-polyhedral preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), where \(Ax\le b\) is TDI, \(A\) is integral, and \(b\) is rational. Then \[P'=\{x:Ax\le\lfloor b\rfloor\}.\] Consequently, the Gomory\text{--}Chv\'atal closure of every rational polyhedron is a rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integral TDI description with rational right-hand side, the Gomory–Chvátal closure is obtained simply by rounding down every right-hand-side entry. In particular, the closure of any rational polyhedron remains rational polyhedral.
assumptions_latex: Ax\le b\text{ is totally dual integral}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P'=\{x:Ax\le\lfloor b\rfloor\};\qquad P\text{ rational polyhedral}\implies P'\text{ rational polyhedral}.

source_evidence.locator: Integer Programming / 5.5. Cutting Planes / Theorem 5.32

knowledge_statements.title: Gomory–Chvátal closure of a TDI system

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier representation of the Gomory–Chvátal closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the first closure of a rational polyhedron by rounded nonnegative aggregations having integral left-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every rational polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), \[P'=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:uAx\le\lfloor ub\rfloor\text{ for every }u\ge0\text{ such that }uA\text{ is integral}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gomory–Chvátal closure of a rational inequality system consists exactly of the points satisfying every rounded nonnegative aggregation whose aggregated coefficient vector is integral.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\text{ is a rational polyhedron}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P'=\{x:uAx\le\lfloor ub\rfloor\text{ for all }u\ge0\text{ with }uA\text{ integral}\}.

source_evidence.locator: Integer Programming / 5.5. Cutting Planes / Proposition 5.31

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier representation of the Gomory–Chvátal closure

directory_assessment.rationale: A general closure-and-cut characterization needs a foundational polyhedral container rather than the cutting-stock-specific cutting-plane node.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the closure of a convex set through integer hulls of containing rational affine half-spaces and its iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. Its Gomory\text{--}Chv\'atal truncation is \[P':=\bigcap_{\substack{P\subseteq H\\ H\text{ a rational affine half-space}}}H_I,\] where \(H_I\) is the integer hull of \(H\). Define \(P^{(0)}:=P\) and \(P^{(i+1)}:=(P^{(i)})'\); \(P^{(i)}\) is the \(i\)-th Gomory\text{--}Chv\'atal truncation of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set P, intersect the integer hulls of all rational affine half-spaces containing P to obtain its Gomory–Chvátal truncation P′. Starting from P, repeated application defines the i-th truncation.
assumptions_latex: H\text{ ranges over rational affine half-spaces containing }P
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P'=\bigcap_{P\subseteq H}H_I,\qquad P^{(0)}=P,\qquad P^{(i+1)}=(P^{(i)})'.

children.title: Encoding Length of Rational Data
children.top_down_role: Size measures for rational vectors, matrices, inequalities, and objective data.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Length of Rational Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit additive binary-size convention for rational scalar, vector, matrix, and linear-program data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a reduced rational number \(p/q\), define \(\lambda(p/q)=1+\lceil\log_2(|p|+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(q+1)\rceil\), where the initial bit accommodates the sign. For \(v\in\mathbb{Q}^k\), define \(\lambda(v)=k+\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda(v_i)\). For \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), define \(\lambda(A)=m+n+mn+\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda(A_{ij})\). For rational linear-program data \((A,b,c)\), define its total encoding length by \(L=\lambda(A)+\lambda(b)+\lambda(c)\). Inequality systems are encoded analogously by including the coefficient arrays, right-hand sides, dimensions, and objective data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under this explicit convention, rational input size is the sum of the binary lengths of reduced numerators, positive denominators, signs, dimensions, and all entries of the matrix, right-hand side, and objective vector.
assumptions_latex: Every rational number is written uniquely as \(p/q\), where \(p\in\mathbb{Z}\), \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The input size of \((A,b,c)\) is \(L=\lambda(A)+\lambda(b)+\lambda(c)\).

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of a reduced rational number.
Total binary encoding length of the rational LP data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controls the encoding size of the determinant of a rational square matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every rational square matrix \(A\), \[\operatorname{size}(\det A)\leq 2\operatorname{size}(A).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The determinant of any rational square matrix has encoding size at most twice the encoding size of the matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{size}(\det A)\leq 2\operatorname{size}(A)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Encoding Size of Rational Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines encoding sizes for integers, reduced rational numbers, rational vectors, and rational matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\in\mathbb Z\), define \(\operatorname{size}(n):=1+\lceil\log(|n|+1)\rceil\). If \(r=p/q\in\mathbb Q\), where \(p,q\in\mathbb Z\) are relatively prime, define \(\operatorname{size}(r):=\operatorname{size}(p)+\operatorname{size}(q)\). For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb Q^n\), define \(\operatorname{size}(x):=n+\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{size}(x_i)\). For \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), define \(\operatorname{size}(A):=mn+\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{size}(a_{ij})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary encoding size is defined componentwise: an integer uses 1 plus the ceiling of the logarithm of one plus its absolute value; a reduced rational uses the combined sizes of its numerator and denominator; a vector or matrix uses the sum of its entry sizes plus its number of entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{size}(n)=1+\lceil\log(|n|+1)\rceil,\quad \operatorname{size}(r)=\operatorname{size}(p)+\operatorname{size}(q),\quad \operatorname{size}(x)=n+\sum_i\operatorname{size}(x_i),\quad \operatorname{size}(A)=mn+\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{size}(a_{ij})

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Encoding-Size Bounds for Vector Addition and Inner Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds encoding growth for two elementary operations on rational vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For all \(x,y\in\mathbb Q^n\), \[\operatorname{size}(x+y)\leq2\bigl(\operatorname{size}(x)+\operatorname{size}(y)\bigr),\qquad \operatorname{size}(x^{\top}y)\leq2\bigl(\operatorname{size}(x)+\operatorname{size}(y)\bigr).\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{size}(x+y)\leq2(\operatorname{size}(x)+\operatorname{size}(y)),\quad \operatorname{size}(x^{\top}y)\leq2(\operatorname{size}(x)+\operatorname{size}(y))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Small-Encoding Optimal LP Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives encoding bounds independent of the objective-data size and a sharper special-case bound for a signed unit right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\). If \(\max\{c^{\top}x:Ax\leq b\}\) has an optimal solution, then it has an optimal solution \(x\) satisfying \[\operatorname{size}(x)\leq4n\bigl(\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(b)\bigr),\] and every component of \(x\) has size at most \(4(\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(b))\). If additionally \(b=e_i\) or \(b=-e_i\) for some unit vector \(e_i\), then there are a nonsingular submatrix \(A'\) of \(A\) and an optimal solution \(x\) such that \[\operatorname{size}(x)\leq4n\operatorname{size}(A').\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever a rational linear program attains its optimum, it has an optimum whose total and componentwise encoding sizes are bounded by the encoding sizes of the constraint matrix and right-hand side. For a signed unit right-hand side, an optimum can instead be bounded using a nonsingular submatrix of the constraint matrix.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb Q^m,\quad c\in\mathbb Q^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{c^{\top}z:Az\leq b\}:\ \operatorname{size}(x)\leq4n(\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(b)),\ \max_j\operatorname{size}(x_j)\leq4(\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(b));\quad b=\pm e_i\Rightarrow\exists A'\subseteq A\text{ nonsingular},\ \exists x\in\operatorname*{argmax}:\operatorname{size}(x)\leq4n\operatorname{size}(A')

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Encoding-Size Bounds for Rational Sums and Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the encoding growth of finite arithmetic expressions over rational numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For all \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\in\mathbb Q\), \[\operatorname{size}\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^n r_i\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{size}(r_i),\qquad \operatorname{size}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n r_i\right)\leq 2\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{size}(r_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any finite collection of rational numbers, the encoding size of their product is at most the sum of their encoding sizes, and the encoding size of their sum is at most twice that sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{size}(r_1\cdots r_n)\leq\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{size}(r_i),\quad \operatorname{size}(r_1+\cdots+r_n)\leq2\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{size}(r_i)

children.title: Polyhedral Object Bit-Size Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bit-complexity control for polyhedral solutions and witnesses.

children.title: Vertex Encoding Size
children.top_down_role: Bit-length control for rational extreme points.

assumptions_latex: Every coefficient has absolute value less than \(2^\ell\), with \(\ell\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every vertex \(v\) satisfies \(\lambda(v)=O\!\left(n^2(\ell+\log n)\right)\).

notation.meaning: An index set of n linearly independent tight inequalities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cramer-Hadamard bit bound for vertices of an integer inequality description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every vertex \(v\) of \(P\), there is an index set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) of cardinality \(n\) such that \(A_I\) is nonsingular and \(v=A_I^{-1}b_I\). In reduced form, every numerator and denominator of \(v_j\) is bounded in absolute value by \(n^{n/2}2^{n\ell}\). Consequently, each coordinate has encoding length \(O(n(\ell+\log n))\), and \(\lambda(v)=O(n^2(\ell+\log n))\). Clearing denominators first gives a polynomial bound in the total encoding length for rational descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vertex is determined by independent tight inequalities, and determinant bounds make its rational encoding polynomial in the dimension and coefficient bit size.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Encoding Size

children.title: Face Description Size
children.top_down_role: Representation size associated with faces and supporting descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is a rational polyhedron described by \(m\) indexed inequalities of total encoding length \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\{x\in P:A_Ix=b_I\}\) for some \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with relative encoding size \(O(m)\) and expanded size at most \(O(L)\).

notation.meaning: Indices of inequalities selected as equalities on the face.
The selected rows and right-hand sides.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Description of a face relative to a fixed rational inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that \(F=\{x\in P:A_i x=b_i\text{ for every }i\in I\}\). Relative to the given description of \(P\), the set \(I\) can be encoded by an \(m\)-bit incidence vector. If the defining equalities are written explicitly, they reuse rows of \((A,b)\), so their total coefficient encoding length is at most \(L\), up to dimension and indexing overhead. Thus no coefficients of superpolynomial bit length are required to specify a face of a rationally described polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face is specified by declaring selected original inequalities tight; indices require linear space, and an expanded description reuses at most the original input size.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Description Size

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Vertex Size Implies a Bounded Inequality Description
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts a uniform encoding bound on the vertices of a rational polytope into a uniform encoding bound on defining inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a rational polytope and let \(T\in\mathbb N\) satisfy \(\operatorname{size}(v)\leq T\) for every vertex \(v\) of \(P\). Then \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\) for an inequality system in which every inequality \(a^{\top}x\leq\beta\) satisfies \[\operatorname{size}(a)+\operatorname{size}(\beta)\leq 75n^2T.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every vertex of a rational polytope has encoding size at most T, then the polytope has an inequality description whose individual inequalities have combined coefficient and right-hand-side size at most 75 n squared T.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a rational polytope}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial bit bounds for exact rational LP status and optimality witnesses.
