children.title: Face Recognition
children.top_down_role: Classification of whether a candidate structure exposes a face.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a face of \(P\) if and only if there exist \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that \(a^Tx\le\beta\) is valid for \(P\) and \(F=\{x\in P:a^Tx=\beta\}\).

notation.meaning: Supporting inequality used to expose the face.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition criterion for nonempty faces of a polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(F\) is a face of \(P\) if and only if there are \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) for which \(a^Tx\le\beta\) is valid for \(P\) and
\[F=\{x\in P:a^Tx=\beta\}.\]
Equivalently, \(F\) is the nonempty maximizer set of some linear functional over \(P\). Taking \(a=0\) recognizes the improper face \(F=P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty subset is a face exactly when it is the equality set of a valid supporting inequality, equivalently a linear-functional maximizer set.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Recognition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of a Polyhedral Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization by an exposed maximizing set and by tight inequalities from a subsystem of a fixed description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) be a polyhedron and let \(F\subseteq P\). The following are equivalent: \(F\) is a face of \(P\); there exists a vector \(c\) such that \(\delta:=\max\{cx:x\in P\}\) is finite and \(F=\{x\in P:cx=\delta\}\); and there is a subsystem \(A'x\le b'\) of \(Ax\le b\) such that \(F=\{x\in P:A'x=b'\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of a polyhedron is a face exactly when it is the maximizing set of a linear functional with finite maximum, and exactly when it is the nonempty set obtained by making all inequalities in some subsystem tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a face of }P\iff \exists c:\ \delta:=\max_{x\in P}cx<\infty,\ F=\{x\in P:cx=\delta\}\iff \exists(A',b'):\ A'x\le b'\text{ is a subsystem of }Ax\le b,\ F=\{x\in P:A'x=b'\}\ne\varnothing.

source_evidence.locator: Linear Programming / 3.1. Polyhedra / Proposition 3.4

knowledge_statements.statement_title: The Maximizer Set of a Bounded Linear Objective Is a Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial structure of the optimizer set of a linear functional over a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\ne\varnothing\) be a polyhedron and let \(c\) be a vector. If \(\max\{cx:x\in P\}\) is finite, then \[\left\{x\in P:cx=\max_{y\in P}cy\right\}\] is a face of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a linear objective has a finite maximum over a nonempty polyhedron, the set of all maximizing points is a face of that polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}cx\text{ is a face of }P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes nonempty minimal faces through equality systems obtained from defining inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\) be a polyhedron and let \(\varnothing\neq F\subseteq P\). Then \(F\) is a minimal face of \(P\) if and only if \(F=\{x:A'x=b'\}\) for some subsystem \(A'x\leq b'\) of \(Ax\leq b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty subset of the polyhedron is a minimal face exactly when it is the solution set obtained by making every inequality in some subsystem tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a minimal face of }P\iff\exists\text{ a subsystem }A'x\leq b'\text{ of }Ax\leq b\text{ such that }F=\{x:A'x=b'\}

children.title: Facet Recognition
children.top_down_role: Classification of whether an exposed face has facet status.

knowledge_statements.title: Facet Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Codimension-one criterion for a nonempty tight face of a finite-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron of affine dimension \(d\geq 1\), and let \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) be valid for \(P\). If \(F=\{x\in P:a^\top x=\beta\}\neq\varnothing\), then
\[
F\text{ is a facet of }P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \dim F=d-1.
\]
Equivalently, \(F\) is a facet if and only if \(F\neq P\) and \(F\) contains \(d\) affinely independent points. Thus, after validity and properness are established, facet recognition amounts to checking that the tight points have affine dimension \(d-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid inequality defines a facet exactly when its tight set is proper and has dimension one less than the polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron with \(d=\dim P\geq 1\).
The inequality \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) is valid for \(P\), and \(F=\{x\in P:a^\top x=\beta\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a facet of \(P\) if and only if \(\dim F=d-1\), equivalently if and only if \(F\neq P\) and \(F\) contains \(d\) affinely independent points.

notation.meaning: tight face of the valid inequality

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines facets of a polyhedron and the valid inequalities that expose them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron. A facet of \(P\) is a maximal proper face of \(P\). An inequality \(c^{\top}x\leq\delta\) is facet-defining for \(P\) if it is valid for \(P\) and \(\{x\in P:c^{\top}x=\delta\}\) is a facet of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A facet is a maximal proper face. A valid inequality is facet-defining when its equality set in the polyhedron is a facet.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^{\top}x\leq\delta\text{ is facet-defining for }P\iff (\forall x\in P,\ c^{\top}x\leq\delta)\land\{x\in P:c^{\top}x=\delta\}\text{ is a facet of }P

source_evidence.locator: Linear Programming / 3.1. Polyhedra / Definition 3.7

knowledge_statements.title: Facets and Facet-Defining Inequalities

children.title: Dimension-Based Recognition
children.top_down_role: Geometric recognition organized by affine dimension and supporting structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For any base point \(v^1\in V\), \(\dim P=\operatorname{rank}[v^2-v^1\ \cdots\ v^m-v^1]\). For a nonempty subset \(W\subseteq V\), the same formula applied to \(W\) gives \(\dim\operatorname{conv}(W)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-rank recognition for polyhedra supplied by finite point generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V=\{v^1,\ldots,v^m\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)\). Form the displacement matrix
\[
D=[v^2-v^1\ \cdots\ v^m-v^1].
\]
Then
\[
\dim P=\operatorname{rank}(D).
\]
More generally, if \(W\subseteq V\) is nonempty, choose \(w^0\in W\); the affine dimension of \(\operatorname{conv}(W)\) equals the rank of the matrix whose columns are \(w-w^0\) for \(w\in W\setminus\{w^0\}\). Hence dimensions of generator-defined faces are recognized by exact linear algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dimension of a finite convex hull equals the rank of generator differences from any chosen base point.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Based Recognition

children.title: Recognition Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational difficulty of identifying faces or facets.

knowledge_statements.title: Recognition Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity bound for facet recognition from a rational finite-generator representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v^1,\ldots,v^m\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(v^1,\ldots,v^m\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), and let \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) have rational, binary-encoded data. Validity is checked by testing \(a^\top v^i\leq\beta\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). If the inequality is valid, define
\[
I_{\mathrm{tight}}=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:a^\top v^i=\beta\}.
\]
Writing \(d=\dim P\), the inequality defines a facet exactly when the affine dimension of \(\{v^i:i\in I_{\mathrm{tight}}\}\) is \(d-1\). Exact rational rank computations therefore decide validity and facet status in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rational finite-generator description, validity and facet status can be decided in polynomial bit time by evaluating every generator and computing exact affine ranks.
assumptions_latex: \(v^1,\ldots,v^m\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and the rational inequality \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) are given in binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validity and facet recognition are decidable in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length by evaluating all generators and computing the affine dimension of the tight generators.

notation.meaning: rational polytope given by finite generators
indices of generators satisfying the inequality at equality

children.title: Inequality Transfer Calculus
children.top_down_role: Transfer of inequalities among related dimensions, formulations, and faces.

children.title: Inequality Lifting
children.top_down_role: Transfer of inequalities into enlarged variable spaces or higher-dimensional settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Inequality Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single binary-variable lifting when the polytope is generated by its zero and one slices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_0,P_1\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty polytopes and define
\[
P=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((P_0\times\{0\})\cup(P_1\times\{1\})\bigr).
\]
Suppose \(a^\top x\leq b\) is valid for \(P_0\). Then
\[
a^\top x+\alpha y\leq b
\]
is valid for \(P\) if and only if
\[
\alpha\leq b-\max\{a^\top x:x\in P_1\}.
\]
Consequently, the largest valid coefficient in this lifting form is
\[
\alpha^*=b-\max\{a^\top x:x\in P_1\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a polytope is generated by its binary zero and one slices, the largest valid lifting coefficient is determined by maximizing the original left-hand side over the one slice.
assumptions_latex: The inequality \(a^\top x\leq b\) is valid for \(P_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted inequality \(a^\top x+\alpha y\leq b\) is valid for \(P\) exactly when \(\alpha\leq b-\max\{a^\top x:x\in P_1\}\).

notation.meaning: slice associated with the binary value zero
slice associated with the binary value one

children.title: Polyhedral Projection
children.top_down_role: Transfer of descriptions from lifted spaces to original coordinates.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+k}\) is a polyhedron described by \(Ax+By\leq d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^k,\ Ax+By\leq d\}\), and this image is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate projection of a finitely described polyhedron, equivalently existential elimination of auxiliary variables.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^k:Ax+By\leq d\}.
\]
The coordinate projection of \(Q\) onto the \(x\)-space is
\[
\pi_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\text{ there exists }y\in\mathbb{R}^k\text{ such that }Ax+By\leq d\}.
\]
This set is a polyhedron. Thus projecting a polyhedral formulation is equivalent to eliminating its auxiliary variables while retaining exactly those \(x\) that admit a feasible extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a polyhedron eliminates auxiliary coordinates existentially and produces another polyhedron containing exactly the extendable retained-coordinate points.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Projection

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

children.title: Face Restriction
children.top_down_role: Specialization of inequalities or descriptions to exposed substructures.

knowledge_statements.title: Face Restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of a valid inequality to a nonempty face of the same polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a nonempty face of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(a^\top x\leq b\) be valid for \(P\). The restricted inequality is valid for \(G\). If
\[
F=\{x\in P:a^\top x=b\},
\]
then its tight set on \(G\) is \(G\cap F\), which is either empty or a face of \(G\). When \(G\cap F\neq\varnothing\), the restricted inequality defines a facet of \(G\) exactly when
\[
\dim(G\cap F)=\dim G-1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a valid inequality to a face preserves validity, and the restricted tight set is the intersection with the original tight face.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron and \(G\) is a nonempty face of \(P\).
The inequality \(a^\top x\leq b\) is valid for \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restriction is valid for \(G\), and its tight set is \(G\cap F\), where \(F=\{x\in P:a^\top x=b\}\); this set is empty or a face of \(G\).

notation.meaning: face to which the inequality is restricted
ambient tight face of the inequality

children.title: Strength-Preservation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing whether transformed inequalities retain validity or strength.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polytope, \(G\) is a face of \(P\), and \(\pi\) is a linear projection.
Facet strength is interpreted as defining a proper codimension-one face in the relevant polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validity can survive restriction or projection while facetness fails whenever the transferred tight set has codimension other than one; explicit simplex and self-restriction examples exhibit this collapse.

notation.meaning: projection onto the first two coordinates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete codimension-collapse boundaries showing that validity transfer does not imply preservation of facet strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Facetness is not automatically preserved by restriction or projection. For
\[
T=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\},
\]
the inequality \(z\geq0\) defines a facet, but under \(\pi(x,y,z)=(x,y)\) its tight facet projects onto all of \(\pi(T)\), so it yields no proper projected face. Likewise, if a facet-defining inequality \(a^\top x\leq b\) is restricted to its own face \(G=\{x\in P:a^\top x=b\}\), equality holds throughout \(G\), so the restriction is not facet-defining for positive-dimensional \(G\). Strength persists only when the transferred tight set has codimension one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection or restriction may preserve validity but destroy facetness when the transferred tight set becomes the whole image or loses codimension one.
knowledge_statements.title: Strength-Preservation Boundaries

children.title: Canonical Combinatorial Inequality Families
children.top_down_role: Rank, cover, clique, cut, odd-set, and related structure-indexed families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every structure-indexed inequality \(x(S)\leq r_{\mathcal{F}}(S)\) is valid for \(P(\mathcal{F})\); rank, clique, cut, cover, and odd-set inequalities arise by replacing the generic bound with the sharper model-specific combinatorial bound.

notation.meaning: maximum feasible cardinality within an index set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common validity principle for structure-indexed inequality families; model-specific facet criteria are excluded.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Preliminaries on polyhedra and linear and integer programming p. 59

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite, let \(\mathcal{F}\subseteq2^E\), and define
\[
P(\mathcal{F})=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\in\mathcal{F}\}.
\]
For each \(S\subseteq E\), set \(r_{\mathcal{F}}(S)=\max\{|F\cap S|:F\in\mathcal{F}\}\). Then the structure-indexed inequality
\[
x(S)\leq r_{\mathcal{F}}(S)
\]
is valid for \(P(\mathcal{F})\). Canonical rank and clique inequalities instantiate this template directly, while cover, cut, and odd-set inequalities use analogous model-specific counting or parity bounds. Validity follows from the bound holding for every feasible incidence vector; facetness requires additional family-specific conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical combinatorial inequalities encode counting, capacity, separation, or parity bounds that hold for every feasible incidence vector in a structured family.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Combinatorial Inequality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional definition and face characterization of a rational integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is integral if
\[
P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n).
\]
Equivalently, every nonempty face of \(P\) contains an integer point. If \(P\) is pointed, these conditions are also equivalent to every vertex of \(P\) belonging to \(\mathbb{Z}^n\). In particular, a rational polytope is integral exactly when all of its vertices are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational polyhedron is integral when it equals the convex hull of its integer points, equivalently when every nonempty face contains an integer point; for pointed polyhedra this is also equivalent to all vertices being integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is integral exactly when every nonempty face of \(P\) contains an integer point; if \(P\) is pointed, this is also equivalent to every vertex of \(P\) being integral.

notation.meaning: integer lattice in the ambient space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Bounded-Coefficient Description of Integer Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The describing matrix depends only on the fixed integral constraint matrix; the rational right-hand side may vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), there exists an integral matrix \(M\), all of whose entries have absolute value at most \(n^{2n}\Xi(A)^n\), such that for every \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) there exists a rational vector \(d\) satisfying \(\{x:Ax\le b\}_I=\{x:Mx\le d\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed integral constraint matrix A, one bounded-coefficient integral matrix M provides the inequality normals needed to describe the integer hull for every rational right-hand side b; only the rational vector d changes with b.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M\text{ integral}:\ \max_{i,j}|M_{ij}|\le n^{2n}\Xi(A)^n\ \land\ \forall b\in\mathbb Q^m\ \exists d\text{ rational}:\ \{x:Ax\le b\}_I=\{x:Mx\le d\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of rational integral polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric and optimization characterizations with finite-optimum qualifications; the supporting-hyperplane conditions concern integral vectors on the hyperplanes, not necessarily in their exposed faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a rational polyhedron. The following are equivalent: (a) \(P\) is integral; (b) every face of \(P\) contains a vector in \(\mathbb{Z}^n\); (c) every minimal face of \(P\) contains a vector in \(\mathbb{Z}^n\); (d) every supporting hyperplane of \(P\) contains a vector in \(\mathbb{Z}^n\); (e) every rational supporting hyperplane of \(P\) contains a vector in \(\mathbb{Z}^n\); (f) for every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\) for which \(\max\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\) is finite, the maximum is attained by an integral vector; and (g) for every \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) for which that maximum is finite, its value is an integer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rational polyhedron, integrality is equivalent to the stated face and supporting-hyperplane conditions, to integral attainment of every finite linear maximum, and to integer optimal values for every integral objective having a finite maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (a)--(g) are equivalent}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximity and Bounded-Distance Improvement for an Integer Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two proximity conclusions for a nonempty integer hull, expressed through the matrix parameter \(\Xi(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), and suppose \(P_I\ne\varnothing\). (a) If \(y\) is optimal for \(\max\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\), then there is an optimal integral solution \(z\) of \(\max\{c^Tx:x\in P_I\}\) satisfying \(\|z-y\|_\infty\le n\Xi(A)\). (b) If \(y\) is a feasible integral but nonoptimal solution for \(\max\{c^Tx:x\in P_I\}\), then some feasible integral \(z\in P_I\) satisfies \(c^Tz>c^Ty\) and \(\|z-y\|_\infty\le n\Xi(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integer constraint matrix with nonempty integer hull, an LP optimum has an optimal integral solution within infinity distance n times Xi(A). Moreover, every feasible integral nonoptimum admits a strictly improving feasible integral point within the same distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(a) }\exists z\in P_I\cap\mathbb Z^n:\ z\text{ is optimal and }\|z-y\|_\infty\le n\Xi(A);\qquad \text{(b) }\exists z\in P_I\cap\mathbb Z^n:\ c^Tz>c^Ty,\ \|z-y\|_\infty\le n\Xi(A).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\neq\varnothing\), its integer hull is
\[
P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n).
\]
The set \(P_I\) is a rational polyhedron satisfying \(P_I\subseteq P\) and
\[
P_I\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n.
\]
Every vertex of \(P_I\) is integral. Geometrically, passing from \(P\) to \(P_I\) removes precisely those fractional regions that are unnecessary for representing convex combinations of feasible integer points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integer hull is the convex hull of a rational polyhedron's integer points; it is polyhedral, integral, and preserves exactly those integer points.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Hull Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5.1. The Integer Hull of a Polyhedron p. 105
5.21 The integer hull and cutting planes p. 83

children.title: Integral-Description Exactness
children.top_down_role: Conditions connecting continuous descriptions to integer-hull representations.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is a nonempty rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The description is integer-hull exact exactly when \(P=P_I\), equivalently when the linear and integer optimization values agree for every rational objective having a finite maximum over \(P\).

notation.meaning: polyhedron defined by the linear description

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness of a rational linear description relative to its integer hull and all bounded rational objectives.

source_refs.locator: Section 5.1. The Integer Hull of a Polyhedron p. 105

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) be rational and let \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\neq\varnothing\). The description is integer-hull exact when
\[
P=P_I.
\]
This equality holds if and only if, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) for which the maximum over \(P\) is finite,
\[
\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\}=\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\}.
\]
Thus universal equality of bounded linear and integer optimization values characterizes exactness of the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear description is integer-hull exact precisely when it equals its integer hull, equivalently when all bounded rational objectives have no integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Description Exactness

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5.1. The Integer Hull of a Polyhedron p. 105

children.title: Nonintegral Boundary Cases
children.top_down_role: Regimes where a rational description fails to capture integral geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(P\) has an integral inequality description, it has fractional vertices and \(P_I=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}^2:x_1+x_2\leq1\}\neq P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral coefficients and right-hand sides alone do not guarantee an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}^2:2x_1+2x_2\leq3\}.
\]
All displayed coefficients and right-hand sides are integral, yet \((3/2,0)\) and \((0,3/2)\) are fractional vertices, so \(P\) is not integral. Its integer points satisfy \(x_1+x_2\leq1\), and hence
\[
P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^2)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}^2:x_1+x_2\leq1\}\subsetneq P.
\]
Therefore integrality of the written data does not imply integer-hull exactness; additional structural conditions on the system are necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality system may have entirely integral data yet possess fractional vertices and strictly contain the convex hull of its integer points.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonintegral Boundary Cases

children.title: Unimodular Systems
children.top_down_role: Matrix structures with determinant-based integrality properties.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is unimodular exactly when every nonsingular \(m\times m\) submatrix has determinant in \(\{-1,1\}\).

notation.meaning: Submatrix of A formed by columns indexed by B.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the full-row-rank maximal-minor convention for a unimodular integer matrix system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) satisfy \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\). The system of columns of \(A\) is unimodular if, for every set \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\), either \(\det(A_B)=0\) or \(|\det(A_B)|=1\). Equivalently, every column basis of \(A\) is a lattice basis of \(\mathbb{Z}^m\). This convention concerns maximal minors; it is weaker than total unimodularity, which constrains minors of every order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-row-rank integer matrix is unimodular when every nonsingular maximal square submatrix has determinant plus or minus one.
knowledge_statements.title: Unimodular Systems

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unimodular matrices and elementary unimodular transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines unimodular square matrices and the elementary column operations generating unimodular transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A square matrix \(U\) is unimodular if \(U\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) and \(\det U\in\{-1,1\}\). Right multiplication of a matrix having \(n\) columns by the three stated types of unimodular matrices respectively negates one column, exchanges two columns, or subtracts one column from another. A finite sequence of these operations is a unimodular transformation. Products of unimodular matrices are unimodular. Moreover, a square matrix is unimodular if and only if it can be obtained from \(I_n\) by such transformations, equivalently, if and only if it is a product of matrices of the three stated types.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square integer matrix is unimodular when its determinant is 1 or -1. Negating a column, exchanging two columns, and subtracting one column from another are elementary unimodular transformations. Products of unimodular matrices remain unimodular, and precisely the unimodular matrices can be generated from the identity using these operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U\text{ is unimodular}\iff \det U\in\{-1,1\}\iff U\text{ is obtainable from }I_n\text{ by the stated elementary column transformations}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unimodular column reduction to a nonsingular block
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a block normal form for a full-row-rank rational matrix under a unimodular change of columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) have linearly independent rows. Then there exists a unimodular matrix \(U\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) such that \(AU=\begin{pmatrix}B&0\end{pmatrix}\), where \(B\in\mathbb Q^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational matrix with linearly independent rows can be transformed by a unimodular change of columns into a nonsingular square block followed by zero columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n},\ \det U\in\{-1,1\},\ \exists B\in\mathbb Q^{m\times m}:\ \det B\ne0\text{ and }AU=\begin{pmatrix}B&0\end{pmatrix}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse closure and lattice automorphisms of unimodular matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States inverse closure and preservation of the integer lattice under left or right multiplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every unimodular matrix \(U\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\), its inverse \(U^{-1}\) is unimodular. Furthermore, \(x\mapsto Ux\) is a bijection on integer column vectors \(\mathbb Z^n\), and \(x\mapsto xU\) is a bijection on integer row vectors \(\mathbb Z^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse of a unimodular matrix is unimodular. Left multiplication on integer column vectors and right multiplication on integer row vectors both bijectively map the integer lattice onto itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U^{-1}\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n},\ \det(U^{-1})\in\{-1,1\},\text{ and multiplication by }U\text{ on either side is bijective on the corresponding }\mathbb Z^n.

children.title: Totally Unimodular Systems

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is totally unimodular exactly when every square submatrix has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\).

notation.meaning: A square submatrix using row set I and column set J.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite integer-matrix definition, including minors of every order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer matrix \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular if every square submatrix \(A_{I,J}\), including those of orders smaller than \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\), satisfies \(\det(A_{I,J})\in\{-1,0,1\}\). In particular, applying the definition to the \(1\times1\) minors implies \(A_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}\) for every entry. The property is invariant under transposition, row or column permutation, and multiplication of a row or column by \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is totally unimodular when every square minor, of every possible order, has determinant zero, one, or minus one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral primal–dual optimum characterization of total unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent characterization by integral attainment of both primal and dual optima whenever their common optimal value is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\). Then \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if, for every \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), whenever the optimal value in \[\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}=\min\{b^Ty:A^Ty\ge c,\ y\ge0\}\] is finite, both optima are attained by integral vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral matrix is totally unimodular exactly when every finite primal-dual pair with integral data has integral optimal solutions on both sides.
assumptions_latex: \text{the common primal-dual optimal value is finite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff \text{both optima are attained by integral vectors for every such }b,c.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for TDI requiring a suitably supported optimal dual solution for every integral objective whose dual problem attains an optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). children.title: Unimodularity Recognition

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if it satisfies the stated signed row-partition predicate.

notation.meaning: An arbitrary subset of row indices.
A partition of R into positively and negatively signed rows.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ghouila-Houri signed-row characterization, used as an exact recognition criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(A\in\{-1,0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular if and only if, for every row set \(R\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), there is a partition \(R=R_+\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_-\) such that, for every column \(j\), \[\sum_{i\in R_+}A_{ij}-\sum_{i\in R_-}A_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}.\] Thus total unimodularity is equivalent to the existence of an admissible signing for every selected row set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ghouila-Houri recognition says every selected row set must admit signs making each signed column sum zero, one, or minus one.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is regular exactly when it has a totally unimodular real representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid definition with its standard totally unimodular representation equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matroid \(M\) is regular if it is representable over every field \(\mathbb{F}\). Equivalently, \(M\) has a real matrix representation that, after scaling nonzero columns, can be chosen totally unimodular: a set of elements is independent in \(M\) exactly when the corresponding columns are linearly independent. Consequently, the same column-dependence structure survives reduction over every field.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is obtainable from graphic matroids, cographic matroids, and \(R_{10}\) by \(1\)-, \(2\)-, and \(3\)-sums.

Matroid k-sum operation for k equal to 1, 2, or 3.

Let \(A\) be an integral matrix. A subdeterminant of \(A\) is \(\det B\), where \(B\) is any square submatrix of \(A\) selected by arbitrary row and column index sets. Define

\]

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-monoid definition of an integer cone generated by integral vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^d\), its integer cone is the additive monoid \[\operatorname{intcone}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k z_i s_i:k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0},\ s_i\in S,\ z_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\right\}.\] The empty sum gives \(0\in\operatorname{intcone}(S)\). If \(S\) is finite, say \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_r\}\), the same set is \(\{\sum_{i=1}^r z_i s_i:z\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^r\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integer cone generated by integral vectors consists of all finite linear combinations using nonnegative integer coefficients, including the zero combination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{intcone}(S)\) consists exactly of all finite nonnegative integer combinations of elements of \(S\).

children.title: Integral Generation

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lattice-point generation property for a finite integral conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite integral generator system \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_k\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^d\) has the integral generation property if every \(x\in\operatorname{cone}(S)\cap\mathbb{Z}^d\) admits coefficients \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) satisfying \(x=\sum_{i=1}^k z_i s_i\). Equivalently, \[\operatorname{cone}(S)\cap\mathbb{Z}^d=\operatorname{intcone}(S).\] Thus no lattice point of the real cone requires fractional generator coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral generation means every lattice point in a real cone can be expressed with nonnegative integer coefficients on the given integral generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integral generation holds exactly when \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\cap\mathbb{Z}^d=\operatorname{intcone}(S)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists G\subseteq C\cap\mathbb Z^n\text{ finite}:\ C=\operatorname{cone}(G)\ \land\ \forall g\in G\;\forall i,\ |g_i|\le\Xi(A)

children.title: Minimal Generating Sets
children.top_down_role: Irredundancy and minimality issues for integral cone generators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) is minimal exactly when every \(h\in H\) is indispensable for generating \(M\).

notation.meaning: The nonnegative integer span of a set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion-minimal generation of an affine integer monoid, not minimum-cardinality generation over another coefficient domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\) be an affine monoid. A finite set \(H\subseteq M\) is a generating set if \[M=\mathbb Z_+H:=\left\{\sum_{h\in H}\lambda_hh:\lambda_h\in\mathbb Z_+\right\}.\] It is a minimal generating set if no proper subset generates \(M\); equivalently, for every \(h\in H\), one has \(h\notin\mathbb Z_+(H\setminus\{h\})\). When \(M=C\cap\mathbb Z^d\) for a pointed rational cone \(C\), this inclusion-minimal generating set is the Hilbert basis of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generating set of an integer monoid is minimal when every generator is indispensable. For lattice points in a pointed rational cone, this set is its Hilbert basis.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Generating Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and inclusion-minimality equivalence are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports either the definition or the additional identification with the Hilbert basis of a pointed rational cone.

children.title: Integer-Decomposition Property
children.top_down_role: Integral decomposition behavior across dilated polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(kP\cap\mathbb Z^d=(P\cap\mathbb Z^d)+\cdots+(P\cap\mathbb Z^d)\) with \(k\) summands.

notation.meaning: The scalar dilation of the polytope.
The lattice points of the polytope.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard integer-decomposition property for lattice polytopes and all positive integral dilations.

source_refs.locator: 5.19 The integer rounding and decomposition properties p. 82

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lattice polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) has the integer-decomposition property if, for every integer \(k\ge 1\) and every \(z\in kP\cap\mathbb Z^d\), there exist \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\in P\cap\mathbb Z^d\) such that \[z=z_1+\cdots+z_k.\] Equivalently, the lattice points in every dilation satisfy \[kP\cap\mathbb Z^d=\underbrace{(P\cap\mathbb Z^d)+\cdots+(P\cap\mathbb Z^d)}_{k\text{ summands}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every lattice point in every positive integral dilation of the polytope must be a sum of the same number of lattice points from the original polytope.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Decomposition Property

source_witnesses.locator: 5.19 The integer rounding and decomposition properties p. 82

children.title: Dilation Structure
children.top_down_role: Scaling regimes relevant to integral decomposition.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(kP+\ell P=(k+\ell)P\), while equality between the corresponding lattice-point sets is an additional integer-decomposition property.

notation.meaning: Scalar dilation by a nonnegative integer.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar and Minkowski structure of integral dilations, separating convex-set equality from lattice-point decomposition.

source_refs.locator: 5.19 The integer rounding and decomposition properties p. 82

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and an integer \(k\ge 0\), define \(kP:=\{kx:x\in P\}\), with \(0P:=\{0\}\). Convexity gives \[kP+\ell P=(k+\ell)P\qquad(k,\ell\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}).\] Consequently, \[(kP\cap\mathbb Z^d)+(\ell P\cap\mathbb Z^d)\subseteq (k+\ell)P\cap\mathbb Z^d.\] Equality need not hold; equality generated from \(P\cap\mathbb Z^d\) across all positive dilation levels is precisely the additional decomposition structure captured by integer decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty convex set, scalar dilations add exactly as sets. Their lattice points always add into the next dilation, but the reverse inclusion requires an additional integer-decomposition property.
knowledge_statements.title: Dilation Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 5.19 The integer rounding and decomposition properties p. 82

children.title: Controlled Rounding
children.top_down_role: Structural guarantees supporting integer recovery from fractional points.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rounding is controlled when \(y\in P\cap(\mathbb Z^I\times\mathbb R^{d-|I|})\) and \(|y_i-x_i|\le\Delta_i\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic feasibility-preserving coordinatewise rounding predicate; the tree does not specify a stronger named rounding theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), a point \(x\in P\), integral-coordinate indices \(I\subseteq\{1,ldots,d\}\), and tolerances \(\Delta_i\ge0\) for \(i\in I\). A point \(y\) is a controlled rounding of \(x\) relative to \((P,I,\Delta)\) if \[y\in P,\qquad y_i\in\mathbb Z\ \ (i\in I),\qquad |y_i-x_i|\le\Delta_i\ \ (i\in I).\] Thus control requires both preservation of feasibility and an explicit error bound; coordinatewise nearest-integer rounding alone does not satisfy the condition unless its rounded point remains in \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A controlled rounding preserves feasibility, makes the designated coordinates integral, and respects specified coordinatewise error bounds. Ordinary componentwise rounding need not preserve feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Controlled Rounding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic predicate is plausible, but the taxonomy does not determine that this is the intended controlled-rounding notion, and no source resolves that ambiguity. In addition, the statement writes the index set as \(\{1,ldots,d\}\), which does not denote the intended \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\).

children.title: Rounding Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral settings where decomposition or controlled recovery breaks down.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1,1,1)\in2R_h\cap\mathbb Z^3\) but it is not a sum of two points of \(R_h\cap\mathbb Z^3\).

notation.meaning: The Reeve lattice tetrahedron of height h.
The first two standard unit vectors in three dimensions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reeve tetrahedra exhibit failure of lattice-point decomposition already at the second dilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(h\ge2\), let \[R_h=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,h)\}.\] The lattice point \((1,1,1)\) belongs to \(2R_h\), since it has coefficients \(1-1/h\), \(1-1/h\), and \(1/h\) on the three nonzero vertices, whose sum is \(2-1/h\le2\). However, \(R_h\cap\mathbb Z^3\) consists only of its four vertices, and no sum of two such vertices equals \((1,1,1)\). Hence \(R_h\) fails the integer-decomposition property at dilation \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Reeve tetrahedron has a lattice point in its second dilation that cannot be expressed as the sum of two lattice points from the tetrahedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Rounding Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Reeve-tetrahedron example is a relevant counterexample and the counterexample content kind fits this failure leaf, but the exact construction and its asserted lattice-point description have no inspectable citation.

children.title: Chvátal–Gomory Cuts
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic strengthening structures associated with rational linear systems.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) and all components of \(x\) are required to be integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\lambda^{\mathsf T}A)x\le\lfloor\lambda^{\mathsf T}b\rfloor\) is valid for \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n\).

notation.meaning: The integer hull of the relaxation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier form of a Chvátal–Gomory cut for a pure-integer linear relaxation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), with \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) intended. If \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(c:=\lambda^{\mathsf T}A\in\mathbb Z^{1\times n}\), then \(cx\le\lambda^{\mathsf T}b\) is valid for \(P\). Because \(cx\) is integral at every integer-feasible point, the strengthened inequality \[cx\le\left\lfloor\lambda^{\mathsf T}b\right\rfloor\] is valid for \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n\). The multiplier \(\lambda\), together with the integrality of \(c\), is a directly checkable certificate of validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative combination of relaxation rows whose left side is integral can have its right side rounded down, producing an inequality valid for every integer-feasible point.

children.title: Gomory Fractional Cuts
children.top_down_role: Tableau-derived cutting structures for pure integer settings.

assumptions_latex: \(x_B+\sum_{j\in N}a_jx_j=b\), where every variable is nonnegative and integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j\in N}(a_j-\lfloor a_j\rfloor)x_j\ge f_0\) is valid for the integer solutions of the tableau row.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical pure-integer Gomory fractional cut derived from one simplex-tableau row.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a tableau row \[x_B+\sum_{j\in N}a_jx_j=b,\] where \(x_B\) and all \(x_j\) are nonnegative integers, and let \(f_0:=\{b\}\in(0,1)\). Taking fractional parts of the row implies that every integer solution satisfies the Gomory fractional cut \[\sum_{j\in N}\{a_j\}x_j\ge f_0.\] Here \(\{a_j\}=a_j-\lfloor a_j\rfloor\). The row, the declared integrality of its variables, and the nonintegrality of \(b\) form a checkable validity certificate; the current basic solution with \(x_j=0\) violates the cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: From a pure-integer tableau row with a fractional right side, the fractional coefficient parts yield a valid inequality violated by the current basic solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Gomory Fractional Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is consistent with the stated pure-integer tableau convention and the certificate role is defensible, but no citation with a specific locator supports the formula, hypotheses, or convention.

children.title: Gomory Mixed-Integer Cuts
children.top_down_role: Gomory-family strengthening structures for mixed-integer settings.

assumptions_latex: \(x_B+\sum_{j\in N}a_jx_j=b\), with \(x_B\) integer and all nonbasic variables nonnegative.
\(I\subseteq N\) indexes integer variables, \(C=N\setminus I\) indexes continuous variables, and \(f_0=\{b\}\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed Gomory mixed-integer inequality is valid for every mixed-integer solution of the tableau row.

notation.meaning: Integer and continuous nonbasic index sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized single-row Gomory mixed-integer cut under the stated tableau sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_j:=\{a_j\}\) for \(j\in I\). Every mixed-integer solution of the row satisfies \[\sum_{\substack{j\in I\\ f_j\le f_0}}f_jx_j+\frac{f_0}{1-f_0}\sum_{\substack{j\in I\\ f_j>f_0}}(1-f_j)x_j+\sum_{\substack{j\in C\\ a_j\ge0}}a_jx_j-\frac{f_0}{1-f_0}\sum_{\substack{j\in C\\ a_j<0}}a_jx_j\ge f_0.\] This is the normalized Gomory mixed-integer cut for the convention \(x_B+\sum_ja_jx_j=b\). It is violated by the associated basic solution in which all nonbasic variables vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer tableau row yields a piecewise-scaled inequality, using fractional parts for integer variables and signed coefficients for continuous variables, that cuts off the fractional basic solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Gomory Mixed-Integer Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed normalized mixed-integer cut is convention-dependent. Without a source fixing the tableau sign convention and normalization, its coefficient formula cannot be accepted reliably.

children.title: Arithmetic-Family Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Containment, strength, and applicability relations among arithmetic cut families.

assumptions_latex: All cut families are compared for the same linear relaxation and the same declared integer variables.
Tableau rows are valid equations for that formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pure-integer fractional cuts admit Chvátal–Gomory interpretations, while single-row mixed-integer Gomory cuts are split cuts; converse statements require formulation qualifications.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-cut relationships under a fixed formulation, not equality of closures across arbitrary extended formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed pure-integer formulation, a Gomory fractional cut obtained from a tableau row can be represented as a Chvátal–Gomory cut after expressing that row as a valid aggregation of the formulation. For a fixed mixed-integer formulation, every single-row Gomory mixed-integer cut is valid for a split disjunction and hence belongs to \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{split}}\). These statements compare generated inequalities, not unrestricted closures: reverse containments can fail for a fixed tableau, and changing or extending the formulation can change which tableau cuts are obtainable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pure-integer Gomory fractional cuts have Chvátal–Gomory interpretations, and single-row mixed-integer Gomory cuts are split cuts. Reverse comparisons depend on the formulation and available tableau rows.
knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic-Family Comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualified family relationships are plausible and fit a comparison leaf, but they are nontrivial formulation-dependent claims. No inspectable comparison source is supplied to establish their precise scope.

children.title: Disjunctive Lift-Project Cut Family
children.top_down_role: Strengthening families derived from disjunctions and lifted reformulations.

children.title: Split Cuts
children.top_down_role: Strengthening structures derived from split disjunctions.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a polyhedron with integer-variable indices \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every inequality valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(P\cap(D^0\cup D^1))\) is a split cut for the specified split disjunction.

notation.meaning: The two sides of the split disjunction.
The split hull associated with the disjunction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Split cuts for a mixed-integer relaxation using an integral primitive direction on integer coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Extend \(\pi\) by zeros outside \(I\), and define the split disjunction \[D^0:=\{x:\pi^{\mathsf T}x\le\pi_0\},\qquad D^1:=\{x:\pi^{\mathsf T}x\ge\pi_0+1\}.\] Every point satisfying the declared integrality lies in \(D^0\cup D^1\). The associated split hull is \[P^{\pi,\pi_0}:=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((P\cap D^0)\cup(P\cap D^1)\bigr).\] An inequality is a split cut for this disjunction if it is valid for \(P^{\pi,\pi_0}\); it cuts the relaxation when it is not valid for all of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A split disjunction excludes one open unit-width slab in an integral direction. Any inequality valid for the convex hull of the two remaining pieces is a split cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Split Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The split-disjunction and split-hull definition is standard and fits the definition leaf, but it lacks a cited source. The scope note also calls the direction primitive while the assumptions require only a nonzero integral direction; a source or explicit convention is needed to settle that discrepancy.

children.title: Disjunctive Cuts
children.top_down_role: Inequality families obtained from broader disjunctive structures.

assumptions_latex: \(D^1,\ldots,D^q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) satisfy every intended integer-feasible point belonging to \(\bigcup_{t=1}^qD^t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An inequality is a disjunctive cut when it is valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{t=1}^q(P\cap D^t))\) but not for all of \(P\).

notation.meaning: The alternatives of the valid disjunction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite valid disjunctions and cuts obtained from their convexified union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D^1,\ldots,D^q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) form a valid disjunction for the intended integer-feasible set, meaning every such point lies in \(\bigcup_{t=1}^qD^t\). For a relaxation \(P\), define the disjunctive hull \[P_D:=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{t=1}^q(P\cap D^t)\right).\] An inequality \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) is a disjunctive cut generated by this disjunction if it is valid for \(P_D\). It is proper relative to \(P\) when some point of \(P\) violates it. Split cuts are the two-term special case arising from a split disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disjunctive cut is valid for the convex hull of the pieces obtained by intersecting a relaxation with every alternative of a valid finite disjunction.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-disjunction formulation is coherent, matches the plain statement, and has the correct definition role, but no source with a specific locator supports the selected convention for disjunctive cuts and properness.

children.title: Lift–Project Cut Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Lifted reformulation hierarchies followed by projection to the original space.

assumptions_latex: \(P^0=P\subseteq[0,1]^n\) is a relaxation of a binary-feasible set.
At each round, every coordinate split \(x_i=0\) or \(x_i=1\) is imposed and convexified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{r+1}\subseteq P^r\), every binary-feasible point remains in every level, and \(P^n\) equals the binary hull.

notation.meaning: The relaxation after r lift–project rounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential coordinate-disjunction hierarchy; named lift–project systems may use stronger simultaneous operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\subseteq[0,1]^n\), set \[L_i(Q):=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((Q\cap\{x:x_i=0\})\cup(Q\cap\{x:x_i=1\})\bigr).\] Define \(P^0:=P\) and, for \(r\ge0\), \[P^{r+1}:=\bigcap_{i=1}^n L_i(P^r).\] Then \(P^{r+1}\subseteq P^r\), and \(P\cap\{0,1\}^n\subseteq P^r\) for every \(r\). After at most \(n\) rounds, all coordinate disjunctions have been recursively convexified and \[P^n=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\{0,1\}^n).\] This recursion provides a rank-indexed lift–project cut hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly convexifying every binary coordinate disjunction gives nested relaxations that retain all binary-feasible points and reach their convex hull within at most the number of variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Lift–Project Cut Hierarchy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record defines one particular coordinate-disjunction closure and asserts finite convergence to the binary hull after at most \(n\) rounds. That theorem-level conclusion is operator-sensitive and is not supported by a source. The representation content kind also understates the role of the finite-convergence claim; the appropriate kind must be settled together with an authoritative hierarchy reference.

children.title: Disjunctive Strength Relations
children.top_down_role: Comparative containment and closure strength across the three families.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron containing the integer-feasible set \(Q_I=Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\).
Every disjunction in each family is valid for \(Q_I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak D_2}(Q)\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak D_1}(Q)\).

notation.meaning: closure obtained by intersecting all relaxations induced by disjunctions in the family

review_flags: A precise authoritative locator for the disjunctive-closure inclusion is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares closure strength by inclusion of the underlying families of valid disjunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a valid disjunction \(D=\bigcup_{j=1}^{k_D}D_j\), set \(T_D(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap D)\), and for a family \(\mathfrak D\) define \(\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak D}(Q)=\bigcap_{D\in\mathfrak D}T_D(Q)\). If \(\mathfrak D_1\subseteq\mathfrak D_2\), then \[Q_I\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak D_2}(Q)\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak D_1}(Q)\subseteq Q.\] Thus enlarging the disjunction family cannot weaken its closure; equality may occur when the added disjunctions contribute no further restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure using every disjunction from a larger family is at least as strong as one using a subfamily.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Strength Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure-inclusion property is mathematically coherent and the property content kind fits the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation. A source specifically supporting disjunctive closures and the reversal of inclusion under enlargement of the disjunction family is required.

children.title: Closure Rank-Convergence Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Structural organization of repeated closure operations and their distance from the integer hull.

children.title: Closure Rank
children.top_down_role: Iteration-depth measures for reaching a target strengthened region.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a closure operator satisfying \(P_I\subseteq\mathcal C(Q)\subseteq Q\) for every relevant relaxation \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal C}(P)=\min\{r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:\mathcal C^r(P)=P_I\}\), with value \(+\infty\) if the set is empty.

notation.meaning: integer hull of the initial relaxation
the r-fold iterate of the closure operator

review_flags: A closure-specific source is needed to certify the rank convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the number of closure rounds needed to reach the pure-integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal C^0(P)=P\) and \(\mathcal C^{r+1}(P)=\mathcal C(\mathcal C^r(P))\) for \(r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). The \(\mathcal C\)-rank of \(P\) is \[\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal C}(P)=\min\{r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:\mathcal C^r(P)=P_I\}.\] If no finite iterate equals \(P_I\), its rank is \(+\infty\). In particular, the rank is zero exactly when \(P=P_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure rank is the least number of closure rounds required to obtain the integer hull, or infinity if no finite round suffices.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Rank

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent and correctly includes zero and infinite rank, and definition is the appropriate content kind. The closure-rank convention nevertheless has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Iterated Closure Structure
children.top_down_role: Nested geometry produced by repeated closure operations.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is monotone and satisfies \(P_I\subseteq\mathcal C(Q)\subseteq Q\) whenever \(P_I\subseteq Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I\subseteq P^{(r+1)}\subseteq P^{(r)}\subseteq P\) for every \(r\ge0\), and \(P^{(\infty)}=\bigcap_{r\ge0}P^{(r)}\).

notation.meaning: the relaxation after r closure rounds
the limiting intersection of all finite iterates

review_flags: A general closure-calculus source is required for the stated operator framework.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the recursive, nested structure common to valid cutting-plane closures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(P^{(0)}=P\) and recursively define \(P^{(r+1)}=\mathcal C(P^{(r)})\) for \(r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). Then every valid integer point survives every round and the iterates form a descending chain: \[P_I\subseteq P^{(r+1)}\subseteq P^{(r)}\subseteq P.\] The infinite iterate is defined by \(P^{(\infty)}=\bigcap_{r=0}^{\infty}P^{(r)}\). Finite convergence occurs precisely when some \(P^{(r)}\) equals \(P_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated closure application creates nested relaxations containing the integer hull; their limiting closure is the intersection of all rounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Iterated Closure Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursive iterates, descending inclusions, and limiting intersection are consistent with the stated contractive closure assumptions, and property fits the leaf. No source with a specific closure-calculus locator is supplied.

children.title: Integer-Hull Convergence
children.top_down_role: Structural behavior of closure sequences approaching the integer hull.

assumptions_latex: All coordinates are required to be integral, and \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) such that \(P^{(r)}_{\mathrm{CG}}=P_I\).

notation.meaning: the r-th Chvátal–Gomory closure of P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convergence of Chvátal–Gomory closures for rational pure-integer polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: 5.21 The integer hull and cutting planes p. 83

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P^{(0)}_{\mathrm{CG}}=P\), and let \(P^{(r+1)}_{\mathrm{CG}}\) be the Chvátal–Gomory closure of \(P^{(r)}_{\mathrm{CG}}\). Then the sequence reaches the integer hull after finitely many rounds: there exists \(r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) such that \[P^{(r)}_{\mathrm{CG}}=P_I.\] Equivalently, every rational pure-integer polyhedron has finite Chvátal–Gomory rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rational polyhedron with all variables integral, finitely many Chvátal–Gomory closure rounds produce its integer hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Hull Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: 5.21 The integer hull and cutting planes p. 83

children.title: Rank Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Families exhibiting large closure depth or slow structural progress.

assumptions_latex: \(P_I\subseteq\mathcal C(Q)\subseteq Q\) for every relevant relaxation \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The existence of \(x^*\in\mathcal C^{r-1}(P)\setminus P_I\) certifies \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal C}(P)\ge r\).
review_flags: A closure-rank source is needed for this witness-certificate formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A surviving fractional point witnesses that fewer than the claimed number of rounds cannot suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To certify the lower bound \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal C}(P)\ge r\), exhibit a point \(x^*\) satisfying \[x^*\in\mathcal C^{r-1}(P)\quad\text{and}\quad x^*\notin P_I.\] Membership in the first set verifies that \(x^*\) survives the first \(r-1\) closure rounds, while nonmembership in \(P_I\) verifies that \(\mathcal C^{r-1}(P)\ne P_I\). Hence no iterate numbered below \(r\) reaches the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noninteger-hull point surviving through round r minus one certifies that the closure rank is at least r.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Lower Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the stated closure assumptions, a point outside the integer hull surviving round r-1 is a valid certificate of rank at least r, and certificate is the correct content kind for this formulation. The witness characterization has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Separation for Inequality Families
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic access to structured and exponentially large cutting families.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{a_i^Tx\le b_i:i\in I\}\) is a rational inequality family defining \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
The query point \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\) is given in binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns either an index \(i\) with \(a_i^Ty>b_i\) or the assertion \(y\in P\).

notation.meaning: possibly exponentially large indexed inequality family
polyhedron defined by every inequality in the family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact strong separation for a rational, explicitly encoded inequality family.

source_refs.locator: * 6.4 Equivalence of Strong Optimization and Separation p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On input \(y\), a strong separation oracle searches the indexed family \(\mathcal F\). If it finds \(i\in I\) with \(a_i^Ty>b_i\), it outputs the violated inequality \(a_i^Tx\le b_i\); otherwise it outputs that \(y\in P\). When this procedure runs in time polynomial in the encoding lengths of \(y\) and the family data, \(\mathcal F\) is polynomial-time separable even if \(|I|\) is exponential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separation oracle either returns an inequality violated by the query point or certifies that every inequality in the family is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation for Inequality Families

source_witnesses.locator: * 6.4 Equivalence of Strong Optimization and Separation p. 174

children.title: Extended-Formulation Complexity Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Lifted representations, projections, compactness, and barriers to concise linear descriptions.

children.title: Lift-Projection Representation Interface
children.top_down_role: Higher-dimensional descriptions projecting to the original feasible region.

children.title: Lifted Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Higher-dimensional linear descriptions associated with a target region.

assumptions_latex: \(Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+k}:A x+B y\le d\}\) is a polyhedron for some \(k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is a lifted description of \(P\) exactly when \(P=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\).

notation.meaning: target polyhedron in the original variables
polyhedron in original and auxiliary variables

review_flags: A precise extended-formulation source locator is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a lifted linear description through coordinate projection onto the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system \(A x+B y\le d\) is a lifted description, or extended formulation, of \(P\) when \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^k,\ A x+B y\le d\}.\] Equivalently, if \(\pi_x(x,y)=x\), then \(\pi_x(Q)=P\). The inequalities describe \(Q\) in the lifted space; equations may be included explicitly or represented separately without being counted as facet inequalities under the usual extension-complexity convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted description represents a polyhedron as the projection of a linear system containing auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Descriptions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection-based definition of a lifted description is mathematically consistent and definition fits the leaf. The additional convention about counting equations and facet inequalities also requires support, but no source is cited.

children.title: Projection Maps
children.top_down_role: Coordinate maps connecting lifted descriptions to original feasible regions.

assumptions_latex: \(\pi(z)=Tz+t\) is an affine map from \(\mathbb R^d\) to \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) represents \(P\) through \(\pi\) exactly when \(\pi(Q)=P\).

notation.meaning: affine projection or linear image map
matrix and translation defining the affine map

review_flags: A precise polyhedral-projection source locator is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allows general affine images, including ordinary coordinate projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An affine map \(\pi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^n\), given by \(\pi(z)=Tz+t\), is a projection map from \(Q\) onto \(P\) when \[\pi(Q)=\{Tz+t:z\in Q\}=P.\] In the coordinate form \(z=(x,y)\), the standard projection is \(\pi_x(x,y)=x\). Surjectivity is required only after restricting the map to \(Q\); injectivity is not required, so several lifted points may represent the same point of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection map sends every lifted feasible point into the target polyhedron and reaches every target point, without requiring a unique lift.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine-image condition is precise and the definition content kind fits the leaf. Because some sources reserve projection for coordinate or linear projections while using affine image more generally, an inspectable source is required for the stated terminology and representation convention.

children.title: Auxiliary Variable Spaces
children.top_down_role: Additional coordinate systems used to expose compact structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An auxiliary variable space is valid for a system \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times Y\) when \(\pi_x(Q)=P\).
review_flags: A source explicitly treating auxiliary spaces in extended formulations is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates original coordinates from variables introduced solely to obtain a compact formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An auxiliary variable space for \(P\) is a finite-dimensional space \(Y=\mathbb R^k\) whose coordinates supplement the original space \(X=\mathbb R^n\). A linear system defines \(Q\subseteq X\times Y\), and the auxiliary space is valid for that representation when \[P=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}.\] The variables in \(Y\) need not have unique values for a given \(x\), and feasibility in \(P\) depends only on the existence of at least one lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables occupy an added space in which a linear system is built; existentially eliminating them recovers exactly the original polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Variable Spaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separation of original and auxiliary spaces and the existential projection condition are internally consistent, and definition fits the leaf. No source explicitly supporting this auxiliary-space formulation is supplied.

children.title: Lift–Projection Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relationships among lifted dimension, description size, and projected geometry.

assumptions_latex: Extension size counts inequalities, while equations and auxiliary dimension are recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min\{m:\exists Q\text{ with }m\text{ inequalities and an affine }\pi\text{ such that }\pi(Q)=P\}\).
review_flags: A precise extension-complexity source locator is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes the inequality-count benefit obtainable by lifting and projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extension complexity of \(P\) is \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min\{m:\exists Q=\{z:Cz\le d,\ Ez=f\},\ C\text{ has }m\text{ rows},\ \exists\pi\text{ affine},\ \pi(Q)=P\}.\] Hence any lifted description with \(m\) inequalities proves \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\le m\), whereas a lower bound on \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\) rules out every lift with fewer inequalities, regardless of its auxiliary dimension. A smaller projected description may therefore be obtained by accepting additional variables and equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension complexity measures the fewest lifted inequalities needed to project onto a polytope, exposing the tradeoff between extra variables and inequality count.
knowledge_statements.title: Lift–Projection Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives the standard inequality-count interpretation of extension complexity and uses it to express the lift-projection tradeoff. Principle is acceptable for this tradeoff leaf, although the displayed formula itself is definitional. A precise extension-complexity source and locator are missing.

children.title: Compositional State-Space Formulation Family
children.top_down_role: Extended descriptions assembled from compositional and state-space structure.

children.title: Decomposition-Based Formulations
children.top_down_role: Extended descriptions assembled from separable or compositional structure.

assumptions_latex: \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\le b_i\}\) are nonempty polyhedra for \(i=1,\ldots,k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection onto \(x\) of the homogenized block formulation equals \(P\).

notation.meaning: scaled copy of the component-i point
convex hull of the component union

review_flags: A source for the disjunctive decomposition formulation and its recession assumptions is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex-hull decomposition using one homogenized block per component polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every \(P_i\) is a polytope, then \(P\) is the projection onto \(x\) of \[x=\sum_{i=1}^k x^i,\qquad A_i x^i\le b_i\lambda_i\ \ (i=1,\ldots,k),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1,\qquad \lambda_i\ge0.\] Indeed, positive \(\lambda_i\) scale points of \(P_i\), while zero-weight blocks contribute only zero because the component recession cones are trivial. Thus the lifted system composes separate component descriptions into a formulation of their convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex hull of finitely many polytopes is represented by scaled component formulations whose nonnegative weights sum to one.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed homogenized formulation is valid under the statement's stronger condition that every component is a polytope, and representation fits the leaf. The formal assumptions instead introduce general nonempty polyhedra, for which recession behavior requires additional conditions or a more general formulation. The requested source is necessary to settle and document the intended scope.

children.title: Dynamic-Programming Formulations
children.top_down_role: Extended descriptions derived from finite state-space representations.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite acyclic directed graph with source \(s\) and sink \(t\).
Each arc \(a\in A\) has a label \(\ell_a\in\mathbb R^n\), and feasible objects correspond to \(s\)-\(t\) paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection of the unit \(s\)-\(t\) flow polytope under \(x=\sum_{a\in A}\ell_a f_a\) is the convex hull of path-label vectors.

notation.meaning: unit flow variable on arc a
arc label contributing to the represented object

review_flags: A source for the dynamic-programming network formulation is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents an acyclic dynamic program through its state-transition flow polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b_s=1\), \(b_t=-1\), and \(b_v=0\) for \(v\notin\{s,t\}\). Define the lifted system \[Bf=b,\qquad f\ge0,\qquad x=\sum_{a\in A}\ell_a f_a.\] Because the unit \(s\)-\(t\) flow polytope of an acyclic graph is the convex hull of incidence vectors of \(s\)-\(t\) paths, its projection is \[\operatorname{conv}\left\{\sum_{a\in p}\ell_a:p\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path in }G\right\}.\] Thus states and transitions yield an extended formulation for the dynamic program's feasible-output polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An acyclic dynamic program becomes a unit-flow formulation whose projection is the convex hull of vectors encoded by source-to-sink paths.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Programming Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The path-flow projection is the appropriate representation for an acyclic dynamic program, and representation fits the leaf. The sign convention for the node-arc incidence matrix must be specified to justify the stated supply vector, and no source for the network-flow formulation or path decomposition is cited.

children.title: State-Transition Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral encodings of state transitions underlying dynamic programs.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Transition Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layered acyclic state-transition formulation and its projection onto accumulated decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a layered acyclic digraph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and arc labels \(g_a\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The state-transition polyhedron is \[Q(D)=\left\{y\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}:\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}y_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}y_a=b_v\quad(v\in V)\right\},\] where \(b_s=1\), \(b_t=-1\), and \(b_v=0\) otherwise. Under the projection \(x=\sum_{a\in A}g_a y_a\), its image is \[\operatorname{conv}\left\{\sum_{a\in P}g_a:P\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path in }D\right\}.\] Thus feasible paths encode discrete objects while flow variables provide an extended formulation of their convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit-flow polyhedron on a layered acyclic state graph projects to the convex hull of the decision vectors encoded by source-to-sink paths.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite layered acyclic digraph with designated vertices \(s,t\).
Each arc \(a\in A\) has a label \(g_a\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left\{\sum_{a\in A}g_a y_a:y\in Q(D)\right\}=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\sum_{a\in P}g_a:P\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\right\}.\)

notation.meaning: Unit source-to-sink flow polyhedron of the state graph.
Arcs leaving and entering vertex v.
Decision contribution attached to arc a.
