children.title: Composition Size Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Description-size consequences of decomposition width or state-space growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Composition Size Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive size under serial composition and multiplicative state growth under synchronous product composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For layered state graphs \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\), serial composition obtained by identifying consecutive terminal and initial states has \[|A|=\sum_{i=1}^k |A_i|\quad\text{and}\quad |V|\leq\sum_{i=1}^k|V_i|.\] By contrast, a synchronous product whose layer \(j\) stores every tuple of component states has at most \(\prod_{i=1}^k |V_{i,j}|\) states in that layer and at most \(\prod_{i=1}^k |A_{i,j}|\) simultaneous transitions between consecutive layers. Consequently, serially composable subproblems yield additive formulation size, whereas retaining all joint component states can produce multiplicative, hence exponential-in-\(k\), size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Serial state-space composition has additive size, while synchronous composition may multiply component state and transition counts, becoming exponential in the number of components.
assumptions_latex: Each \(D_i=(V_i,A_i)\) is a finite layered state graph.
Synchronous transitions are tuples of component transitions occurring in the same layer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|A_{\mathrm{serial}}|=\sum_i|A_i|\), whereas \(|V_{\mathrm{sync},j}|\leq\prod_i|V_{i,j}|\) and \(|A_{\mathrm{sync},j}|\leq\prod_i|A_{i,j}|\).\)

notation.meaning: States of component i in layer j.
Transitions of component i leaving layer j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the tradeoff leaf, and the additive and product counts are plausible under the stated serial and synchronous constructions. A source is required because the precise composition operations, size convention, and conditions behind exponential growth are model-dependent.

children.title: Symmetry in Extended Formulations
children.top_down_role: Effects of invariance requirements and symmetry breaking on lifted descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry in Extended Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariance condition for a lifted formulation under a group acting on the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act linearly on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(gP=P\) for every \(g\in G\). An extension \((Q,\pi)\), with \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\pi(Q)=P\), is \(G\)-symmetric if for every \(g\in G\) there exists an affine automorphism \(\widetilde g\) of \(Q\) such that \[\pi(\widetilde g(y))=g\pi(y)\qquad(y\in Q).\] Requiring this equivariance restricts the admissible extensions; a symmetry-breaking formulation may still project to \(P\) but need not admit compatible lifts \(\widetilde g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended formulation is symmetric when every original-space symmetry lifts to an affine automorphism commuting with projection; symmetry breaking removes this requirement.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite group acting linearly on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((Q,\pi)\text{ is }G\text{-symmetric}\iff(\forall g\in G)(\exists\widetilde g\in\operatorname{AffAut}(Q))\;\pi\circ\widetilde g=g\circ\pi.\)

notation.meaning: Symmetry group acting on the represented polytope.
Affine lift of the action of g to the extension.
Projection from the lifted space to the original space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivariance condition matches the stated topic and the condition content kind is appropriate. No citation or inspectable locator is supplied for this particular affine-automorphism definition of a symmetric extension.

children.title: Extension Complexity-Nonnegative Rank Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Measures and representation correspondences governing compact lifts.

children.title: Extension Complexity
children.top_down_role: Size measures for linear extended formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Extension Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facet-count definition for nonempty polytopes, allowing equations without charging them as inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), an extended formulation is a finite linear system \[Q=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:Ey=f,\;Gy\leq h\}\] together with an affine map \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(\pi(Q)=P\). Its size is the number of inequalities, after redundant inequalities are removed; equations are not counted. The extension complexity of \(P\) is \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min\{\text{number of inequalities in an extended formulation of }P\}.\] Equivalently, the minimum may be taken over extensions \(Q\) and counts the facets of \(Q\) relative to its affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension complexity is the minimum number of inequalities in any higher-dimensional polyhedron that projects affinely onto the given nonempty polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min\{|I|:P=\pi(\{y:Ey=f,\;G_Iy\leq h_I\})\}.\)

notation.meaning: Affine projection realizing P as the image of Q.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is locally appropriate and clearly states that equations are not charged. It still requires an authoritative citation with a specific definition, section, theorem, or page locator; none is attached.

children.title: Nonnegative Rank
children.top_down_role: Nonnegative factorization complexity associated with polyhedral slack structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorization definition over the nonnegative reals, including the zero-matrix convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{p\times q}\), its nonnegative rank is \[\operatorname{rank}_{+}(M)=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}:M=TU,\;T\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{p\times r},\;U\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{r\times q}\right\}.\] Equivalently, it is the least \(r\) for which there exist nonnegative vectors \(t_1,\ldots,t_r\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{p}\) and \(u_1,\ldots,u_r\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{q}\) satisfying \(M=\sum_{k=1}^{r}t_k u_k^{\mathsf T}\). The convention \(\operatorname{rank}_{+}(0)=0\) is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative rank of a nonnegative matrix is the smallest inner dimension of a factorization into two entrywise nonnegative matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_{+}(M)=\min\{r:M=TU,\;T\geq0,\;U\geq0\}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The factorization definition and zero-matrix convention are precise, and definition is the correct content kind. The record has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Slack-Matrix Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between lifted descriptions and nonnegative factorizations.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polytope containing at least two points.
\(P=\{x\in\operatorname{aff}(P):Ax\leq b\}\) is an irredundant relative-facet description, and \(v_1,\ldots,v_q\) are all vertices of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_{+}(S)\), where \(S_{ij}=b_i-A_iv_j\).

notation.meaning: Row normal of relative-facet inequality i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Yannakakis correspondence for nonempty polytopes that are not singletons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polytope with at least two points, and write \[P=\{x\in\operatorname{aff}(P):Ax\leq b\},\] where the rows give an irredundant description by all facets relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\). Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_q\) be all vertices of \(P\), and define the slack matrix \(S\) by \(S_{ij}=b_i-A_i v_j\). Then \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_{+}(S).\] The value is invariant under positive row scaling, vertex ordering, and the chosen irredundant relative-facet description. Hence the minimum inequality size of a lift equals the minimum inner dimension of a nonnegative factorization of its slack matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every nontrivial polytope, extension complexity equals the nonnegative rank of any irredundant relative-facet-versus-vertex slack matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Slack-Matrix Correspondence

children.title: Correspondence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation settings requiring qualifications to the standard complexity connection.

knowledge_statements.title: Correspondence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of the unmodified polytope slack-matrix equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equality \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_{+}(S)\) in its facet-versus-vertex form presupposes a nonempty polytope with vertices and a finite relative-facet description. It does not apply verbatim to an unbounded polyhedron, because vertices alone do not encode recession directions; an appropriate generalized slack matrix must also represent extreme rays. Degenerate zero-dimensional cases require a separate convention because their slack matrix can be empty or zero while formulation-size conventions may count no inequalities. Likewise, adding redundant rows or nonvertex columns preserves the represented polytope but changes the matrix presentation, so invariance claims require the corresponding rows or columns to be redundant in the factorization sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic correspondence needs a bounded nontrivial polytope; unbounded sets require recession data, and zero-dimensional or redundant presentations require explicit conventions.
assumptions_latex: The basic correspondence uses a facet-versus-vertex slack matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ unbounded}\Rightarrow\text{vertex slacks alone do not determine the full extension problem};\quad \dim P=0\Rightarrow\text{a separate size convention is required}.\)

notation.meaning: Slack matrix used in the polytope correspondence.
Recession cone of an unbounded polyhedron P.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the leaf, but the claims about generalized slack matrices for unbounded polyhedra, recession-ray data, zero-dimensional conventions, and redundant presentations are convention-sensitive. No source is supplied from which the exact boundary statement can be verified.

children.title: Compact Formulation Size-Bound Family
children.top_down_role: Constructive compactness results and barriers to concise formulations.

children.title: Compact Formulation Constructions
children.top_down_role: Structural families admitting concise extended descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(Q=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:Ey=f,\;Gy\leq h\}\) is an integral polytope with \(m\) inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(X)\) and \(\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{conv}(X))\leq m\).

notation.meaning: Finite family of feasible discrete vectors.
Affine decoding map from the lifted space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction principle for deriving small lifts from exact integral encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be finite, and let \[Q=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:Ey=f,\;Gy\leq h\}\] be an integral polytope described using \(m\) inequalities. Suppose an affine map \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(\pi(Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^d)=X\). Then \[\pi(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(X)\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{conv}(X))\leq m.\] Network-flow, dynamic-programming, and decomposition constructions can instantiate this principle by providing a compact integral lifted polytope and an affine decoding map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact integral lifted polytope whose integer points decode exactly to the feasible discrete vectors gives an extended formulation of their convex hull, with size bounded by its inequality count.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Formulation Constructions

children.title: Formulation Size Upper Bounds
children.top_down_role: Quantitative compactness guarantees for explicit formulation families.

knowledge_statements.title: Formulation Size Upper Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper bounds obtained by exhibiting a valid lifted linear description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polytope. If there exist matrices and vectors defining \[Q=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:Ey=f,\;Gy\leq h\}\] and an affine map \(\pi\) such that \(\pi(Q)=P\), then \[\operatorname{xc}(P)\leq \#\operatorname{rows}(G).\] Therefore, for a family \((P_n)\), an explicit construction with at most \(f(n)\) inequalities proves \(\operatorname{xc}(P_n)\leq f(n)\). The count concerns inequalities rather than auxiliary variables or equations, although those quantities may be reported separately when measuring the encoding length of an implementable formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any explicit lift with m inequalities proves that extension complexity is at most m; a family of such lifts supplies an asymptotic upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a polyhedron satisfying \(\pi(Q)=P\) for an affine map \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\leq\#\operatorname{rows}(G)\).

notation.meaning: Member n of a polytope family.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim is a direct upper-bound consequence of the stated extension-complexity convention, and complexity_bound is the correct role for this leaf. No authoritative source with a specific locator is cited.

children.title: Formulation Size Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Quantitative barriers to concise linear descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Formulation Size Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bounds transferred from nonnegative-rank bounds on slack matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a nonempty polytope with at least two points and slack matrix \(S\). Any proof that every nonnegative factorization \(S=TU\) has inner dimension at least \(L\) establishes \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_{+}(S)\geq L.\] For a family \((P_n)\), a bound \(\operatorname{rank}_{+}(S_n)\geq f(n)\) rules out every extended formulation of \(P_n\) having fewer than \(f(n)\) inequalities, independently of the number of auxiliary variables. Thus nonnegative-rank arguments provide formulation-size lower bounds against arbitrary linear lifts, not merely a prescribed formulation template.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower bound on the nonnegative rank of a polytope's slack matrix rules out every linear extended formulation with fewer inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polytope with at least two points.
\(S\) is a facet-versus-vertex slack matrix of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_{+}(S)\geq L\Rightarrow\operatorname{xc}(P)\geq L.\)

notation.meaning: Proposed lower bound on factorization dimension.
Slack matrix of the nth polytope in a family.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound transfer is mathematically aligned with the nonnegative-rank correspondence, and complexity_bound fits the leaf. It depends on the uncited Yannakakis correspondence and has no independent authoritative locator.

children.title: Compactness Separation Results
children.top_down_role: Contrasts between classes with compact lifts and classes requiring large formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Separation Results
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal separation between small original-space descriptions and small lifted descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polytope \(P\), let \(\operatorname{fc}(P)\) denote the minimum number of inequalities in any description of \(P\) within its own affine hull. Always \[\operatorname{xc}(P)\leq\operatorname{fc}(P),\] because \(P\) itself is an admissible extension. A family \((P_n)\) exhibits a compactness separation when \(\operatorname{fc}(P_n)\) and \(\operatorname{xc}(P_n)\) have asymptotically different growth; for example, \(\operatorname{fc}(P_n)=2^{\Omega(n)}\) and \(\operatorname{xc}(P_n)=n^{O(1)}\). Such a result certifies that auxiliary variables yield polynomial-size lifted formulations despite exponentially large direct descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension complexity never exceeds direct facet complexity, and a compactness separation occurs when lifts are asymptotically much smaller than every original-space description.
assumptions_latex: Direct descriptions and extensions count inequalities relative to their affine hulls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\leq\operatorname{fc}(P)\); a separation family may satisfy \(\operatorname{fc}(P_n)=2^{\Omega(n)}\) and \(\operatorname{xc}(P_n)=n^{O(1)}\).\)

notation.meaning: Minimum original-space inequality count for P.
Minimum lifted inequality count for P.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inequality between lifted and direct formulation sizes is coherent under the stated relative-affine-hull convention, and property is an acceptable role for the separation leaf. The notation \(\operatorname{fc}\) and the term 'compactness separation' are not sourced, so their intended convention cannot be confirmed.

children.title: Polyhedral Failure Boundaries

children.title: Relaxation Fractionality-Gap Boundary
children.top_down_role: Divergence between continuous relaxations and discrete feasible solutions.

children.title: Fractional Extreme Points
children.top_down_role: Nonintegral vertex structures appearing in continuous relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractionality of vertices in a relaxation of an integer feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) be a discrete feasible set and let \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron satisfying \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\subseteq R\). A point \(x^*\in R\) is a fractional extreme point of the relaxation if \(x^*\) is an extreme point of \(R\) and \(x^*\notin\mathbb{Z}^n\). Equivalently, \(x^*\) cannot be expressed as \(x^*=\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\) for distinct \(u,v\in R\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), yet at least one coordinate of \(x^*\) is nonintegral. Its existence proves that \(R\) is not an integral polyhedron and hence \(R\neq\operatorname{conv}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional extreme point is a nonintegral vertex of a polyhedral relaxation; its existence proves that the relaxation is not the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname{ext}(R)\setminus\mathbb{Z}^n\Rightarrow R\text{ is nonintegral and }R\neq\operatorname{conv}(X).\)

notation.meaning: Polyhedral relaxation of the discrete feasible set.
Set of extreme points of R.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the fractional-extreme-point leaf, introduces the relaxation and integer set, and correctly distinguishes a nonintegral vertex from an integral extreme point. No authoritative polyhedral-integrality source or inspectable locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to the polyhedra P_sub and P_cut as defined in the surrounding formulation context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: P_{\mathrm{sub}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{cut}}. Moreover, there exist examples for which P_{\mathrm{sub}}\subsetneq P_{\mathrm{cut}}, and P_{\mathrm{cut}} can have fractional extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: P_sub is contained in P_cut; the containment is strict in some examples, and P_cut can have fractional extreme points.

children.title: Integrality-Gap Measures
children.top_down_role: Quantitative comparisons between relaxation values and discrete optima.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative and additive gaps for a minimization relaxation with positive integer optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_I\subseteq X_R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be integer and relaxed feasible sets, and let \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Define \(z_I(c)=\inf\{c^\top x:x\in X_I\}\) and \(z_R(c)=\inf\{c^\top x:x\in X_R\}\). When \(0<z_R(c)\le z_I(c)<\infty\), the multiplicative integrality gap is \(g(c)=z_I(c)/z_R(c)\). Whenever both optima are finite, the additive gap is \(\Delta(c)=z_I(c)-z_R(c)\ge0\). For an instance class \(\mathcal I\), its worst-case gap is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}g_I\), restricted to instances satisfying the positivity convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integrality gap compares the integer optimum with the relaxation optimum, either by their ratio or difference; a class gap is the supremum over admissible instances.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(c)=z_I(c)/z_R(c)\) and \(\Delta(c)=z_I(c)-z_R(c)\ge0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ratio and additive-gap conventions are mathematically coherent for minimization, but no inspectable source is supplied. The scope note also says "positive integer optimum," whereas the statement requires a positive relaxation optimum and a finite integer optimum, not an integer-valued optimum.

children.title: Gap Instance Families
children.top_down_role: Structured examples exhibiting persistent or large relaxation gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap Instance Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete graphs witness the asymptotic factor-two gap of the standard vertex-cover LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the unweighted vertex-cover instance on \(K_n\), consider the relaxation \(\min\sum_{v}x_v\) subject to \(x_u+x_v\ge1\) for every edge \(uv\) and \(x_v\ge0\). The assignment \(x_v=1/2\) has value \(n/2\), and summing all edge constraints shows every relaxed solution has value at least \(n/2\). Every integral vertex cover of \(K_n\) contains at least \(n-1\) vertices. Hence \(z_R=n/2\), \(z_I=n-1\), and the ratio \(z_I/z_R=2-2/n\) tends to \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete graphs make the standard vertex-cover LP asymptotically a factor two too optimistic: its value is n/2 while the integer optimum is n−1.
assumptions_latex: The standard edge-constraint LP relaxation for unweighted vertex cover is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_I/z_R=2-2/n\to2\) as \(n\to\infty\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Relaxation Exactness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions separating integral relaxations from genuinely fractional regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Exactness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness characterized uniformly over linear objectives for a bounded relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_I\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and finite, and let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polytope with \(X_I\subseteq P\). Then the relaxation is exact for every linear minimization objective precisely when \(P=\operatorname{conv}(X_I)\): \[\min_{x\in P}c^\top x=\min_{x\in X_I}c^\top x\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb R^n \iff P=\operatorname{conv}(X_I).\] Thus any point of \(P\setminus\operatorname{conv}(X_I)\) permits a separating linear objective whose relaxed value is strictly better than the integer value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded relaxation is exact for every linear objective exactly when it equals the convex hull of its integer feasible points.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polytope containing \(X_I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(X_I)\) if and only if all linear-objective optimum values agree.

children.title: Exponential Facet Complexity
children.top_down_role: Families lacking concise descriptions in their natural spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Facet Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural-space inequality descriptions can require exponentially many facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\binom n2}\) be the symmetric traveling-salesperson polytope, the convex hull of incidence vectors of Hamiltonian cycles of \(K_n\). For each nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V(K_n)\), every tour satisfies the cut inequality \(x(\delta(S))\ge2\). For the standard nontrivial ranges of \(S\), these inequalities yield exponentially many distinct facets: the number is \(2^{\Omega(n)}\). Consequently, every irredundant linear inequality description of \(P_n\) in its original edge-variable space contains \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) inequalities, although extended formulations are a separate complexity measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The traveling-salesperson polytope has exponentially many facets in its natural edge-variable space, so no polynomial-size irredundant description exists there.
assumptions_latex: \(P_n\) is represented in the original \(\binom n2\) edge variables.
Descriptions use linear inequalities without auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{facets}(P_n)=2^{\Omega(n)}\), implying natural-space description size \(2^{\Omega(n)}\).

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in S
sum of edge variables over F

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A natural-space exponential facet lower bound is the correct kind of complexity statement for this leaf, but the claimed TSP facet family is left as "standard nontrivial ranges" and no authoritative locator is supplied. The exact facet conditions and resulting count require a source.

children.title: Polyhedral Oracle Hardness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral interfaces whose computational status obstructs effective use.

children.title: Membership Hardness
children.top_down_role: Computational barriers to deciding point inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Membership Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary for deciding membership in an explicitly encoded polyhedron family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of rational polyhedra \(\mathcal P=\{P_s\subseteq\mathbb R^{n(s)}\}\), indexed by binary strings \(s\), define \(\mathrm{MEM}_{\mathcal P}=\{(s,x):x\in\mathbb Q^{n(s)},\ x\in P_s\}\). The family has NP-hard membership if this language is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions, with input length equal to the binary encoding length of \((s,x)\). Membership hardness concerns exact rational membership; it does not by itself imply hardness of weak membership, which allows a prescribed numerical tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership is hard when deciding whether an encoded rational point belongs to an indexed polyhedron is NP-hard under polynomial-time reductions.
assumptions_latex: The index \(s\) and point \(x\) have finite binary encodings.
Membership is interpreted exactly over rational data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{MEM}_{\mathcal P}\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement proposes a reasonable exact-membership language, but the cited section concerns optimization from membership and does not reliably establish this indexed-language NP-hardness convention. Moreover, the conclusion asserts that the language is NP-hard although the body only defines what that phrase would mean. A source supporting the exact rational encoding and hardness formulation is required.

children.title: Separation Hardness
children.top_down_role: Computational barriers to producing separating witnesses.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary for producing a violated valid inequality or confirming membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an indexed family of rational polyhedra \(\mathcal P=\{P_s\subseteq\mathbb R^{n(s)}\}\), the strong separation problem takes rational \((s,y)\) and must either certify \(y\in P_s\) or return rational \((a,\beta)\) such that \(a^\top x\le\beta\) for every \(x\in P_s\) but \(a^\top y>\beta\). The family has NP-hard strong separation when a polynomial-time algorithm for this task would yield a polynomial-time algorithm for an NP-hard language, under the stated binary encoding model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong separation is hard when producing a valid inequality violated by a given point, or confirming membership, would solve an NP-hard problem.
assumptions_latex: The polyhedron index and query point are rationally encoded.
A separating inequality must have a rational finite encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation for \(\mathcal P\) is NP-hard in the binary encoding model.

source_refs.locator: * 6.4 Equivalence of Strong Optimization and Separation p. 174

The class \(\mathcal C\) and ambient-dimension convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recognition of \(\mathcal C\) is called NP-hard precisely when \(\mathrm{REC}_{\mathcal C}\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary for recognizing whether encoded data defines a member of a polyhedron class.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a fixed class of rational polyhedra, and let \(D=(A_D,b_D)\) encode a rational inequality system in a specified ambient dimension. Define \(P(D)=\{x:A_Dx\le b_D\}\) and \(\mathrm{REC}_{\mathcal C}=\{D:P(D)\in\mathcal C\}\). Recognition of \(\mathcal C\) is called NP-hard when \(\mathrm{REC}_{\mathcal C}\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions measured in the binary encoding length of \(D\). This differs from point membership because the input is an entire polyhedral description rather than a query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognition of a fixed polyhedron class is called NP-hard when deciding whether a rational inequality system defines a member of that class is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.title: Recognition Hardness

children.title: Oracle Intractability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Consequences of hard interfaces for effective polyhedral access.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) belongs to a family of nonempty, bounded, well-described rational polyhedra.
Computation uses the rational bit model with the required encoding bounds available to the oracle algorithms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{SEP}_{\mathrm{strong}}\equiv_T^p\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{strong}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation and linear optimization share a polynomial-time boundary for well-described rational polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: * 6.4 Equivalence of Strong Optimization and Separation p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a family of nonempty, bounded, well-described rational polyhedra for which the required polynomial encoding bounds are supplied to the oracle algorithms. In the rational bit model, strong separation over each \(P\in\mathcal P\) is polynomial-time oracle reducible to strong linear optimization over \(P\), and strong linear optimization is polynomial-time oracle reducible to strong separation. Thus \(\mathrm{SEP}_{\mathrm{strong}}\equiv_T^p\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{strong}}\). Consequently, if either problem is NP-hard, a polynomial-time algorithm for the other would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). This equivalence does not by itself cover exact membership or numerical oracles lacking the required encoding guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For well-described rational polytopes with the required encoding bounds, strong separation and strong linear optimization are polynomial-time oracle equivalent, so hardness transfers between them.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Intractability Boundaries

children.title: Exceptional Polyhedral Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric edge cases requiring distinct representations and certificates.

children.title: Empty Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Representation and certification issues for regions with no feasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empty feasibility regime for a finite linear inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), the polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) is empty when no vector satisfies all inequalities, equivalently \(P=\varnothing\). By the inequality form of Farkas' lemma, emptiness is equivalent to the existence of \(y\in\mathbb R_+^m\) such that \(A^\top y=0\) and \(b^\top y<0\). Such a multiplier is a finite certificate that the defining system is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is empty when its inequalities have no common solution; a nonnegative Farkas multiplier certifies this infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\varnothing\iff\exists y\ge0:\ A^\top y=0,\ b^\top y<0\).

notation.meaning: polyhedron defined by the inequality system

children.title: Unbounded Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Recession structure and representation issues for unbounded regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unboundedness characterized by a nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) be nonempty. Its recession cone is \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:Ad\le0\}\). The polyhedron is unbounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\) contains a nonzero vector. Equivalently, there exist \(x_0\in P\) and \(d\ne0\) such that \(x_0+td\in P\) for every \(t\ge0\). For a minimization objective \(c\), such a ray proves objective unboundedness below when additionally \(c^\top d<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is unbounded exactly when it has a nonzero recession direction; a cost-decreasing recession ray certifies an unbounded objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is unbounded}\iff\exists d\ne0:\ Ad\le0\).

children.title: Lower-Dimensional Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Affine-hull and relative-interior issues for non-full-dimensional regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedra whose affine hull is proper in the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is lower-dimensional in its stated ambient space when \(\dim(P)=\dim(\operatorname{aff}P)<n\). Equivalently, there exist \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that \(a^\top x=\beta\) for every \(x\in P\). If \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), lower dimensionality means that some nontrivial affine equality is valid throughout \(P\), whether or not that equality appears explicitly among the input constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is lower-dimensional when its affine hull is a proper affine subspace of the declared ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(P)<n\iff\exists(a,\beta),\ a\ne0:\ a^\top x=\beta\ \forall x\in P\).

children.title: Edge-Case Certificates
children.top_down_role: Witness formats suited to empty, unbounded, or dimension-deficient regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) is defined by a finite real inequality system.
For an unboundedness certificate, a feasible point \(x_0\in P\) is supplied.
For the lower-dimensionality certificate, \(P\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated multiplier, ray, and paired-validity witnesses certify emptiness, unboundedness, and lower dimensionality, respectively.

notation.meaning: normal and right-hand side of a valid affine equality
nonnegative multipliers certifying the two opposite valid inequalities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit witnesses for emptiness, unboundedness, and failure of full dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\). Emptiness is certified by \(y\ge0\) satisfying \(A^\top y=0\) and \(b^\top y<0\). Given \(x_0\in P\), unboundedness is certified by \(d\ne0\) satisfying \(Ad\le0\). Given nonempty \(P\), lower dimensionality is certified by \(a\ne0\), \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), and multipliers \(u,v\ge0\) satisfying \(A^\top u=a\), \(b^\top u\le\beta\), \(A^\top v=-a\), and \(b^\top v\le-\beta\). The last conditions certify \(a^\top x=\beta\) for every \(x\in P\). Each displayed witness is checkable using linear algebra and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Farkas multiplier certifies emptiness, a feasible base point with a nonzero recession direction certifies unboundedness, and nonnegative multipliers for two opposite valid inequalities certify a universally valid affine equality and hence lower dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Case Certificates

children.title: Computational Representation Models
children.top_down_role: Models connecting combinatorial instances, numerical data, primitive operations, and computational cost.

children.title: Bit-Level Turing Computation Model
children.top_down_role: Binary encoding and exact computation with finite strings and rational data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite-string objects used as inputs and outputs in the Turing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An alphabet is a finite set \(A\) with \(|A|\ge 2\) and \(\sqcup\notin A\). For \(n\ge 0\), \(A^n\) is the set of length-\(n\) strings over \(A\), where \(A^0\) consists of the unique empty string, and \(A^*:=\bigcup_{n\ge0}A^n\). A language over \(A\) is any subset \(L\subseteq A^*\); its elements are words. If \(x\in A^n\), then \(\operatorname{size}(x):=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alphabet is a finite set of at least two symbols that excludes the designated blank symbol. Strings are finite symbol sequences; the unique length-zero string is empty, and A* is the set of all finite strings. A language is any subset of A*, and the size of a string is its length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^*=\bigcup_{n\ge0}A^n,\quad A^0=\{\varepsilon\},\quad L\subseteq A^*,\quad x\in A^n\Rightarrow\operatorname{size}(x)=n.

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.1. Turing Machines / Definition 15.1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary input size for rational data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding lengths for integer and rational inputs, independent of a particular formal machine model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer \(a\) can be represented in binary using \(O(\log(|a|+2))\) bits. A rational number is represented by separately encoding its numerator and denominator. For an instance \(x\) with rational data, \(\operatorname{size}(x)\) is the total number of bits required by these binary representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer has logarithmic-length binary encoding, while a rational is encoded through its numerator and denominator. The size of a rational-data instance is the total number of encoding bits.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is an instance with rational data}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{size}(x)\text{ is the total binary encoding length, and integer }a\text{ requires }O(\log(|a|+2))\text{ bits.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic One-Tape Simulation of a Two-Tape Machine
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An output-preserving one-tape simulation exists with quadratic running-time overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $A$ be an alphabet and let
\[
\Phi:\{0,\ldots,N\}\times(A\cup\{\sqcup\})^2\to\{-1,\ldots,N\}\times(A\cup\{\sqcup\})^2\times\{-1,0,1\}^2
\]
be a two-tape Turing machine. Then there exist an alphabet $B\supseteq A$, an integer $N'$, and a one-tape Turing machine
\[
\Phi':\{0,\ldots,N'\}\times(B\cup\{\square\})\to\{-1,\ldots,N'\}\times(B\cup\{\square\})\times\{-1,0,1\}
\]
such that, for every $x\in A^*$,
\[
\operatorname{output}(\Phi',x)=\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{time}(\Phi',x)=O\!\left(\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)^2\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every two-tape Turing machine can be simulated by a one-tape Turing machine over an extended alphabet. On every input, the simulator has the same output and at most quadratic running-time overhead.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists B\supseteq A\;\exists N'\;\exists\Phi'\;\forall x\in A^*:\ \operatorname{output}(\Phi',x)=\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x)\ \land\ \operatorname{time}(\Phi',x)=O\!\left(\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)^2\right).

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.2. Church's Thesis / Theorem 15.5

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic One-Tape Simulation of a Two-Tape Machine

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Computational Problems and Polynomial-Time Turing Computation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines total relational search problems, their computation by Turing machines, the functional and decision special cases, and polynomial-time computability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an alphabet \(A\), a computational problem is a pair \((X,R)\) such that \(X\subseteq A^*\), \(R\subseteq X\times A^*\), and \(\forall x\in X\,\exists y\in A^*:(x,y)\in R\). A Turing machine \(\Phi\) computes \((X,R)\) if, for every \(x\in X\), it halts and \((x,\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x))\in R\). It is polynomial-time for \((X,R)\) if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that \(\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)\le p(\operatorname{size}(x))\) for every \(x\in X\). If every \(x\in X\) has exactly one related output, then \(R\) defines a function \(f:X\to A^*\), and \(\Phi\) computes \(f\). If \(X=A^*\) and \(f:A^*\to\{0,1\}\), then \(\Phi\) decides \(L:=\{x\in A^*:f(x)=1\}\). A function is polynomial-time computable, or a language polynomial-time decidable, if an appropriate polynomial-time Turing machine exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computational problem assigns at least one admissible output string to every input in its input language. A Turing machine computes the problem when it halts on every permitted input and returns an admissible output. Polynomial time is a uniform polynomial bound in input length. Unique admissible outputs define function computation, while Boolean functions on all strings define language decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ computes }(X,R)\iff\forall x\in X:\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)<\infty\ \land\ (x,\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x))\in R;\quad \Phi\text{ is polynomial-time for }(X,R)\iff\exists p\text{ polynomial}\ \forall x\in X:\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)\le p(\operatorname{size}(x)).

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.1. Turing Machines / Definition 15.3

knowledge_statements.title: Computational Problems and Polynomial-Time Turing Computation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Turing Machine for a Computational Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a two-tape oracle machine with a special query state, relation-valued answers, and output-length-sensitive query cost; the stated answer rule applies to queries in the oracle domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $A$ be an alphabet, $\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}$, and let $(X,R)$ be a computational problem with $X\subseteq A^*$. An oracle Turing machine using $(X,R)$ is a function
\[
\Phi:\{0,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A^2\to\{-2,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A^2\times\{-1,0,1\}^2,
\qquad N\in\mathbb Z_+.
\]
Its computation follows the two-tape model, with accumulated time initially $0$ and transition value $-2$ designating an oracle call. At such a call, let $q\in A^k$ be the string in cells $1,\ldots,k$ of the second tape, where
\[
k=\min\{j\in\mathbb N:t_j^{(i)}=\sqcup\}-1.
\]
If $q\in X$, choose some $y\in A^*$ with $(q,y)\in R$, write $y$ in the initial cells of the second tape followed by a blank, increase accumulated time by $1+|y|$, set $n^{(i+1)}=n^{(i)}+1$, and leave the remaining configuration components unchanged. In every other case accumulated time increases by $1$. The computation ends when the state is $-1$; its accumulated time is then $\operatorname{time}(\Phi,w)$ for the machine input $w$, and output is defined as in the two-tape model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle Turing machine is a two-tape machine with a special oracle-call transition. Its query is the second-tape string preceding the first blank. When that query belongs to the oracle domain, the oracle may return any related output, writes it followed by a blank, charges one step plus the output length, and resumes at the successor of the calling state. Other steps cost one, and state -1 halts. The extract supplies an oracle-answer rule only for queries in the domain X.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is an alphabet and }\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}
(X,R)\text{ is a computational problem with }X\subseteq A^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ defines a two-tape computation with oracle-call value }-2;\ q\in X\text{ permits some answer }y\text{ with }(q,y)\in R\text{ at cost }1+|y|,\text{ while other steps cost }1\text{ and state }-1\text{ halts.}

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.2. Church's Thesis / Definition 15.6

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Turing Machine for a Computational Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Tape Turing Machine and Its Computation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a deterministic two-tape machine with integer-indexed tapes, separate heads, and halting state -1.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $A$ be an alphabet, $\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}$, and $N\in\mathbb Z_+$. A two-tape Turing machine is a function
\[
\Phi:\{0,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A^2\to\{-1,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A^2\times\{-1,0,1\}^2.
\]
For $x\in A^*$, its computation is the finite or infinite sequence $(n^{(i)},s^{(i)},t^{(i)},\pi^{(i)},\rho^{(i)})_{i\ge0}$ initialized by $n^{(0)}=0$, $\pi^{(0)}=\rho^{(0)}=1$, the symbols of $x$ in cells $1,\ldots,|x|$ of the first tape, and blanks elsewhere on both tapes. If $n^{(i)}\ne-1$ and
\[
\Phi(n^{(i)},s^{(i)}_{\pi^{(i)}},t^{(i)}_{\rho^{(i)}})=(m,\sigma,\tau,\delta,\epsilon),
\]
then the next configuration has state $m$, writes $\sigma$ and $\tau$ in the scanned cells, leaves all other cells unchanged, and moves the heads to $\pi^{(i)}+\delta$ and $\rho^{(i)}+\epsilon$. The computation terminates upon reaching state $-1$; its time and output are defined as in the one-tape model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-tape Turing machine has finite control, two integer-indexed tapes, and an independently moving head on each tape. The input initially occupies the first tape, while the second tape is blank. Each nonhalting transition reads both scanned symbols, changes state, writes on both tapes, and moves each head by -1, 0, or 1. State -1 terminates the computation; time and output follow the one-tape conventions.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is an alphabet and }\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ together with the initialization and update rules determines a finite or infinite computation that terminates when the control state reaches }-1.

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.2. Church's Thesis / Definition 15.4

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Tape Turing Machine and Its Computation

children.title: Turing Machine Cost Model
children.top_down_role: Finite-string computation measured through discrete machine operations.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite binary word \(x\in\{0,1\}^*\).
The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and transition function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_M(x)\) equals the number of transitions before halting, and \(S_M(x)\) equals the number of distinct work-tape cells visited.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic bit-complexity model for finite binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and input \(x\in\{0,1\}^*\), the time cost \(T_M(x)\) is the number of transition steps executed before \(M\) halts. Its space cost \(S_M(x)\) is the number of distinct work-tape cells visited during that computation; read-only input cells are excluded. An algorithm has worst-case time \(T(n)\) and space \(S(n)\) when every input of length \(n\) halts within those respective bounds. Thus arithmetic on encoded integers is charged according to the bit-level transitions required, rather than as a single operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Turing cost model counts elementary transitions and visited work cells on binary inputs, so arithmetic cost depends on operand encoding length.
knowledge_statements.title: Turing Machine Cost Model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Turing-machine cost-model leaf and is internally precise, but no inspectable source is cited for the selected multitape, read-only-input, and work-tape-space conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Turing Machine, Computation, Time, and Output
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a deterministic one-tape Turing machine with a bi-infinite tape and its finite or infinite execution on a finite input string.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be an alphabet and \(\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}\). A Turing machine is a function \(\Phi:\{0,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A\to\{-1,�\ldots,N\}\times\bar A\times\{-1,0,1\}\) for some \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\). On input \(x\in A^*\), the initial instruction is \(0\), the symbols of \(x\) occupy tape positions \(1,\ldots,\operatorname{size}(x)\), all other positions are blank, and the head is at position \(1\). Each transition changes the instruction, writes one symbol, and moves the head by \(-1\), \(0\), or \(1\). If instruction \(-1\) is reached after \(i\) transitions, then \(\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x):=i\), and the output is the tape prefix in positions \(1,\ldots,k\), where \(k\) is one less than the first nonnegative tape position containing a blank. If instruction \(-1\) is never reached, then \(\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x):=\infty\) and \(\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x)\) is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic one-tape Turing machine uses the current instruction and scanned symbol to choose the next instruction, symbol to write, and a movement left, stationary, or right. The finite input begins at tape position 1 and all other positions are blank. Reaching instruction -1 defines halting time and an output given by the tape prefix before its first blank. A nonhalting computation has infinite runtime and undefined output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)<\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x)\in A^*,\qquad \operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)=\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x)\text{ is undefined}.

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.1. Turing Machines / Definition 15.2

knowledge_statements.title: Turing Machine, Computation, Time, and Output

children.title: Binary Encoding Length
children.top_down_role: Instance-size measurement for binary-encoded combinatorial and rational data.

assumptions_latex: Integers use signed binary notation without leading zeroes, except that zero is encoded by one bit.
A rational number is represented in reduced numerator-denominator form with positive denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell(a)=1+\lceil\log_2(|a|+1)\rceil\) and \(\ell(p/q)=\ell(p)+\ell(q)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed signed-binary convention; alternative conventions differ only by additive constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\in\mathbb Z\), define its signed binary encoding length by \(\ell(a)=1+\lceil\log_2(|a|+1)\rceil\), where the first bit accounts for sign. If \(r=p/q\in\mathbb Q\) is represented uniquely with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\), define \(\ell(r)=\ell(p)+\ell(q)\). For a finite vector or matrix of rational entries, its encoding length is the sum of the entry lengths plus a fixed self-delimiting encoding of its dimensions. Polynomial-time bounds are measured as functions of this total length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary encoding length counts the bits for signed integers, reduced rational numerators and denominators, and the dimensions and entries of finite arrays.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Encoding Length

children.title: Exact Rational Arithmetic
children.top_down_role: Exact numerical computation with attention to operand representation.

assumptions_latex: Each rational is stored as a reduced pair \((p,q)\in\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
Integer operations are performed exactly, without rounding or overflow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operations \(+,-,\times,\div\) and comparison return exact reduced rational results whenever division is defined.

notation.meaning: reduced representation of a rational number

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical exact arithmetic on reduced rational pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent \(p/q\in\mathbb Q\) by coprime integers \((p,q)\) with \(q>0\). For operands \(p/q\) and \(r/s\), compute addition as \((ps+rq)/(qs)\), multiplication as \((pr)/(qs)\), and division, when \(r\ne0\), as \((ps)/(qr)\); subtraction is analogous. After each operation, divide numerator and denominator by their greatest common divisor and make the denominator positive. Compare two rationals by the exact sign of \(ps-rq\). The output is therefore the canonical reduced result, while bit cost depends on the lengths of all intermediate integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact rational arithmetic stores reduced fractions, applies integer formulas, normalizes by a greatest common divisor, and compares by cross multiplication without rounding.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Rational Arithmetic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and exact rational formulas are mathematically sound, but the only citation is specifically located at a section on encoding lengths and does not clearly support the arithmetic and normalization algorithm. A source locator covering exact rational operations and comparison is required.

children.title: Machine Operation-Cost Models
children.top_down_role: Machine and operation-count models used in combinatorial and numerical analysis.

children.title: Random-Access Machine Model
children.top_down_role: Memory-access assumptions used in combinatorial runtime analysis.

assumptions_latex: Memory consists of addressable words indexed by nonnegative integers.
The instruction set and word-cost convention are fixed independently of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is \(T_P(x)=\sum_{t=1}^{h(x)}c_t\), where \(c_t\) is the prescribed cost of instruction \(t\).

notation.meaning: number of executed instructions before halting

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General RAM framework encompassing unit-cost and length-sensitive instruction charges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random-access machine has finitely many registers and an unbounded array of addressable words. A fixed program \(P\) applies instructions for loading constants, copying, indirect addressing, branching, comparison, and specified arithmetic operations. Any word can be accessed by its address without scanning preceding memory. If the computation on input \(x\) halts after \(h(x)\) instructions and the cost assigned to its \(t\)-th instruction is \(c_t\), then its running time is \(T_P(x)=\sum_{t=1}^{h(x)}c_t\). A complexity claim in this model must state whether \(c_t\) is uniform or depends on operand lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A RAM directly accesses addressed words and executes a fixed instruction set; its running time sums the costs assigned to executed instructions.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Access Machine Model

children.title: Unit-Cost Arithmetic Model
children.top_down_role: Operation-count analysis treating arithmetic primitives as unit-cost operations.

assumptions_latex: The computation uses a random-access machine.
Every permitted arithmetic, comparison, branch, and memory-access instruction has cost one, regardless of operand magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_P(x)=h(x)\), the number of executed machine instructions.

notation.meaning: executed instruction count on input x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost specialization of the RAM model, including arithmetic on stored words.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the unit-cost arithmetic RAM model, each permitted instruction has cost \(1\), including memory access, comparison, branching, and arithmetic operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and exact division when defined. Consequently, if a program \(P\) executes \(h(x)\) instructions on input \(x\), then \(T_P(x)=h(x)\). The charge is independent of the binary lengths of operands and results. Therefore an operation-count bound in this model is not by itself a bit-complexity bound unless all encountered word lengths are also polynomially bounded in the input encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit-cost model charges one step per permitted RAM operation, even for large operands, so operation counts need not equal bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Cost Arithmetic Model

children.title: Arithmetic-Cost Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes caused by operand size or arithmetic-cost assumptions.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm performs \(N(x)\) arithmetic or memory operations on input \(x\).
Every operand encountered has binary length at most \(B(x)\).
A corresponding bit implementation charges each operation according to operand length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unit-cost polynomiality transfers to bit polynomiality only when both \(N(x)\) and the relevant length-dependent operation costs are polynomial in \(\ell(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer criterion between arithmetic-operation counts and bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm executes \(N(x)\) abstract operations and every intermediate operand has length at most \(B(x)\). If each corresponding bit operation on operands of length at most \(B\) costs at most \(C(B)\), then the implemented running time is bounded by \(O(N(x)C(B(x)))\), up to representation-management overhead. Hence a polynomial unit-cost bound yields a polynomial bit bound when \(N(x)\), \(B(x)\), and \(C(B(x))\) are polynomial in \(\ell(x)\). Without a polynomial bound on intermediate lengths, a polynomial arithmetic-operation count may conceal superpolynomial bit cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operation-count complexity transfers to bit complexity only when intermediate numbers and the bit costs of their operations remain polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic-Cost Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transfer principle is appropriately scoped and mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source supports the stated bit-cost transfer bound or its representation-overhead qualification.

children.title: Explicit Instance Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations listing the relevant instance data directly.

assumptions_latex: An instance is a finite combinatorial object whose primitive data can be listed.
A fixed injective, self-delimiting binary serialization convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The explicit input size is \(\ell(I)=|\operatorname{enc}(I)|\), including every listed primitive datum and structural delimiter.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full listing representation for finite combinatorial instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit encoding of a finite instance \(I\) is an injective, self-delimiting binary string \(\operatorname{enc}(I)\) that lists every primitive component needed to reconstruct \(I\), including dimensions, incidences, coefficients, and objective data when present. Its input size is \(\ell(I)=|\operatorname{enc}(I)|\). A standard explicit encoding must admit deterministic decoding in time polynomial in \(\ell(I)\). Complexity measured under this representation may depend polynomially on the number of listed components and on the binary lengths of their numerical values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit encoding lists all primitive instance data in a decodable binary serialization, and input size is the total serialized bit length.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Instance Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches explicit instance encodings and clearly identifies total serialized bit length, but the decoding requirement and representation conventions have no cited authoritative source.

children.title: Succinct Instance Encodings
children.top_down_role: Compressed representations whose described objects may be much larger than their encodings.

assumptions_latex: A finite object \(I\) is generated by a finite binary description \(d\).
A fixed deterministic interpreter maps valid descriptions to represented instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The succinct size is \(|d|\), which can be exponentially smaller than the size of an explicit listing of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-based representation whose description may be much smaller than its expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a deterministic interpreter \(G\). A succinct encoding of an instance \(I\) is a finite binary description \(d\) satisfying \(G(d)=I\), where \(d\) specifies a circuit, formula, program, or other compact generator rather than listing all components of \(I\). The represented input size is \(|d|\), not the length of an expanded explicit encoding of \(I\). The expansion size may be exponential in \(|d|\); consequently, an algorithm polynomial in the explicit size need not be polynomial in the succinct size. The interpreter \(G\) is part of the representation class and must be fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A succinct encoding uses a fixed compact generator; complexity is measured by the description length, even when the generated explicit instance is exponentially larger.
knowledge_statements.title: Succinct Instance Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly makes the interpreter part of the representation class and says that exponential compression may occur, but no inspectable source supports this representation-sensitive complexity claim.

children.title: Oracle-Access Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations exposing instance information through permitted queries.

assumptions_latex: The instance contains an implicit object accessible through a specified oracle \(O\).
Each legal query and answer has a finite encoding under a fixed query protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle complexity records the number of calls to \(O\), together with any separately charged local computation and query lengths.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box input representation with an explicit query protocol and cost convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle-access encoding specifies an instance through a black box \(O\) and a query domain. On a legal query \(q\), the algorithm receives the exact response \(O(q)\), such as a value, membership answer, separation witness, or optimization result. The oracle protocol fixes the admissible queries, response format, and cost of a call. Query complexity is the number of oracle calls; total complexity additionally charges local computation and, when required, the lengths of queries and responses. Claims made in this representation are relative to the chosen oracle and do not automatically imply complexity bounds for an explicit implementation of \(O\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle encoding exposes instance information through specified queries; complexity must distinguish oracle calls from local work and from implementing the oracle.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Access Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits oracle-access encodings and distinguishes query cost from local and implementation cost, but the broad oracle protocol conventions require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Boolean Problem Interface Family
children.top_down_role: Yes-or-no forms used for classification and reductions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Truth Assignments, Literals, Clauses, and CNF Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the elementary objects and satisfaction semantics of Boolean formulas in conjunctive normal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a finite set of Boolean variables. A truth assignment is a function $T:X\to\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}$, extended to $L:=X\mathbin{\dot\cup}\{\bar x:x\in X\}$ by assigning $\bar x$ the truth value opposite to that of $x$. The elements of $L$ are literals. A clause over $X$ is a set of literals and is satisfied by $T$ if and only if at least one of its literals is true. A family $\mathcal C$ of clauses is satisfiable if and only if some truth assignment satisfies every clause; it represents the conjunctive-normal-form formula $\bigwedge_{C\in\mathcal C}\bigvee_{\ell\in C}\ell$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite set of Boolean variables, a truth assignment assigns true or false to each variable and the opposite value to its negation. A clause is a set of literals interpreted as their disjunction. A family of clauses is satisfiable exactly when one assignment satisfies every clause, and it represents a conjunctive-normal-form formula.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a finite set of Boolean variables.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C\text{ is satisfiable}\iff \exists T:X\to\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}\;\forall C\in\mathcal C\;\exists \ell\in C:\ T(\ell)=\mathrm{true}.

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.4. Cook's Theorem / Definition 15.19

knowledge_statements.title: Truth Assignments, Literals, Clauses, and CNF Satisfiability

children.title: Feasibility Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Problem presentations centered on the existence of admissible objects.

assumptions_latex: Each encoded instance \(I\) determines a candidate domain \(X_I\) and a feasible subset \(F_I\subseteq X_I\).
The Boolean interface receives the encoded instance \(I\), rather than a supplied candidate solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{feas}}(I)=1\) if and only if \(F_I\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential Boolean interface asking whether an encoded instance has any feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each valid encoded instance \(I\), let \(X_I\) be its candidate domain and let \(F_I\subseteq X_I\) be its feasible set. The feasibility interface is the Boolean map \(D_{\mathrm{feas}}\) defined by \(D_{\mathrm{feas}}(I)=1\) if and only if there exists \(x\in X_I\) such that \(x\in F_I\), equivalently if and only if \(F_I\ne\varnothing\). It asks whether a feasible solution exists and does not require the interface to output such a solution. Running time is measured using the declared encoding of \(I\) and machine model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasibility interface returns yes exactly when the encoded instance has at least one feasible solution; it need not produce that solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Interfaces

children.title: Decision Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Binary problem presentations used in classification and reductions.

assumptions_latex: A family of instances is encoded as a language domain \(\mathcal I\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\).
A mathematically specified property \(P(I)\) has a definite truth value for every valid instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decision interface computes \(D_P(I)=1\) if and only if \(P(I)\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General yes-no interface for a property of an encoded instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) be the valid encodings of an instance family and let \(P\) be a property defined on those instances. The associated decision interface is \(D_P:\mathcal I\to\{0,1\}\), with \(D_P(I)=1\) if and only if \(P(I)\) is true. Equivalently, it recognizes the language \(L_P=\{I\in\mathcal I:P(I)\}\). The interface returns only the truth value and need not produce a witness, feasible solution, or optimum. Running time is measured in the length of the complete encoded instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision interface maps each valid encoded instance to yes or no according to a specified property, without requiring a witness or solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record is a precise general definition of a Boolean decision interface and distinguishes decision from witness production, but it has no authoritative citation with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Language-based binary decision-problem interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem is a pair \(\mathcal P=(X,Y)\), where \(X\) is a language decidable in polynomial time and \(Y\subseteq X\). The elements of \(X\) are called instances, those of \(Y\) are yes-instances, and those of \(X\setminus Y\) are no-instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision problem is a pair (X,Y), where X is a language decidable in polynomial time and Y is a subset of X. Elements of X are instances; elements of Y are yes-instances, and elements of X outside Y are no-instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P=(X,Y),\quad X\text{ is decidable in polynomial time},\quad Y\subseteq X;\quad Y\text{ and }X\setminus Y\text{ are respectively the yes- and no-instances}.\)

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.3. P and NP / Definition 15.7

knowledge_statements.title: Decision problem and its instances

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial equivalence of set optimization and threshold decision
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization-to-decision equivalence for integer-weighted feasible subsets, preserving the possibility of infeasibility and the stated hardness transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) and \(\mathcal F'\) be infinite families of finite sets. Given \(E\in\mathcal F\) and \(c:E\to\mathbb Z\), let \(\mathcal P\) minimize \(c(F)\) over sets \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \(F\in\mathcal F'\), or decide that no such set exists. Then \(\mathcal P\) is solvable in polynomial time if and only if the problem of deciding, for an instance \((E,c)\) and an integer \(k\), whether \(\operatorname{OPT}((E,c))\le k\) is solvable in polynomial time. If \(\mathcal P\) is NP-hard, then this threshold decision problem is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integer-weighted feasible-subset optimization over families of finite sets, polynomial-time optimization is equivalent to polynomial-time threshold decision, while allowing that no feasible subset may exist. If the optimization problem is NP-hard, its threshold decision problem is also NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F,\mathcal F'\text{ are infinite families of finite sets}
\{F\subseteq E:F\in\mathcal F'\}\text{ is the feasible-set family, which may be empty}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\in\mathrm P\iff\bigl[(E,c,k)\mapsto(\operatorname{OPT}((E,c))\le k)\bigr]\in\mathrm P;\qquad \mathcal P\text{ NP-hard}\Rightarrow\text{the threshold decision problem is NP-hard.}

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.7. NP-Hard Problems / Proposition 15.44

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial equivalence of set optimization and threshold decision

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the class using logarithmically many random bits, a constant number of nonadaptive proof queries, perfect completeness, and soundness strictly below one half.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y)\) be a decision problem. For a polynomial \(p\), put \(m(x)=\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(x))\rfloor\) and \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log p(\operatorname{size}(x))\rfloor\). Then \((X,Y)\in\operatorname{PCP}(\log n,1)\) if there exist \(k\in\mathbb N\), a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that \(f(x,r)\in\{1,\ldots,m(x)\}^k\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(r\in\{0,1\}^{\ell(x)}\), and a decision problem \((X',Y')\in P\), where \(X'=\{(x,\pi,\gamma):x\in X,\ \pi\in\{1,\ldots,m(x)\}^k,\ \gamma\in\{0,1\}^k\}\), satisfying: if \(x\in Y\), some \(c\in\{0,1\}^{m(x)}\) has \(\Pr_r[(x,f(x,r),c_{f(x,r)})\in Y']=1\); if \(x\notin Y\), every \(c\in\{0,1\}^{m(x)}\) has \(\Pr_r[(x,f(x,r),c_{f(x,r)})\in Y']<\tfrac12\). In both cases \(r\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\ell(x)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision problem is in PCP(log n, 1) when a polynomial-time verifier uses logarithmically many uniformly random bits to select a constant number of proof positions, accepts every yes-instance with probability one for some polynomial-length proof, and accepts any proof for a no-instance with probability strictly less than one half.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a polynomial and \(k\in\mathbb N\) is constant.
The query map \(f\) is polynomial-time computable and returns \(k\) valid proof positions.
The verifier decision problem \((X',Y')\) belongs to \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (X,Y)\in\operatorname{PCP}(\log n,1)\iff\text{the stated perfect-completeness and soundness conditions hold}.

source_evidence.locator: Approximation Algorithms / 16.6. The PCP Theorem / Definition 16.31

source_refs.locator: Approximation Algorithms / 16.6. The PCP Theorem / Definition 16.31

knowledge_statements.title: Definition of PCP(log n, 1)

children.title: Threshold Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Binary comparisons between attainable performance and a specified threshold.

assumptions_latex: Each instance \(I\) has a feasible set \(F_I\) and an objective \(f_I:F_I\to\mathbb Q\).
The rational threshold \(k\in\mathbb Q\) is part of the encoded input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\le}(I,k)=1\) if and only if there exists \(x\in F_I\) such that \(f_I(x)\le k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization threshold convention; the corresponding maximization interface reverses the inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization instance \(I\) with feasible set \(F_I\) and rational-valued objective \(f_I:F_I\to\mathbb Q\), the threshold interface takes an encoded threshold \(k\in\mathbb Q\) and returns \(D_{\le}(I,k)=1\) if and only if there exists \(x\in F_I\) satisfying \(f_I(x)\le k\). If \(F_I\ne\varnothing\) and the minimum of \(f_I\) over \(F_I\) is attained, this is equivalent to \(\min_{x\in F_I}f_I(x)\le k\). For maximization, the corresponding predicate uses \(f_I(x)\ge k\). The encoding length of \(k\) is included in the input size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimization threshold interface returns yes exactly when some feasible solution has objective value at most the encoded threshold; a minimum-value formulation additionally requires attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Interfaces

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On input \(x\), the interface returns some \(y\in R(x)\) when \(R(x)\neq\varnothing\), and returns \(\bot\) otherwise.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A search interface for a polynomially balanced relation \(R\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\) accepts an instance \(x\in\Sigma^*\). If \(R(x)=\{y:(x,y)\in R\}\) is nonempty, it must output one member \(y\in R(x)\); if \(R(x)=\varnothing\), it outputs \(\bot\).
