children.title: Priority-Order Greedy Methods
children.top_down_role: Incremental methods organized by candidate ordering and feasibility preservation.

knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Order Greedy Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic one-pass greedy construction over a hereditary feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite ground set \(E\), a hereditary family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\), and a priority key \(p:E\to\mathbb R\). Order the elements as \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) with \(p(e_1)\geq\cdots\geq p(e_m)\), resolving ties by a specified rule. Initialize \(S_0=\varnothing\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), set \(S_i=S_{i-1}\cup\{e_i\}\) if this set lies in \(\mathcal F\), and otherwise set \(S_i=S_{i-1}\). Output \(S_m\). Stop after every element has been examined once; optimality requires a separate structural certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan candidates in priority order, permanently accept each feasible addition, reject infeasible additions, and return the final feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and membership in \(\mathcal F\) is decidable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(S_m\) belongs to \(\mathcal F\) and is maximal relative to the processed priority scan.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and terminal placement are correct, and heredity makes the final set inclusion-maximal after a complete scan. An authoritative algorithm or greedy-systems locator is nevertheless absent.

children.title: Structural Greedy Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Correctness families based on replacements, safe choices, and structural cuts.

children.title: Exchange-Property Certificates
children.top_down_role: Correctness evidence based on replacing selected objects while preserving feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Property Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies greedy optimality through feasible exchanges that do not decrease total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\), let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and let \(G=\{g_1,ldots,g_r\}\in\mathcal F\) be a greedy output in its selection order. An exchange certificate consists of a certified optimal set \(O_0\in\mathcal F\) and sets \(O_1,ldots,O_r\in\mathcal F\) such that \(\{g_1,ldots,g_i\}\subseteq O_i\) for every \(i\). For each \(i\), either \(g_i\in O_{i-1}\) and \(O_i=O_{i-1}\), or there is an element \(o_i\in O_{i-1}\) such that \(O_i=(O_{i-1}\setminus\{o_i\})\cup\{g_i\}\) and \(w(g_i)\geq w(o_i)\). If \(O_r=G\), these conditions certify that \(G\) is optimal for maximizing total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible sequence that transforms a certified optimum into the greedy output using only nondecreasing-weight exchanges certifies greedy optimality.
assumptions_latex: Every listed set, exchange, and weight comparison is explicitly checkable.
\(O_0\) has an independent certificate of optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exchange data certify that \(G\) is a maximum-total-weight member of \(\mathcal F\).

notation.meaning: feasible set after the ith certified exchange
sum of the weights of elements of S

children.title: Cut-Property Certificates
children.top_down_role: Correctness evidence based on choices certified across structural cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Property Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-spanning-tree safe-edge certificate for a cut respected by the current forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph with edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and let \(A\subseteq E\) be contained in some minimum spanning tree. For a cut \((S,V\setminus S)\) that no edge of \(A\) crosses, let \(e\) be a minimum-weight edge crossing that cut. The tuple \((S,e)\), together with comparisons \(w(e)\leq w(f)\) for every crossing edge \(f\), certifies that \(A\cup\{e\}\) is contained in a minimum spanning tree. Thus \(e\) is a safe greedy choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lightest edge crossing a cut respected by the current forest is certified safe for some minimum spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is contained in a minimum spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a minimum spanning tree containing \(A\cup\{e\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind and MST cut-property statement are mathematically appropriate and sufficiently qualified by the invariant that A lies in an MST. A specific theorem or section locator is required.

children.title: Safe-Choice Certification
children.top_down_role: Connections from structural properties to locally safe greedy selections.

knowledge_statements.title: Safe-Choice Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic certificate that a greedy choice preserves extendibility to an optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with feasible-solution family \(\mathcal X\) and objective \(c:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), let \(A\) be the current partial choice. A candidate \(e\) has a safe-choice certificate when the certificate identifies a certified optimal solution \(X\in\mathcal X\) extending \(A\) and a locally verifiable transformation producing a feasible solution \(X'\in\mathcal X\) that extends \(A\cup\{e\}\) and satisfies \(c(X')\leq c(X)\). These data certify that \(A\cup\{e\}\) extends to an optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A choice is certified safe when a verified transformation inserts it into a certified optimum without increasing the objective.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem with objective \(c\).
\(X\) has an independent certificate of optimality and extends \(A\).
Feasibility of \(X'\), extension of \(A\cup\{e\}\), and the objective comparison are verifiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The enlarged partial choice \(A\cup\{e\}\) extends to an optimal solution.

children.title: Matroid Greedy Characterization
children.top_down_role: Landmark boundary connecting universal weighted greedy correctness with exchange structure.

children.title: Matroid Feasible-Object Regimes
children.top_down_role: Greedy characterization across maximal and fixed-rank feasible objects.

children.title: Independent-Set Regime
children.top_down_role: Greedy behavior over hereditary feasible families without fixed cardinality.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Set Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rado–Edmonds greedy theorem for maximizing nonnegative weight over matroid independent sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and let \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\). Process elements in nonincreasing order of weight and add an element exactly when independence is preserved. The resulting set \(G\in\mathcal I\) maximizes \(w(I)=\sum_{e\in I}w(e)\) over all \(I\in\mathcal I\). Conversely, if a nonempty hereditary system \((E,\mathcal I)\) has this greedy-optimality property for every nonnegative weight function, then \((E,\mathcal I)\) satisfies the augmentation axiom and is a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy maximizes every nonnegative additive weight over independent sets exactly for hereditary systems that are matroids.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal I\) is nonempty and hereditary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Greedy is universally optimal over \(\mathcal I\) if and only if \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.

notation.meaning: sum of element weights in I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and independent-set regime are appropriate, and the forward matroid result is standard. The converse must specify whether universal optimality covers every permitted tie-breaking or an equivalent precise greedy convention, and it needs a Rado–Edmonds theorem locator.

children.title: Basis Regime
children.top_down_role: Greedy behavior over maximal feasible objects of common rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight basis form of the finite matroid greedy theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\) be arbitrary. Process all elements in nonincreasing order of weight, accepting an element whenever independence is preserved, until a maximal independent set \(B_G\) is obtained. Every maximal independent set of a matroid is a basis, and \(B_G\) satisfies \(w(B_G)\geq w(B)\) for every basis \(B\) of \(M\). Unlike independent-set maximization, arbitrary negative weights are permitted because every feasible basis has the same cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scanning arbitrary weights from largest to smallest and preserving independence produces a maximum-weight matroid basis.
assumptions_latex: \(w:E\to\mathbb R\) is additive, with ties resolved arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The greedy output \(B_G\) is a maximum-weight basis of \(M\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the basis regime, and the arbitrary-real-weight maximum-basis statement is correct for finite matroids. No authoritative theorem locator is supplied.

children.title: Maximality-to-Rank Transition
children.top_down_role: Structural passage from arbitrary independent objects to fixed-rank bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximality-to-Rank Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroid augmentation turns inclusion maximality into maximum cardinality within every restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid, let \(X\subseteq E\), and let \(I\subseteq X\) be independent and inclusion-maximal among the independent subsets of \(X\). Then \(|I|=r_M(X)\), where \(r_M(X)=\max\{|J|:J\subseteq X,\ J\in\mathcal I\}\). Consequently, every maximal independent subset of \(X\) is a basis of the restriction \(M|X\), and all such subsets have equal cardinality. This property can fail in a hereditary system that does not satisfy matroid augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a matroid restriction, every inclusion-maximal independent set has maximum possible size and therefore realizes the rank.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq E\), and \(I\subseteq X\) is inclusion-maximal independent in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|I|=r_M(X)\), so \(I\) is a basis of \(M|X\).

children.title: Greedy Weight-Order Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dependence of the characterization on weight and priority models.

children.title: Weighted Greedy Regime
children.top_down_role: Greedy characterization under assigned element weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Greedy Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-ordered greedy algorithm for a finite matroid, with independent-set and basis output conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), an independence oracle, and weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). For maximum-weight independent-set optimization, discard elements of negative weight; for maximum-weight basis optimization, retain all elements. Sort the retained elements so that \(w(e_1)\geq\cdots\geq w(e_m)\), initialize \(S_0=\varnothing\), and set \(S_i=S_{i-1}\cup\{e_i\}\) exactly when this union lies in \(\mathcal I\). After the scan, output \(S_m\). The output is respectively a maximum-weight independent set or a maximum-weight basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort matroid elements by decreasing weight and accept every independence-preserving element; discard negative weights only when a basis is not required.
assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid accessed by an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned set is optimal for the selected independent-set or basis regime.

notation.meaning: accepted set after processing i elements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the weighted greedy regime, and the independent-set and basis conventions are explicitly distinguished rather than conflated. The optimality claims require a specific finite-matroid greedy theorem locator.

children.title: Priority-Ordering Regime
children.top_down_role: Greedy behavior governed by externally specified element priorities.

knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Ordering Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy construction on a finite matroid under a fixed total priority order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and let \(e_1\succ e_2\succ\cdots\succ e_m\) be a total priority order on \(E\). Initialize \(G_0=\varnothing\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), set \(G_i=G_{i-1}\cup\{e_i\}\) if this set belongs to \(\mathcal I\), and otherwise set \(G_i=G_{i-1}\). Output \(G_m\). The output is the lexicographically greatest basis with respect to the priority order. If the order is nonincreasing in weights, then the output is a maximum-weight basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan elements from highest to lowest priority, accepting each feasible element. On a matroid this produces the lexicographically greatest basis and, for weight-ordered priorities, a maximum-weight basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_m\) is the lexicographically greatest basis; a nonincreasing weight order makes \(G_m\) maximum-weight.

notation.meaning: greedy set after processing the first i elements

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Tie-Breaking Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of greedy outcomes or guarantees on equal-priority choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Breaking Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective invariance, but possible solution nonuniqueness, under equal-weight orderings in matroid greedy optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid with weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). Run the greedy basis algorithm using any total order satisfying \(w(e)>w(f)\Rightarrow e\) precedes \(f\). Every permissible ordering of elements tied in weight produces a basis \(B\) satisfying \(w(B)=\max\{w(B'):B'\text{ is a basis of }M\}\). Different tie-breaking orders may produce different bases, but their total weights coincide. Thus tie-breaking affects the selected optimizer, not the optimal objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary ordering within equal-weight classes can change the greedy basis, but every resulting matroid basis has the same optimal total weight.
assumptions_latex: The scan order is nonincreasing in \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every tie-breaking rule returns a maximum-weight basis, although the returned basis need not be unique.

notation.meaning: sum of element weights over basis B

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly distinguishes optimizer sensitivity from objective-value invariance under equal-weight tie breaking and fits the exact leaf. No source or specific locator is supplied for the matroid greedy theorem on which it depends.

children.title: Nonmatroid Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Independence systems lacking the exchange structure needed for universal greedy correctness.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmatroid Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal weight-ordered greedy correctness fails exactly when a finite independence system violates matroid exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite hereditary independence system that is not a matroid. Then there exist \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) with \(|I|<|J|\) and \(I\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I\) for every \(e\in J\setminus I\). Assign weight \(1+\varepsilon\) to elements of \(I\), weight \(1\) to elements of \(J\setminus I\), and weight \(0\) otherwise, where \(\varepsilon>0\) is sufficiently small. Weight-ordered greedy can first select all of \(I\), after which it rejects every element of \(J\setminus I\), while \(J\) has greater weight. Hence universal greedy optimality fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exchange violation admits weights for which greedy commits to a smaller independent set and rejects every improving element, while another feasible set has greater total weight.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal I\) is nonempty and hereditary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a nonnegative weight function for which weight-ordered greedy is not optimal over \(\mathcal I\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary construction is mathematically credible: augmentation failure and sufficiently small positive epsilon make J heavier than I, while a compatible weight order can commit greedy to I. The selected failure_boundary kind fits the topic, but the universal characterization and counterweight construction require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Decomposition Dynamic Programming Family
children.top_down_role: Methods exploiting state structure, subproblem composition, separators, and bounded interfaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization form with an incumbent upper bound and valid lower bounds for subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a collection of active subproblems. Select an active subproblem $F_i$. If $F_i$ is infeasible, delete it; otherwise compute its bound $b(F_i)$. If $b(F_i)\ge U$, delete $F_i$. If $b(F_i)<U$, either solve $F_i$ optimally or partition it into further subproblems and add those subproblems to the active collection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain active subproblems and select one. Delete it if it is infeasible. Otherwise compute its bound. Delete it when the bound is at least the incumbent upper bound; when the bound is strictly smaller, either solve the subproblem optimally or partition it and activate the resulting subproblems.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ is the incumbent objective-value upper bound for a minimization problem}
b(F_i)\text{ is a valid lower bound for subproblem }F_i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_i\text{ is pruned if it is infeasible or }b(F_i)\ge U;\text{ otherwise it is solved or branched into active descendants.}

children.title: State-Resource Dynamic Programming Coupling

children.title: State-Space Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: Dynamic programs organized around explicit combinatorial configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward dynamic programming on a finite acyclic state-transition graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite state set whose feasible transitions form a directed acyclic graph. For each terminal state \(s\), set \(F(s)=g(s)\). Process nonterminal states in reverse topological order and compute \[F(s)=\operatorname{opt}_{a\in A(s)}\bigl(c(s,a)+F(T(s,a))\bigr),\] where \(\operatorname{opt}\) is either minimum or maximum consistently. Store an optimizing action at every processed state. Starting from the initial state \(s_0\), follow stored actions until a terminal state is reached; the resulting policy or path has value \(F(s_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate terminal states, process the acyclic state graph backward, and store an optimal transition at each state. Following stored transitions reconstructs an optimal solution.
assumptions_latex: The state-transition graph is finite and acyclic.
Costs are additively separable across transitions and terminal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The backward recurrence returns the optimal value \(F(s_0)\) and stored actions reconstruct an optimizer.

notation.meaning: optimal continuation value from state s

children.title: Resource-Indexed Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: Dynamic programs indexed by bounded budgets, capacities, or numerical resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Indexed Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon dynamic programming indexed by an integral resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stages \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and integral budgets \(b\in\{0,\ldots,B\}\), let action \(a\in A_i\) consume \(r_i(a)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and yield value \(v_i(a)\). Initialize \(F(0,b)=0\). For increasing \(i\), compute \[F(i,b)=\max_{a\in A_i:\,r_i(a)\le b}\bigl(F(i-1,b-r_i(a))+v_i(a)\bigr).\] Record an optimizing action for each reachable entry. Output \(F(n,B)\), and backtrack through recorded actions to recover an optimal resource-feasible selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Index the table by stage and remaining integral budget. Each transition chooses an action, subtracts its resource use, and adds its value.
assumptions_latex: Resource consumptions and budget \(B\) are nonnegative integers.
Stage rewards are additive and feasibility is determined by total resource consumption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(n,B)\) equals the maximum value attainable with total resource consumption at most \(B\).

notation.meaning: best value through stage i with budget b
resource consumed by action a at stage i
value of action a at stage i

children.title: State-Resource Coupling
children.top_down_role: Dynamic programs whose state dimensions jointly encode structure and resource consumption.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Resource Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bellman states augmented by a discrete resource coordinate when continuation feasibility depends on remaining capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\in S\) describe the structural state and let \(b\in\{0,\ldots,B\}\) be remaining resource. If action \(a\in A(s)\) has resource consumption \(r(s,a)\), immediate value \(c(s,a)\), and successor \(T(s,a)\), then the coupled value function satisfies \[F(s,b)=\operatorname{opt}_{a\in A(s):\,r(s,a)\le b}\bigl(c(s,a)+F(T(s,a),b-r(s,a))\bigr).\] Terminal values are specified for every terminal pair \((s,b)\). The resource coordinate is necessary whenever two histories reaching the same structural state permit different feasible continuations because they leave different resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augment each structural state with remaining resource. Transitions update both coordinates, preserving exactly the history information needed for future feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The structural state is Markovian once remaining resource is included.
Resource consumption is additive and discretely indexed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The product state \((s,b)\) admits a Bellman recurrence that distinguishes continuation sets with different remaining resources.

notation.meaning: optimal continuation value from the coupled state

children.title: Canonical State-Index Dynamic Programming Family

children.title: Subset Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: State organizations indexed by selected or remaining subsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic programming whose states are subsets and whose transitions remove or add one admissible element.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite ground set and let \(F(S)\) denote the optimal value for the subproblem indexed by \(S\subseteq U\). Set \(F(\varnothing)=\beta\). Process subsets in increasing cardinality and compute \[F(S)=\operatorname{opt}_{x\in A(S)}\bigl(F(S\setminus\{x\})+c(S,x)\bigr),\] where \(A(S)\subseteq S\) contains exactly the elements that may be last in a feasible solution for \(S\). Store an optimizing \(x\), output \(F(U)\), and repeatedly remove stored elements to reconstruct an optimizer. Explicit enumeration uses \(2^{|U|}\) subset states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute each subset state from smaller subsets by choosing an admissible last element. Stored choices reconstruct an optimal ordering or subset-structured solution.
assumptions_latex: Optimal solutions admit decomposition by an admissible last element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence computes the optimum for \(U\) using at most \(2^{|U|}\) subset states.

notation.meaning: optimal value for subset state S
admissible final elements for state S

children.title: Interval Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: State organizations indexed by contiguous ranges or nested spans.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up optimization over contiguous intervals with split-based composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ordered input indexed by \(1,\ldots,n\), let \(F(i,j)\) be the optimal value for interval \([i,j]\). Initialize singleton or empty intervals by the problem's base values. For lengths \(\ell=2,\ldots,n\), compute every interval with \(j-i+1=\ell\) using \[F(i,j)=\operatorname{opt}_{i\le k<j}\Phi_{i,k,j}\bigl(F(i,k),F(k+1,j)\bigr),\] where \(\Phi_{i,k,j}\) includes the cost of combining the two subsolutions. Record an optimizing split \(k\). Output \(F(1,n)\) and recursively follow stored splits to reconstruct an optimal decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve short contiguous intervals first, then combine two adjacent subintervals across every possible split. Stored split points reconstruct an optimal decomposition.
assumptions_latex: Every nontrivial feasible interval solution decomposes at a split point.
The objective of a split is determined by its two subproblem values and combination term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bottom-up recurrence computes \(F(1,n)\), the optimal value for the full interval.

notation.meaning: optimal value on interval from i through j

children.title: Sequence Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: State organizations based on prefixes, suffixes, or ordered positions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequence Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prefix-indexed dynamic programming with a finite summary state for sequence decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the input positions be \(1,\ldots,n\), let \(Q\) be a finite summary-state set, and let \(\delta(q,a)\) be the state reached by action \(a\) from state \(q\). Initialize \(F(0,q_0)=0\) and \(F(0,q)=+\infty\) for \(q\ne q_0\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), compute \[F(i,q)=\min_{q'\in Q,\,a:\,\delta(q',a)=q}\bigl(F(i-1,q')+c_i(q',a)\bigr).\] Store minimizing predecessors, choose a permitted terminal state of minimum value, and backtrack to recover an optimal action sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process prefixes in order while retaining a finite state summarizing all relevant past decisions. Predecessor pointers recover an optimal action sequence.
assumptions_latex: The summary state makes future feasibility and costs independent of earlier history.
The total cost is additive across sequence positions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence yields a minimum-cost feasible action sequence over all \(n\) positions.

notation.meaning: minimum cost for the first i positions ending in state q

children.title: Graph-Decomposition Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: State composition over trees, separators, and bounded-width graph representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Decomposition Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Table dynamic programming over a rooted tree decomposition with bounded boundary-state complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\{X_t\}_{t\in V(T)})\) be a rooted tree decomposition of a graph \(G\) of width \(k\). For each node \(t\), construct a table \(D_t\) indexed by realizable boundary summaries \(\sigma\) on bag \(X_t\). Process \(T\) bottom-up: introduce nodes extend compatible child summaries, forget nodes optimize over discarded boundary information, and join nodes combine compatible child entries while correcting duplicated bag contributions. At the root, optimize over accepting summaries and follow stored choices to reconstruct a solution. If each bag has at most \(f(k)\) summaries, a direct implementation uses \(O(|V(T)|f(k)^2)\) combination time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree decomposition localizes graph interactions to bags. Bottom-up tables combine compatible boundary summaries, yielding fixed-parameter running time when the number of summaries depends only on width.
assumptions_latex: A rooted tree decomposition of width \(k\) is supplied.
Feasibility and objective contributions compose through finite bag-boundary summaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatible table composition returns an optimal solution in \(O(|V(T)|f(k)^2)\) time under direct pairwise joins.

notation.meaning: upper bound on boundary summaries per bag

children.title: Numeric Dynamic Programming Approximation Interface

children.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Dynamic Programming
children.top_down_role: Dynamic programs polynomial in numerical magnitudes rather than encoded length alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numeric dynamic programs polynomial in magnitudes of integer data but not necessarily in their bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an integer-valued optimization instance with ordinary combinatorial size \(n\) and a nonnegative numeric parameter \(B\) encoded in binary. A dynamic program with \(O(nB)\) states and polynomial work per state is pseudo-polynomial: its running time is polynomial in \(n\) and the magnitude \(B\), but may be exponential in the input length because \(B\) can be as large as \(2^{\Theta(\log B)}\). It is polynomial-time only when \(B\) is polynomially bounded in the remaining input size or is encoded in unary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A table polynomial in a numeric bound is pseudo-polynomial because the bound's magnitude can be exponential in its binary encoding length.
assumptions_latex: The numeric parameter \(B\) is a nonnegative integer encoded in binary.
The dynamic program has \(O(nB)\) states and polynomial work per state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is polynomial in \(n\) and \(B\), but not necessarily polynomial in the binary input length \(n+\log B\).

notation.meaning: binary encoding length up to constant factors

children.title: Scaling Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Connections from numerical state compression to controlled optimization accuracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value scaling converts a magnitude-dependent exact dynamic program into a polynomial approximation scheme under bounded additive loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a maximization problem selecting at most \(n\) objects with nonnegative values \(v_i\), and suppose an exact dynamic program is polynomial in the sum of integral values. Let \(v_{\max}\) be the value of a feasible singleton, choose \(K=\varepsilon v_{\max}/n\), and define \(v_i'=\lfloor v_i/K\rfloor\). Run the exact dynamic program using \(v_i'\), but return the selected solution evaluated under the original values. If \(v_{\max}\le\mathrm{OPT}\), rounding loses less than \(nK\le\varepsilon\mathrm{OPT}\); hence the returned value is at least \((1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\), while the scaled total is at most \(n^2/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round values to a coarser scale before running an exact numeric dynamic program. The smaller table becomes polynomial in inverse accuracy while losing at most an epsilon fraction.
assumptions_latex: At most \(n\) objects are selected and all values are nonnegative.
The exact dynamic program is polynomial in the total scaled value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaling yields value at least \((1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\) with scaled numeric range at most \(n^2/\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: scaled integral value of object i

source_refs.locator: Polynomial Time Approximation of Real Numbers p. 33

Moreover, the generic problem class is not specified sufficiently to ensure that optimizing the rounded objective returns a solution to which the stated rounding-loss comparison applies. An authoritative approximation-algorithms source with a theorem/section locator and a precisely defined problem class is required.

children.title: Approximation-Scheme Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Scheme Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic conversion of pseudo-polynomial dynamic programming into an approximation scheme by geometric value scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a maximization problem with nonnegative integral item values, optimum [1m[0m\(\mathrm{OPT}>0\), and a pseudo-polynomial dynamic program whose running time is polynomial in the input length and the largest scaled total value. Given [1m[0m\(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choose a computable bound [1m[0m\(L\leq \mathrm{OPT}\leq U\) with [1m[0m\(U/L\) polynomially bounded, set [1m[0m\(K=\varepsilon L/n\), and replace each value [1m[0m\(v_i\) by [1m[0m\(\widehat v_i=\lfloor v_i/K\rfloor\). If the dynamic program optimizes exactly over the scaled instance and its states preserve feasibility, the returned feasible solution has value at least [1m[0m\((1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\), with running time polynomial in the input length and [1m[0m\(1/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling objective values can turn a suitable pseudo-polynomial dynamic program into an FPTAS, provided feasibility survives scaling and rounding loss is bounded by an epsilon fraction of optimum.
assumptions_latex: The scaled dynamic program is exact and polynomial in \(|I|\) and the scaled value bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(S)\geq(1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\) in time \(\operatorname{poly}(|I|,1/\varepsilon)\).

The complexity-bound kind fits the approximation-scheme interface, but the generic theorem is not reliable as written.

children.title: Dynamic Programming Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failure boundaries caused by large interfaces, long-range dependence, or unbounded state dimensions.

children.title: State Explosion
children.top_down_role: Complexity barriers caused by excessive numbers or dimensions of states.

knowledge_statements.title: State Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential growth of distinguishable dynamic-programming states despite a polynomial number of decomposition stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a decomposition have [1m[0m\(m\) stages and an interface [1m[0m\(B_k\) at stage [1m[0m\(k\). Suppose every subset [1m[0m\(S\subseteq B_k\) can occur as a partial-solution signature and, for any distinct [1m[0m\(S,T\subseteq B_k\), some completion is feasible or has a different optimum after signature [1m[0m\(S\) but not after [1m[0m\(T\). Any exact dynamic program that merges partial solutions only when all completions treat them identically must therefore retain at least [1m[0m\(2^{|B_k|}\) states at stage [1m[0m\(k\). Consequently, polynomially many stages do not imply polynomial running time when interface size is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every interface subset has distinguishable future behavior, an exact dynamic program needs exponentially many states even when it has only polynomially many stages.
assumptions_latex: All \(2^{|B_k|}\) subset signatures are realizable and pairwise completion-distinguishable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact state space at stage \(k\) has cardinality at least \(2^{|B_k|}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the counting conclusion is plausible under pairwise completion distinguishability. However, the condition saying a completion is feasible or has a different optimum after one signature but not the other is not formally defined, and no source supports the chosen state-equivalence model.

children.title: Nonseparable Dependence
children.top_down_role: Failure of useful subproblem composition under long-range interactions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonseparable Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of bounded-state decomposition when future contributions depend on the entire partial solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decomposition cut, let [1m[0m\(P\) denote a partial solution and [1m[0m\(Q\) a completion. A state map [1m[0m\(\sigma\) is sufficient only if [1m[0m\(\sigma(P_1)=\sigma(P_2)\) implies that, for every admissible [1m[0m\(Q\), feasibility of [1m[0m\(P_1\cup Q\) equals feasibility of [1m[0m\(P_2\cup Q\) and their objective contributions differ by a constant independent of [1m[0m\(Q\). If every pair of distinct partial solutions is separated by some completion, this implication forces [1m[0m\(\sigma\) to be injective. Thus no compression into fewer states than partial solutions is exact; exponential many partial solutions yield exponential state complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic programming cannot compress partial solutions when some future completion distinguishes every pair by feasibility or relative objective value.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition combines partial solutions \(P\) with admissible completions \(Q\).
Every distinct \(P_1,P_2\) is distinguished by at least one completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every exact sufficient state map \(\sigma\) is injective on the partial solutions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container. A source is needed for the exact sufficient-state equivalence being asserted, including the admissible completion domain and the convention under which objective contributions may differ by a completion-independent constant.

children.title: Interface-Width Barriers
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of decomposition when separators or boundary states become too large.

knowledge_statements.title: Interface-Width Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-space lower bound induced by a decomposition interface carrying independent binary information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an exact dynamic program over a decomposition with an interface of width [1m[0m\(w\). If each interface element carries an independent binary condition and all [1m[0m\(2^w\) assignments are realizable and pairwise distinguishable by completions, then every completion-sufficient state representation contains at least [1m[0m\(2^w\) states. Any implementation explicitly processing every such state requires [1m[0m\(\Omega(2^w)\) time and space at that interface. Hence a running-time form [1m[0m\(f(w)\operatorname{poly}(n)\) is polynomial only when [1m[0m\(f(w)\) is polynomially bounded on the admitted instances; for [1m[0m\(f(w)=2^w\), this includes [1m[0m\(w=O(\log n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interface encoding independent binary choices forces at least two-to-the-width states; exponential-width dependence is polynomial only for logarithmic width.
assumptions_latex: All binary interface assignments are realizable and pairwise completion-distinguishable.
The implementation explicitly stores and processes each sufficient state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Time and space are \(\Omega(2^w)\); if \(w=O(\log n)\), then \(2^w=\operatorname{poly}(n)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary distinguishability argument is plausible but lacks a source and a formal interface model. In this exact terminal container the primary role is a dynamic-programming failure boundary, not merely a complexity bound; a sourced replacement should use content_kind failure_boundary while retaining the quantitative lower bound.

children.title: Augmentative Improvement Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Methods that improve feasible objects through paths, cycles, residual systems, or exchanges.

children.title: Augmenting-Path Methods
children.top_down_role: Improvement families based on path-shaped certificates.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with source \(s\in V\), sink \(t\in V\), and integral capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\).
\(x:E\to\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\) is a feasible integral \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
Residual capacities are defined relative to the current flow \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates, and the output \(x\) is a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-path augmentation for feasible single-commodity flows with integral capacities.

source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Elements of network optimization p. 95

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed network \(G=(V,E)\), integral capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\), a source \(s\in V\), a sink \(t\in V\), and a feasible integral flow \(x\), form the residual network with forward residual capacity \(u_{ij}-x_{ij}\) and reverse residual capacity \(x_{ij}\). While an \(s\)-\(t\) residual path \(P\) exists, set \(\delta=\min_{a\in P}r_a\), increase the flow by \(\delta\) on forward arcs of \(P\), and decrease it by \(\delta\) on reverse arcs. When no such path exists, output \(x\). The procedure terminates, and the final flow is maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly send the bottleneck amount along a source-to-sink residual path. With integral capacities the process terminates, and when no such path remains the feasible flow is maximum.

children.title: Alternating-Path Methods
children.top_down_role: Improvement methods organized around alternating path structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Path Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality augmentation for matchings using paths alternating between unmatched and matched edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite graph [1m[0m\(G=(V,E)\) and a matching [1m[0m\(M\), find a simple path [1m[0m\(P\) whose endpoints are unmatched by [1m[0m\(M\) and whose edges alternate between [1m[0m\(E\setminus M\) and [1m[0m\(M\), beginning and ending outside [1m[0m\(M\). If such a path exists, replace [1m[0m\(M\) by [1m[0m\(M\triangle E(P)\), which is a matching of cardinality [1m[0m\(|M|+1\), and repeat. If no augmenting path exists, output [1m[0m\(M\); by Berge's criterion, it is a maximum-cardinality matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flip matching status along an alternating path between exposed vertices. Each flip adds one matched edge, and absence of such a path characterizes maximum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\triangle E(P)\) has size \(|M|+1\); absence of an augmenting path implies maximum cardinality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and matching statement fit the leaf, and the mathematical claim is standard. No inspectable source locator is supplied for Berge's criterion or the augmentation method, so the record cannot be accepted at candidate-review status.

children.title: Alternating-Cycle Methods
children.top_down_role: Improvement methods organized around alternating cycle structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Cycle Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-preserving exchange along even cycles alternating relative to a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let [1m[0m\(M\) be a matching in a finite graph and let [1m[0m\(C\) be an even cycle whose edges alternate between [1m[0m\(M\) and [1m[0m\(E\setminus M\). Then [1m[0m\(M'=M\triangle E(C)\) is a matching with [1m[0m\(|M'|=|M|\). For edge weights [1m[0m\(w:E\to\mathbb R\), the objective change is [1m[0m\(w(M')-w(M)=w(C\setminus M)-w(C\cap M)\). Thus flipping an alternating cycle is a strict improvement for maximum-weight matching exactly when the total weight of its unmatched edges exceeds that of its matched edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flipping an alternating even cycle preserves matching cardinality; it improves weight exactly when entering edges outweigh leaving edges.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a matching in a finite graph.
\(C\) is an even cycle alternating between unmatched and matched edges.
\(w:E\to\mathbb R\) is additive over edge sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M'=M\triangle E(C)\) is a matching, \(|M'|=|M|\), and \(w(M')-w(M)=w(C\setminus M)-w(C\cap M)\).

notation.meaning: sum of edge weights over an edge set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is acceptable for this feasibility-preserving alternating-cycle exchange, and the displayed weight identity is precise. An authoritative source with a section, theorem, or page locator is still required.

children.title: Alternating-Forest Methods
children.top_down_role: Search organizations maintaining branching collections of alternating structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Forest Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forest-based simultaneous search for matching augmentations, including blossom contraction in general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite graph [1m[0m\(G\) and matching [1m[0m\(M\), initialize a rooted forest at all [1m[0m\(M\)-exposed vertices, labeling roots even. From an even vertex, scan unmatched edges. Reaching an unreached matched vertex adds that edge and its unique matched edge, assigning odd and even labels. An edge joining even vertices in different trees yields an augmenting path. In a general graph, an edge joining even vertices in one tree yields an odd blossom, which is contracted while the search continues. Expand contracted blossoms after augmentation, replace [1m[0m\(M\) by its symmetric difference with the recovered path, and stop when no augmentation exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow alternating trees from exposed vertices; either recover an augmenting path or contract an odd blossom, then expand blossoms after augmentation.
assumptions_latex: Blossom contraction and expansion preserve correspondence of augmenting paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each recovered augmentation increases \(|M|\) by one; exhaustion of the search yields a maximum-cardinality matching.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the compressed blossom-search description relies on a nontrivial contraction-and-lifting invariant and on search exhaustion implying absence of augmenting paths. Those claims require an authoritative algorithm source and a sufficiently specific locator.

children.title: Residual-Network Methods
children.top_down_role: Improvement frameworks expressed through residual feasibility structures.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed multigraph with capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\).
\(x:E\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) is feasible and satisfies \(0\leq x_e\leq u_e\) for every \(e\in E\).
Residual arcs are tagged by their originating arc, so antiparallel original arcs remain distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Capacity-feasible residual circulations represent exactly the capacity-feasible adjustments of \(x\) that preserve its node imbalances.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual representation of capacity-feasible, imbalance-preserving adjustments to a directed flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible flow on a finite directed multigraph \(G=(V,E)\) with capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\). For each original arc \(e=(i,j)\), the residual network \(G_x\) contains a tagged forward residual arc of capacity \(u_e-x_e\) when this quantity is positive and a tagged reverse residual arc of capacity \(x_e\) when \(x_e>0\). Every capacity-feasible residual circulation \(y\) defines a capacity-feasible adjustment of \(x\), obtained by adding flow carried on tagged forward arcs and subtracting flow carried on tagged reverse arcs, and this adjustment preserves all node imbalances. Conversely, if \(x'\) is another feasible flow with the same node imbalances as \(x\), then \(x'-x\) admits such a representation by a capacity-feasible circulation in \(G_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual network records tagged opportunities to increase or decrease each original arc flow. Its capacity-feasible circulations correspond exactly to feasible adjustments that preserve the current node imbalances.

children.top_down_role: Objective-improvement frameworks based on feasible circulations or cycles.

assumptions_latex: The network is finite, capacities are integral and bounded, and \(x\) is a feasible integral circulation.
Each residual reverse arc has the negative of its originating arc's cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates at a minimum-cost feasible circulation.

notation.meaning: sum of residual arc costs on \(C\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative-cycle cancellation for linear-cost feasible circulations with integral capacities.

source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Elements of network optimization p. 95

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite network with integral capacities, linear arc costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R\), and a feasible integral circulation \(x\), assign each forward residual arc its original cost and each reverse residual arc the negative of its originating arc's cost. While the residual network contains a directed cycle \(C\) with \(c(C)<0\), set \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}r_a\) and augment \(\delta\) units around \(C\). This preserves flow conservation, integrality, and capacity feasibility and changes total cost by \(\delta c(C)<0\). Because the bounded integral network has finitely many feasible integral circulations, the procedure terminates. When no negative-cost residual cycle exists, the resulting circulation is minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integral capacitated circulation, repeatedly cancel a negative-cost residual cycle by its bottleneck amount. Every cancellation preserves feasibility and lowers cost; the finite process stops at a minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Improvement Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible circulation with linear arc costs, and let \(G_x\) be its residual network with residual arc costs \(c^x\). The circulation \(x\) is minimum-cost if and only if \(G_x\) contains no directed cycle of negative residual cost. Equivalently, there exists a vertex potential \(\pi:V\to\mathbb R\) such that every residual arc \((i,j)\) satisfies \(c^x_{ij}+\pi_i-\pi_j\geq0\). Feasibility of \(x\), together with such a potential, is a polynomially checkable optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible circulation is minimum-cost exactly when its residual network has no negative-cost directed cycle, equivalently when vertex potentials make every residual reduced cost nonnegative.

children.title: Exchange-Graph Augmentation

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Graph Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic augmentation using directed exchanges between elements of a feasible set and its complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let [1m[0m\(E\) be finite, [1m[0m\(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) a feasible family, and [1m[0m\(S\in\mathcal F\). Construct a directed exchange graph whose vertices encode elements of [1m[0m\(S\) and [1m[0m\(E\setminus S\), with an arc whenever the corresponding elementary removal-addition transition is admissible; add source and sink incidences for admissible initial and terminal exchanges. Find a directed source-to-sink path [1m[0m\(P\), translate its ordered exchanges into an update [1m[0m\(S'\), and verify [1m[0m\(S'\in\mathcal F\) and objective improvement. Repeat until no improving path exists. Optimality from path absence requires a problem-specific exchange theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent admissible element swaps by directed arcs, follow a source-to-sink exchange path, and apply its exchanges; feasibility and optimality require problem-specific exchange laws.
assumptions_latex: Exchange arcs correctly encode admissible elementary transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An improving exchange path produces a feasible improved set \(S'\); path absence certifies optimality only under an additional exchange theorem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the topic, but for an arbitrary feasible family the elementary arcs, source and sink incidences, ordered path-to-update operation, and feasibility invariant are not defined by the supplied data. The record correctly acknowledges that optimality is problem-specific, but an authoritative instantiated exchange-graph source is needed before a reliable mathematical statement can be selected.

children.title: Augmentation Optimality Boundary
children.top_down_role: Optimality witnesses from absent augmentations and boundaries involving cycling or infinitesimal progress.

children.title: Augmentation Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Optimality evidence based on the absence of admissible improving augmentations.

knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate for finite minimization under an augmentation-complete neighborhood system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite feasible set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(A(x)\subseteq X\) be the admissible augmentations from \(x\). Assume augmentation completeness: whenever \(x\) is not globally optimal, some \(y\in A(x)\) satisfies \(f(y)<f(x)\). Then
\[
x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in X}f(z)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(y)\ge f(x)\ \text{for every }y\in A(x).
\]
Thus a feasible point \(x\), together with verifiable inequalities \(f(y)\ge f(x)\) for all admissible augmentations, is an optimality certificate relative to an augmentation-complete system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a complete augmentation system, a feasible solution is globally optimal exactly when no admissible augmentation improves its objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is optimal if and only if \(f(y)\ge f(x)\) for every \(y\in A(x)\).

notation.meaning: set of feasible augmentations available from x

children.title: Cycling Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where repeated augmentations revisit prior states without durable progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycling Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal cycling example for non-strict augmentative improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\{a,b\}\), let \(f(a)=f(b)=0\), and define \(A(a)=\{b\}\) and \(A(b)=\{a\}\). An augmentation rule that accepts non-increasing moves and selects the unique available augmentation produces
\[
a,b,a,b,\ldots,
\]
although the objective never improves. Hence acceptance of non-strict augmentations does not imply finite termination, even on a finite feasible set. A strict-decrease rule or an anti-cycling rule that forbids this repeated-state mechanism is sufficient to exclude the displayed cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing equal-value augmentations can make a finite-state method alternate forever unless strict progress or an anti-cycling rule excluding repeated states is imposed.
assumptions_latex: The augmentation rule accepts moves satisfying \(f(y)\le f(x)\).
No visited-state or anti-cycling restriction is enforced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated sequence is periodic and does not terminate.

children.title: Infinitesimal-Progress Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where improving augmentations fail to yield adequate discrete progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinitesimal-Progress Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict improvement without a uniform progress bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\in\mathbb{N},\ n\ge1\}\), let \(f(x)=x\), and permit from \(x_n=1/n\) only the augmentation \(x_n\mapsto x_{n+1}=1/(n+1)\). Starting from \(x_1\), every iteration strictly decreases the objective because \(f(x_{n+1})<f(x_n)\), yet no finite iterate equals the unique minimizer \(0\). Therefore strict descent alone does not ensure finite termination on an infinite feasible set; a positive progress bound, discreteness condition, or separate convergence argument is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly improving steps may shrink toward zero and approach an optimum forever without attaining it in finitely many iterations.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set may be infinite.
No uniform positive lower bound on objective improvement is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_n)\downarrow0\), but \(x_n\ne0\) for every finite \(n\).

children.title: Complementary-Slackness-Guided Methods
children.top_down_role: Exact optimization families maintaining compatible primal and dual structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary-Slackness-Guided Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual stopping principle for standard-form linear optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal problem \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\). A complementary-slackness-guided method maintains or constructs primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\), and modifies them until
\[
x_j\bigl(c_j-(A^{\mathsf T}y)_j\bigr)=0\qquad\text{for every }j.
\]
At that stopping point, \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\); weak duality then makes \(x\) primal optimal and \(y\) dual optimal. Thus feasibility plus complementary slackness is an exact termination certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal-dual methods become exact when feasible primal and dual solutions satisfy complementary slackness, forcing equality of their objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complementary slackness implies \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\) and optimality of both solutions.

notation.meaning: vector of dual slacks or reduced costs

children.title: Dual Price-Update Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Methods driven by improvements in dual prices or potentials.

children.title: Dual-Ascent Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods organized around monotone improvement of dual-side objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Ascent Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible ascent scheme for a concave dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a dual problem \(\max\{q(y):y\in D\}\), initialize any \(y^0\in D\). At iteration \(k\), an ascent oracle either certifies that \(y^k\) maximizes \(q\) over \(D\), or returns a feasible update \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\alpha_k d^k\in D\) satisfying \(q(y^{k+1})>q(y^k)\), where \(\alpha_k>0\). In the latter case continue; in the former stop and output \(y^k\) and the dual value \(q(y^k)\). For a primal minimization problem, every iterate supplies the valid lower bound \(q(y^k)\le p^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual ascent repeatedly makes feasible dual updates that increase the dual objective; every iterate gives a lower bound for primal minimization.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) is a concave dual function on the feasible set \(D\).
The ascent oracle returns a strict feasible improvement or a valid optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual values strictly increase before termination, and each satisfies \(q(y^k)\le p^*\).

children.title: Price-Adjustment Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods organized around changes to prices or potentials guiding primal choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Price-Adjustment Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path price adjustment on the reachable part of a residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite residual digraph with reduced arc costs \(c_\pi(u,v)=c(u,v)+\pi(u)-\pi(v)\ge0\), and fix a source \(s\in V\). Let \(R\subseteq V\) be the vertices reachable from \(s\), and for each \(v\in R\) let \(d(v)\) be its shortest-path distance from \(s\) under \(c_\pi\). Define
\[
\pi'(v)=\begin{cases}\pi(v)+d(v),&v\in R,\\\pi(v),&v\notin R.\end{cases}
\]
For every residual arc \((u,v)\in E\) with \(u,v\in R\),
\[
c_{\pi'}(u,v)=c_\pi(u,v)+d(u)-d(v)\ge0.
\]
Moreover, every arc \((u,v)\) satisfying \(d(v)=d(u)+c_\pi(u,v)\) is tight under the updated prices. The price-adjustment step outputs \(\pi'\) with these reachable-region properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shortest-path distances adjust the prices of reachable vertices, preserve nonnegative reduced costs on residual arcs between reachable vertices, and make shortest-path predecessor arcs tight.
assumptions_latex: Each updated vertex belongs to the reachable set \(R\) and therefore has finite distance from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \((u,v)\in E\) with \(u,v\in R\), the update satisfies \(c_{\pi'}(u,v)\ge0\).

notation.meaning: set of vertices reachable from the designated source

children.title: Dual-Progress Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degeneracy, stalled improvement, or scaling effects limiting price-based progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Progress Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stalling caused by an update family that cannot express joint ascent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\max\{y_1+y_2:y_1-y_2\le0,\ y_2-y_1\le0,\ 0\le y_1\le1,\ 0\le y_2\le1\}.
\]
At \(y=(0,0)\), increasing either coordinate alone violates one equality-inducing constraint, so a dual method restricted to positive single-coordinate adjustments reports no feasible improving update. Nevertheless the joint direction \(d=(1,1)\) is feasible up to step length \(1\) and reaches the optimum \((1,1)\). Thus absence of progress within a restricted price-update family need not certify dual optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual method can stall below optimum when its allowed updates omit a feasible improving joint direction.
assumptions_latex: Updates may increase at most one coordinate per iteration.
A stalled update search is not supplemented by a global dual-optimality test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coordinatewise stalling occurs at \((0,0)\), although the optimal dual value is attained at \((1,1)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restricted-coordinate stalling example is mathematically valid and fits the failure-boundary container, but no source or locator supports the stated boundary phenomenon.

children.title: Reduced-Cost Methods
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial optimization methods guided by costs transformed through dual information.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative-cycle cancellation for integral minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an integral feasible circulation \(x\) with integral capacities and costs, form its residual digraph and assign each residual arc its residual cost \(c_x(a)\). If the residual digraph contains a directed cycle \(C\) with \(\sum_{a\in C}c_x(a)<0\), augment \(x\) around \(C\) by the minimum residual capacity on \(C\), then rebuild the residual digraph. Stop when no negative-cost residual cycle exists and output \(x\). The stopping condition is equivalent to optimality of the feasible circulation; integrality keeps all generated circulations integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cycle cancellation improves an integral feasible circulation along negative residual cycles and stops exactly when no such improving cycle remains.
assumptions_latex: Capacities, costs, and the initial feasible circulation are integral.
The problem is a finite capacitated minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When no negative residual cycle exists, the current circulation \(x\) is minimum-cost.

notation.meaning: cost of residual arc a at x

children.title: Feasible-Potential Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods maintaining potentials compatible with dual feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Potential Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential invariant and optimality principle for minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible circulation \(x\), let \(G_x\) be its residual digraph. A vertex potential \(\pi\) is feasible when every residual arc \((u,v)\) satisfies
\[
c_\pi(u,v)=c_x(u,v)+\pi(u)-\pi(v)\ge0.
\]
Summing reduced costs around any directed residual cycle cancels all potential terms, so every residual cycle then has nonnegative original cost. Consequently no improving circulation augmentation exists and \(x\) is minimum-cost. Feasible-potential methods preserve these inequalities while modifying the primal circulation and use their joint satisfaction as the optimality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible-potential methods maintain nonnegative residual reduced costs; when the condition holds on every residual arc, it excludes negative cycles and certifies minimum cost.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi\) is defined on every residual-network vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(c_\pi(u,v)\ge0\) on every residual arc, then \(x\) is minimum-cost.

notation.meaning: residual digraph of the circulation x

children.title: Cost-Potential Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural links between transformed costs, feasible potentials, and admissible improvements.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Potential Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-sensitive complementary-slackness condition for capacitated minimum-cost flow with nonfixed arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be a feasible flow on a finite directed network with arc costs \(c_a\), strictly separated bounds \(\ell_a<u_a\), and vertex potentials \(\pi\). Define
\[
\bar c_a=c_a+\pi(\operatorname{tail}(a))-\pi(\operatorname{head}(a)).
\]
Cost-potential compatibility requires, for every arc \(a\),
\[
x_a=\ell_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\ge0,\qquad
\ell_a<x_a<u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a=0,\qquad
x_a=u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\le0.
\]
Equivalently, every forward and backward residual arc has nonnegative reduced cost. A feasible flow and potential satisfying these conditions certify that the flow is minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each nonfixed arc, reduced cost is nonnegative at its lower bound, zero in its interior, and nonpositive at its upper bound; these compatibility conditions certify minimum cost.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) satisfies flow conservation and \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every arc \(a\).
Every arc has strictly separated bounds \(\ell_a<u_a\).
Potentials \(\pi\) are unrestricted real vertex labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed sign conditions are equivalent to nonnegative reduced costs on all residual arcs and imply minimum cost of \(x\).

notation.meaning: strictly separated lower and upper bounds on arc flow

children.title: Lagrangian Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Problem representations formed by pricing selected constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound representation for constrained minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
p^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
For multipliers \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), define the Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)\) and the relaxed value
\[
q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda).
\]
Every primal-feasible \(x\) satisfies \(L(x,\lambda)\le f(x)\), hence \(q(\lambda)\le p^*\). Maximizing \(q(\lambda)\) over nonnegative multipliers gives the Lagrangian dual bound \(d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)\le p^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalizing relaxed inequalities with nonnegative multipliers yields a tractable infimum that lower-bounds a minimization problem’s optimal value.
assumptions_latex: The primal problem is a minimization problem with constraints \(g_i(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(\lambda)\le d^*\le p^*\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\).

children.title: Lagrangian Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Objective bounds supported by feasible multiplier choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain certificate for a Lagrangian lower bound and optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be finite and consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\). A certificate consists of \(\lambda\ge0\), a point \(z\in X\), and the value
\[
q=L(z,\lambda)=\min_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda).
\]
The equality can be verified by evaluating \(L(x,\lambda)\ge q\) for all \(x\in X\). Then every primal-feasible \(x\) satisfies \(f(x)\ge q\), so \(q\) is a certified lower bound. If a feasible point \(\hat x\) also satisfies \(f(\hat x)=q\), then \(\hat x\) is optimal and the primal-dual gap is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative multiplier and verified relaxed minimizer certify a lower bound; a feasible solution attaining it is globally optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda\ge0\), and all relaxed inequalities have the form \(g_i(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\le p^*\); moreover, \(f(\hat x)=q\) for feasible \(\hat x\) certifies optimality.

notation.meaning: verified minimizer of the Lagrangian over X

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Decomposition Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable minimization with linear coupling constraints and a Lagrangian master problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the primal problem be \(\min\{\sum_{k=1}^q c_k^{\mathsf T}x_k:\sum_{k=1}^q A_kx_k=b,\ x_k\in X_k\}\), where each \(X_k\) is nonempty. Dualizing only the coupling equality with multiplier \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\) gives
\[g(\lambda)=-\lambda^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_{k=1}^q\inf_{x_k\in X_k}(c_k^{\mathsf T}+\lambda^{\mathsf T}A_k)x_k.\]
Thus evaluation of \(g(\lambda)\) decomposes into \(q\) independent subproblems, while the master interface computes \(\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}g(\lambda)\). Every finite \(g(\lambda)\) is a lower bound on the primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing shared linear constraints separates the problem into independent block subproblems; a multiplier master problem maximizes their combined lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The primal objective is bounded below whenever a finite optimal value is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(\lambda)\le p^*\) for every \(\lambda\) with finite \(g(\lambda)\), and evaluating \(g\) separates across the blocks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-pivot simplex algorithm for an inequality-form LP, initialized at a vertex with a nonsingular active basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and a vertex \(x\) of \(P=\{z:Az\le b\}\), choose \(J\) with \(|J|=n\), \(A_J\) nonsingular, and \(A_Jx=b_J\). Define \(y\) by \(y^{\top}A=c^{\top}\) and \(y_k=0\) outside \(J\). If \(y\ge0\), return \((x,y)\). Otherwise choose the least \(i\in J\) with \(y_i<0\), and choose \(w\) satisfying \(A_{J\setminus\{i\}}w=0\) and \(a_iw=-1\). If \(Aw\le0\), return \(w\). Otherwise let \(\lambda=\min\{(b_j-a_jx)/(a_jw):a_jw>0\}\), choose the least minimizing \(j\), replace \(J\) by \((J\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}\), set \(x\leftarrow x+\lambda w\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a vertex and nonsingular active basis, compute the corresponding dual multipliers. Return primal and dual feasible vectors when the multipliers are nonnegative; otherwise use least-index leaving and entering choices to pivot, or return an improving recession direction when no blocking constraint exists.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb R^m,\quad c\in\mathbb R^n
x\in P:=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:Az\le b\}\text{ is a vertex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns either }(x,y)\text{ with }x\in P,\ y\ge0,\ y^{\top}A=c^{\top},\text{ or }w\text{ with }Aw\le0\text{ and }c^{\top}w>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The stated least-index simplex algorithm terminates after at most \(\binom{m}{n}\) iterations. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). Start from a basis matrix \(B\) with nonbasic index set \(N\), \(x_B=B^{-1}b\ge0\), and \(x_N=0\). At each iteration compute \(y^{\mathsf T}=c_B^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}\) and \(\bar c_j=c_j-y^{\mathsf T}A_j\) for \(j\in N\). If every \(\bar c_j\ge0\), return the current basic feasible solution. Otherwise select \(j\in N\) with \(\bar c_j<0\), set \(d=B^{-1}A_j\), and, when some \(d_i>0\), select a leaving basic index by minimizing \((x_B)_i/d_i\) over those indices, using the fixed anticycling rule to break ties. Pivot and repeat. If no \(d_i>0\), return the ray \(r\in\mathbb R^n\) defined by \(r_j=1\), \(r_B=-d\), and all other components zero; it satisfies \(Ar=0\), \(r\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}r=\bar c_j<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal simplex maintains primal feasibility, enters a variable with negative reduced cost, and uses the ratio test to preserve nonnegativity. It terminates at an optimum or returns a feasible improving ray proving unboundedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). Start from a basis matrix \(B\) with nonbasic index set \(N\), basic values \(x_B=B^{-1}b\), and reduced costs \(\bar c_j=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}A_j\ge0\) for every \(j\in N\). If \(x_B\ge0\), return the current optimal solution. Otherwise select a row \(r\) with \((x_B)_r<0\) according to the fixed anticycling rule. For \(\bar a_{rj}=(B^{-1}A_j)_r\), select an entering index from \(\{j\in N:\bar a_{rj}<0\}\) minimizing \(\bar c_j/(-\bar a_{rj})\), with ties resolved by that rule, and pivot. If the eligible set is empty, return the resulting primal-infeasibility certificate. Repeating these pivots preserves nonnegative reduced costs and, under the finite anticycling rule, terminates at an optimal basis or with primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual simplex maintains dual feasibility while repairing negative basic variables. With a finite anticycling rule, it terminates at an optimal basis or produces a primal-infeasibility certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Revised Simplex Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-factorization implementation of primal simplex without storing a full tableau.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), maintain a nonsingular basis \(B\) and a factorization permitting solves with \(B\) and \(B^{\mathsf T}\). Compute \(x_B=B^{-1}b\), solve \(B^{\mathsf T}y=c_B\), and price nonbasic columns by \(\bar c_j=c_j-A_j^{\mathsf T}y\). If all \(\bar c_j\ge0\), return \(x\). Otherwise choose \(j\) with \(\bar c_j<0\), solve \(Bd=A_j\), apply the primal ratio test, replace the leaving basis column by \(A_j\), and update or refactor the basis factors. The generated basis sequence equals that of tableau simplex under identical pivot choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Revised simplex reproduces simplex pivots using linear solves and updated basis factors instead of maintaining the complete tableau.
assumptions_latex: The initial basis is nonsingular and primal feasible.
Basis solves and factor updates are performed exactly for the mathematical algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Identical entering and leaving choices produce the same bases as primal tableau simplex.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Variant Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility- and representation-based choice among simplex variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear program and a proposed initial basis, select the pivot regime from the maintained invariant. If \(B^{-1}b\ge0\), primal simplex can preserve primal feasibility. If the reduced costs satisfy \(\bar c_N\ge0\), dual simplex can preserve dual feasibility. If both conditions hold, the basis is already optimal. If neither holds, a feasibility-restoration phase or another initialization procedure is required before either invariant-preserving method applies. Independently, revised implementations are appropriate when basis solves and sparse factorization updates are preferable to storing the full tableau; this implementation choice does not alter the underlying primal or dual feasibility invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose primal or dual simplex according to which feasibility invariant the initial basis satisfies; choose revised storage according to the desired linear-algebra representation.
assumptions_latex: The linear program is expressed in equality form with nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal feasibility selects a primal regime, dual feasibility selects a dual regime, and absence of both requires initialization.

children.title: Simplex Initialization

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase-I construction of a primal-feasible basis for equality-form linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), first multiply rows by \(-1\) where necessary so that \(b\ge0\). Introduce artificial variables \(a\ge0\) and solve the Phase-I problem
\[\min\{\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}a:Ax+a=b,\ x\ge0,\ a\ge0\},\]
starting from the artificial basis. If its optimum is positive, declare the original system infeasible. If the optimum is zero, pivot zero-valued artificial basic variables out whenever possible; delete redundant rows when no original-column pivot exists. Remove all artificial columns and return the resulting feasible basis for the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phase I adds artificial variables, minimizes their sum, and either constructs an original feasible basis or certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Phase I is solved to optimality with a terminating pivot rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero Phase-I optimum yields a feasible original basis after cleanup; a positive optimum proves infeasibility.

children.title: Basis Degeneracy
