knowledge_statements.title: Basis Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of a basic feasible solution in standard equality form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\) has row rank \(m\). A feasible basis \(B\) defines \(x_B=B^{-1}b\) and \(x_N=0\). This basic feasible solution is degenerate with respect to \(B\) exactly when at least one component of \(x_B\) is zero. Equivalently, fewer than \(m\) basic variables are strictly positive. A feasible point is a degenerate vertex when it has a feasible basis exhibiting this condition; consequently, multiple bases may represent the same vertex, and a zero-length pivot may change the basis without changing the feasible point or objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic feasible solution is degenerate when at least one basic variable equals zero, allowing basis changes that do not move the represented vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) consists of \(m\) linearly independent columns of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy holds if and only if \((B^{-1}b)_i=0\) for some basic index \(i\).

children.title: Anticycling Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Anticycling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of simplex under Bland's least-index pivot rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider simplex applied to a finite-dimensional standard-form linear program. At each nonoptimal primal-feasible basis, choose as entering variable the eligible nonbasic variable of smallest index, and among all ratio-test minimizers choose as leaving variable the eligible basic variable of smallest index. Then no basis can recur. Because only finitely many bases exist, the algorithm terminates after finitely many pivots, either at an optimal basis or with a valid unboundedness conclusion. The assertion remains relevant under degeneracy, where arbitrary eligible pivot choices can otherwise revisit a previous basis and cycle indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bland's least-index choices prevent repeated bases, so simplex terminates finitely even when degenerate pivots are possible.
assumptions_latex: The linear program has finitely many variables and constraints.
Entering and leaving choices follow Bland's least-index rule consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No basis repeats, and the simplex run terminates after finitely many pivots.

notation.meaning: A simplex basis, drawn from finitely many column subsets.

children.title: Initialization Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Obstructions arising from infeasible, unstable, or poorly conditioned starting structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Initialization Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which direct primal-simplex initialization or Phase I cannot supply a feasible basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Direct primal simplex cannot start from a proposed nonsingular basis \(B\) when \(B^{-1}b\not\ge0\), because its primal-feasibility invariant already fails. Phase I separates this recoverable initialization failure from infeasibility: for
\[\min\{\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}a:Ax+a=b,\ x\ge0,\ a\ge0\},\]
a strictly positive optimal value means that no \(x\ge0\) satisfies \(Ax=b\), so no primal-feasible basis exists. For example, \(x=-1\) with \(x\ge0\) is infeasible, and every Phase-I construction retains positive artificial mass. A zero optimum may still require removal of zero artificial basic variables or redundant rows before ordinary simplex begins.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible proposed basis only blocks direct initialization; a positive Phase-I optimum establishes that no feasible basis exists at all.
assumptions_latex: Rows have been sign-normalized so the displayed artificial basis is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B^{-1}b\not\ge0\) blocks direct primal initialization, while a positive Phase-I optimum certifies infeasibility.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal B\) contains precisely the size-\(m\) column bases admitted by the chosen feasibility regime.
For the network specialization, the underlying graph is finite and connected after orientations are ignored, and one incidence-matrix row is deleted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every admissible single-column basis pivot corresponds to an edge of \(H\); for a reduced node-arc incidence matrix, these edges are spanning-tree exchanges.

notation.meaning: Reduced node-arc incidence matrix in the network specialization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis adjacency represented as an exchange graph, with reduced-incidence bases specialized to spanning trees.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.6. The Network Simplex Algorithm p. 232
Chapter 3. Elements of network optimization p. 95

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have row rank \(m\), and let \(\mathcal B\) be the family of size-\(m\) column index sets whose submatrices are nonsingular and satisfy the chosen feasibility condition. Define the basis-exchange graph \(H\) with vertex set \(\mathcal B\), joining \(B,B'\in\mathcal B\) when \(|B\setminus B'|=|B'\setminus B|=1\). Every admissible simplex pivot that replaces one basis column moves along an edge of \(H\); a degenerate pivot may traverse such an edge while representing the same polyhedral vertex. For a connected directed graph, delete one row of its node-arc incidence matrix to obtain the full-row-rank reduced incidence matrix \(\widetilde D\). Its column bases correspond to spanning trees, and exchanging one basis column amounts to adding one non-tree arc, forming its fundamental cycle, and deleting one tree arc from that cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Admissible bases form an exchange graph in which simplex pivots replace one column. For a connected graph's reduced incidence matrix, bases are spanning trees and pivots are tree-edge exchanges along fundamental cycles.
knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Pivoting Structures

children.title: Network-Simplex Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Simplex structure specialized to network optimization settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Simplex Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-basis simplex interface for minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible minimum-cost flow with a spanning-tree basis, compute node potentials \(\pi\) so every basic arc \((u,v)\) has zero reduced cost \(\bar c_{uv}=c_{uv}+\pi_u-\pi_v\). If all nonbasic arcs satisfy the appropriate reduced-cost sign at their active lower or upper bounds, output the flow. Otherwise choose a violating nonbasic arc and insert it into the tree, creating a unique fundamental cycle. Augment flow around that cycle until an arc reaches a bound, delete a bound-reaching cycle arc to restore a spanning tree, update potentials, and repeat. With an anticycling rule, finite termination yields an optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network simplex prices arcs with node potentials and pivots by adding an arc, augmenting on its fundamental cycle, and deleting a saturated tree arc.
assumptions_latex: The network-flow instance has a feasible tree-structured basis.
Arc bounds and supplies are finite where required by the pivot.
A deterministic anticycling rule handles degenerate pivots.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination with no reduced-cost violation yields an optimal feasible flow.

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of arc from u to v.

children.title: Graph-Induced Basis Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between graph objects, feasible bases, and admissible pivots.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Induced Basis Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spanning-tree characterization of bases of a connected graph's reduced incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected directed graph, let \(D\in\mathbb R^{V\times E}\) be its node-arc incidence matrix, and delete one row to obtain \(\widetilde D\). Then \(\operatorname{rank}(\widetilde D)=|V|-1\). For any \(T\subseteq E\) with \(|T|=|V|-1\), the square submatrix \(\widetilde D_T\) is nonsingular if and only if the underlying undirected edges in \(T\) form a spanning tree of \(G\). Consequently, linear-programming bases of the reduced flow-conservation equations correspond exactly to spanning trees, before bound-status data for nonbasic arcs are added.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonsingular column bases of a connected graph's reduced incidence matrix are exactly its spanning trees.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and connected after arc orientations are ignored.
\(D\) uses one \(+1\) and one \(-1\) in each non-loop arc column.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det(\widetilde D_T)\neq0\) if and only if \(T\) is a spanning tree.

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix with one row deleted.
A set of candidate basis arcs.

children.title: Network Pivot Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate or repetitive pivot behavior specific to graph-structured bases.

assumptions_latex: The entering arc and current tree determine a fundamental cycle \(C\) and its unit signed augmentation direction \(d\in\{-1,0,1\}^{E}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pivot is degenerate exactly when \(\theta=0\); then \(x+\theta d=x\), although a basis exchange may occur.

notation.meaning: fundamental cycle created by the entering arc

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy for a primal network-simplex pivot on a capacitated minimum-cost flow basis.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Network Flow Algorithms - An Overview p. 20
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible tree solution on an arc set \(E\), and let a nonbasic entering arc induce a fundamental cycle \(C\). Orient \(C\) in the augmentation direction and define \(d\in\{-1,0,1\}^{E}\) by \(d_e=1\) on forward cycle arcs, \(d_e=-1\) on backward cycle arcs, and \(d_e=0\) off \(C\). The maximal feasible step is \[\theta=\min\bigl(\{u_e-x_e:e\in C,\ d_e=1\}\cup\{x_e-\ell_e:e\in C,\ d_e=-1\}\bigr).\] The network pivot is degenerate exactly when \(\theta=0\). In that case an arc attaining the minimum may leave the tree, so the basis may change while the primal flow remains \(x+\theta d=x\) and its objective value is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network pivot is degenerate when its maximum feasible augmentation around the oriented fundamental cycle is zero. The tree basis may then change even though the flow and objective value do not.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Pivot Degeneracy

children.title: Central-Cut Ellipsoid Methods
children.top_down_role: Ellipsoid localization based on cuts passing through the current center.

knowledge_statements.title: Central-Cut Ellipsoid Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One exact-arithmetic update for a halfspace whose boundary passes through the ellipsoid center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an ellipsoid \(E(a,A)=\{x:(x-a)^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}(x-a)\le1\}\), where \(A\succ0\), and a central cut \(g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le0\) with \(g\ne0\). Set \[q=\frac{Ag}{\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}},\qquad a^+=a-\frac{q}{n+1},\qquad A^+=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\left(A-\frac{2}{n+1}\frac{Agg^{\mathsf T}A}{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\right).\] Replace \(E(a,A)\) by \(E(a^+,A^+)\). The latter contains \(E(a,A)\cap\{x:g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le0\}\); iteration stops under the prescribed feasibility, volume, or accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect the current ellipsoid with a center-passing halfspace and replace it by the displayed smaller enclosing ellipsoid, repeating until the chosen stopping test holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(a,A)\cap\{x:g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le0\}\subseteq E(a^+,A^+)\).

notation.meaning: ellipsoid with center a and positive-definite shape matrix A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Definiteness and Norm Bounds for Ellipsoid Iterates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and magnitude bounds for iterates of the preceding finite-precision central-cut ellipsoid method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\), \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), \(x_0\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), and \(R\in\mathbb{Q}_+\) with \(R\ge2\). Suppose \((A_k,x_k)\) is generated by the stated finite-precision ellipsoid method with \(A_0=R^2I\) and \(p=\left\lceil6N+\log(9n^3)\right\rceil\). For every \(k\in\{0,1,\ldots,N\}\), \(A_k\) is positive definite and \[\|x_k\|\le \|x_0\|+R2^k,\qquad \|A_k\|\le R^2 2^k,\qquad \|A_k^{-1}\|\le R^{-2}4^k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every generated shape matrix remains positive definite, and the center, matrix, and inverse-matrix norms satisfy the stated exponential bounds.
assumptions_latex: (A_k,x_k)\text{ are generated by the stated finite-precision ellipsoid iteration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_k\succ0,\quad \|x_k\|\le\|x_0\|+R2^k,\quad \|A_k\|\le R^2 2^k,\quad \|A_k^{-1}\|\le R^{-2}4^k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-Volume Enclosing Ellipsoid of a Central Half-Ellipsoid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact enclosing-ellipsoid formula for a halfspace cut whose boundary passes through the ellipsoid center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\), \(A=A^\top\succ0\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\). Define \[E'=\{z\in E(A,x):a^\top z\ge a^\top x\},\qquad b=\frac{Aa}{\sqrt{a^\top Aa}}.\] The minimum-volume ellipsoid containing \(E'\) is \(E(A',x')\), where \[A'=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\left(A-\frac{2}{n+1}bb^\top\right),\qquad x'=x+\frac{1}{n+1}b.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The displayed rank-one shape update and center shift give the minimum-volume ellipsoid enclosing the retained central half of an ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(A',x')\text{ is the minimum-volume ellipsoid containing }\{z\in E(A,x):a^\top z\ge a^\top x\}

children.title: Deep-Cut Ellipsoid Methods
children.top_down_role: Ellipsoid localization using separators positioned beyond the current center.

knowledge_statements.title: Deep-Cut Ellipsoid Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic update for a normalized cut that strictly excludes the current center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(E(a,A)\), \(A\succ0\), and a valid cut \(g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le-\alpha\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\), where \(g\ne0\) and \(0<\alpha<1\). Put \(q=Ag/\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\) and set \[a^+=a-\frac{1+n\alpha}{n+1}q,\qquad A^+=\frac{n^2(1-\alpha^2)}{n^2-1}\left(A-\frac{2(1+n\alpha)}{(n+1)(1+\alpha)}\frac{Agg^{\mathsf T}A}{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\right).\] Then replace the current ellipsoid by \(E(a^+,A^+)\), which contains the cut intersection; stop according to the specified feasibility or accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deep cut excludes the current center by positive normalized depth; the displayed update encloses the surviving intersection more tightly than the corresponding central update.
assumptions_latex: The target set lies in the displayed halfspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(a,A)\cap\{x:g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le-\alpha\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\}\subseteq E(a^+,A^+)\).

children.title: Ellipsoid Cut-Strength Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes distinguishing central cuts from stronger separating cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoid Cut-Strength Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized classification of parallel ellipsoid cuts by signed displacement from the center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E(a,A)\) with \(A\succ0\) and \(g\ne0\), write a parallel cut uniquely in normalized form \[g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le-\alpha\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}.\] Its signed parameter classifies its strength: \(\alpha=0\) is central; \(0<\alpha<1\) is deep; and \(-1/n<\alpha<0\) is shallow but yields a strict ellipsoidal volume reduction under the standard update. At \(\alpha=-1/n\) that update returns the original ellipsoid, while \(\alpha\le-1/n\) supplies no strict progress guarantee from this update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized signed offset alpha classifies a cut as central, deep, or shallow and identifies when the standard ellipsoid update guarantees strict progress.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha>0\) is deep, \(\alpha=0\) central, and \(-1/n<\alpha<0\) shallow with strict standard-update progress.

notation.meaning: signed cut offset measured in the ellipsoid norm

children.title: Deep-Cut Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Geometric limits on safely exploiting stronger cut information.

knowledge_statements.title: Deep-Cut Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric boundary for the normalized deep-cut update, including empty and lower-dimensional intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E(a,A)\) be full-dimensional and consider \(g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le-\alpha\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\). For \(0\le\alpha<1\), the surviving intersection can be full-dimensional and the standard deep-cut shape matrix is positive definite. If \(\alpha=1\), the intersection is at most the single boundary point \(a-Ag/\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\); if \(\alpha>1\), it is empty. Consequently, the full-dimensional deep-cut update is valid only for \(\alpha<1\), and the limiting or empty cases require separate termination or dimension-reduction handling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized depth below one permits a full-dimensional update; depth one leaves at most one boundary point, and greater depth makes the ellipsoid-cut intersection empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha=1\) gives an intersection of dimension zero or less, and \(\alpha>1\) gives the empty intersection.

source_refs.locator: Section 3.2, The Central-Cut Ellipsoid Method, p. 86

source_witnesses.locator: Section 3.2, The Central-Cut Ellipsoid Method, p. 86

children.title: Shallow-Cut Ellipsoid Methods
children.top_down_role: Ellipsoid variants accommodating weak geometric separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Shallow-Cut Ellipsoid Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ellipsoid update accepting a weak cut whose retained halfspace contains the current center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(E(a,A)\), \(A\succ0\), and a valid shallow cut \(g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le\beta\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\), where \(g\ne0\) and \(0<\beta<1/n\). Set \(q=Ag/\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\) and \[a^+=a-\frac{1-n\beta}{n+1}q,\qquad A^+=\frac{n^2(1-\beta^2)}{n^2-1}\left(A-\frac{2(1-n\beta)}{(n+1)(1-\beta)}\frac{Agg^{\mathsf T}A}{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\right).\] Replace \(E(a,A)\) by \(E(a^+,A^+)\). The new ellipsoid contains the retained intersection and has strictly smaller volume.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently shallow valid cut may contain the old center yet still supports a strict-volume-reduction ellipsoid update when its normalized weakness is below one over the dimension.
assumptions_latex: The target set satisfies the displayed cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(a,A)\cap\{x:g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le\beta\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\}\subseteq E(a^+,A^+)\) and \(\det A^+<\det A\).

children.title: Implicit Optimization Oracle Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Ellipsoid methods as engines for optimization over implicitly described regions.

children.title: Implicit Feasible-Region Optimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization settings where feasible regions are accessed without explicit constraint listings.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a possibly empty bounded rational polytope represented by a specified exact oracle model.
The rational encoding and geometric bounding conventions of the oracle model are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Return \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\), or certify \(P=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear optimization over a bounded rational polytope accessed through a specified oracle rather than explicit inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact implicit feasible-region optimization problem consists of a rational objective \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), a possibly empty bounded rational polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) represented by a specified exact oracle, and rational encoding and geometric bounds sufficient for that oracle model. Its task is to certify \(P=\varnothing\), or to return \(x^\star\in P\) satisfying \[c^{\mathsf T}x^\star=\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}.\] Weak optimization is a distinct problem and requires separately specified feasibility, objective, norm, and oracle-error tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the exact model, optimize a rational linear objective over a bounded rational polytope given through an exact oracle, returning an exact optimizer or certifying that the polytope is empty. Weak optimization requires a separately specified tolerance model.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Feasible-Region Optimization

children.title: Separation-Oracle Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions that use separation access to support implicit optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Oracle Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong optimization from strong separation for well-described rational polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a bounded rational polytope with known polynomial encoding and bounding data. Suppose a strong separation oracle, on rational input \(y\), either asserts \(y\in P\) or returns rational \((a,\beta)\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in P\). Then, for every \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), the ellipsoid method solves strong linear optimization over \(P\), or detects \(P=\varnothing\), using a number of oracle calls and rational arithmetic operations polynomial in the dimension and input encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a suitably encoded bounded rational polytope, strong separation oracle access suffices to solve exact linear optimization in oracle-polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a bounded rational polytope with polynomially bounded description and geometric data.
The separation oracle returns polynomially encoded strong separators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong optimization over \(P\) is polynomial-time reducible to strong separation over \(P\).

children.title: Optimization-Oracle Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions connecting optimization access to other oracle capabilities.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Oracle Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation from strong optimization for well-described rational polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty bounded rational polytope with known polynomial encoding and bounding data. Suppose a strong optimization oracle returns, for each \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), a point maximizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\) and the exact optimum value. Then strong separation for rational query points is computable with polynomially many oracle calls and rational arithmetic operations: for each \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\), the reduction either confirms \(y\in P\) or produces rational \((a,\beta)\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for all \(x\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a well-described rational polytope, an exact linear-optimization oracle can be used to implement exact separation in oracle-polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty bounded rational polytope with polynomially bounded encoding data.
The optimization oracle returns exact rational optimum data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation over \(P\) is polynomial-time reducible to strong optimization over \(P\).

children.title: Oracle Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation and complexity conditions governing equivalence among oracle models.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a well-described bounded rational polytope.
Strong separation and strong optimization use exact rational inputs and outputs with polynomially bounded encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SEP}_{\mathrm{strong}}(P)\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{strong}}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial oracle equivalence in the strong rational-polyhedral regime and the boundary against transferring it to unmatched oracle models.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.4, Equivalence of Strong Optimization and Separation, p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every well-described bounded rational polytope \(P\), strong separation and strong linear optimization are mutually polynomial-time oracle reducible: \[\operatorname{SEP}_{\mathrm{strong}}(P)\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{strong}}(P).\] This conclusion is model-specific: it does not imply an equivalence after replacing either side by a weak oracle, omitting polynomial encoding bounds, or allowing uncontrolled oracle error. Any weak equivalence requires its own matched accuracy, norm, geometric-radius, and error hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong separation and exact linear optimization are polynomially equivalent for well-described bounded rational polytopes. The theorem does not transfer automatically to weak or mismatched oracle models.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Equivalence Regimes

children.title: Ellipsoid Numerical Validity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Dependence on rational size, geometric bounds, precision, and separation quality.

children.title: Rational Encoding Size
children.top_down_role: Input-length effects arising from rational polyhedral data.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Encoding Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary input length used by rational polyhedral and ellipsoid complexity bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(z\), define \(\langle z\rangle=1+\lceil\log_2(|z|+1)\rceil\). For a reduced rational \(r=p/q\) with \(q>0\), define \(\langle r\rangle=\langle p\rangle+\langle q\rangle\). The encoding size of a rational vector or matrix is the sum of its entries' encoding sizes together with dimensions and structural indices. An oracle algorithm is polynomial-time in rational input data only when its arithmetic-operation count and every intermediate and output bit length are bounded polynomially in this total encoding size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational encoding size counts the binary lengths of reduced numerators and denominators; polynomial-time claims must also control intermediate and output bit lengths.
assumptions_latex: Every rational is stored in reduced numerator-denominator form with positive denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Input length is the summed binary encoding length, and bit complexity must be polynomial in that length.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of an integer
binary encoding length of a reduced rational

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Encoding-Size Bound for an Optimal Integral Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a small-encoding optimum when optimization over the integer hull attains its maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb Q^n:Ax\le b\}\) be a rational polyhedron. If \(\max\{c^Tx:x\in P_I\}\) has an optimal solution, then it has an optimal integral solution \(x\) satisfying \(\operatorname{size}(x)\le 13n\bigl(\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(b)\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever linear optimization over the integer hull of a rational polyhedron attains an optimum, an optimal integral solution exists whose encoding size is at most 13n times the combined encoding size of A and b.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb Q^n:Ax\le b\}\text{ is a rational polyhedron}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\in P_I\cap\mathbb Z^n:\ x\text{ is optimal and }\operatorname{size}(x)\le 13n\bigl(\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(b)\bigr).

children.title: Geometric Bounding Data
children.top_down_role: Outer-radius, inner-radius, and dimensional information relevant to localization.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and represented in a feasibility-oracle model.
Euclidean balls and rationally encoded centers and radii are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The supplied data satisfy \(K\subseteq B(a_0,R)\) and \(K\ne\varnothing\Longrightarrow B(a_1,r)\subseteq K\), with polynomially bounded encodings and \(\log_2(R/r)\).

notation.meaning: closed Euclidean ball centered at a with radius rho
inner radius bound for the nonempty branch
rational centers for the outer and inner balls

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner- and outer-radius promises supporting finite ellipsoid iteration bounds for empty-or-full-dimensional convex feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex feasibility instance \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has usable full-dimensional geometric bounding data when rational centers \(a_0,a_1\in\mathbb Q^n\) and rational radii \(0<r\le R\) are supplied with the promise \[K\subseteq B(a_0,R),\qquad K\ne\varnothing\Longrightarrow B(a_1,r)\subseteq K.\] The data are polynomially usable when the binary encodings of \(a_0,a_1,r,R\) and the quantity \(\log_2(R/r)\) are polynomially bounded by the instance length. This promise excludes nonempty lower-dimensional feasible sets; handling such sets requires a separately specified affine-hull or width model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Usable full-dimensional bounding data give an encoded outer ball and promise an encoded inner ball whenever the convex set is nonempty, with a polynomially controlled radius ratio. Nonempty lower-dimensional sets require a separate model.

children.title: Finite-Precision Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by approximate arithmetic and finite numerical representation.

assumptions_latex: The feasible region is a bounded convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
Every computed separating inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\) has coefficient error at most \(\eta\), and every ellipsoid update has cumulative arithmetic error at most \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-precision validity requires explicit error budgets and geometric margins.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical validity boundary for oracle-based ellipsoid iterations, not a floating-point implementation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a queried point \(y\notin K\), suppose the exact oracle admits a normalized valid cut \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}y-\beta\geq\gamma>0\). A finite-precision oracle and update remain logically valid only when their certified errors are smaller than the available separation and containment margins; in particular, a sufficient local requirement is \(\eta+\rho<\gamma\). If no positive lower bound on \(\gamma\) is available, or if rounding can move a retained point of \(K\) outside the computed halfspace, the usual exact-arithmetic volume-reduction argument does not certify feasibility, infeasibility, or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ellipsoid guarantees survive finite precision only when certified oracle and update errors stay below the available separation and containment margins.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the scalar condition η+ρ<γ is not justified by the stated error model: coefficient error needs a norm and a bound on relevant points, while update error and cut violation must be expressed in compatible units. The cited optimization-from-separation section does not specifically support this finite-precision condition. A source and a precise numerical model are required.

children.title: Separation-Quality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence on the accuracy and reliability of separating information.

assumptions_latex: The feasible region is a convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
The oracle is queried at \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only cuts satisfying the stated validity and depth conditions support the corresponding ellipsoid guarantee.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact, weak, and unusable separation responses.

source_refs.locator: * 6.4 Equivalence of Strong Optimization and Separation p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact separation response at \(y\) is either the assertion \(y\in K\), or a pair \((a,\beta)\) with \(a\neq0\), \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\) for every \(x\in K\), and \(a^{\mathsf T}y>\beta\). A weak response with tolerance \(\varepsilon\) may instead certify \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\leq\varepsilon\), or return a cut whose promised violation is at least the specified tolerance. A cut that excludes a feasible point, has uncertified coefficient error, or has depth below the algorithm's required threshold cannot be used to invoke the corresponding optimization-from-separation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A usable separator must be valid for every feasible point and must separate the query by the depth required by the chosen oracle model.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Quality Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: * 6.4 Equivalence of Strong Optimization and Separation p. 174

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and exact-separation portion fit the leaf. The cited sections must be inspected to determine the supported formulation.

children.title: Encoding-to-Geometry Transfer
children.top_down_role: Connections between symbolic input size and usable geometric bounds.

assumptions_latex: The polytope is \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\), where \(A\) and \(b\) are rational.
The total binary encoding length of \((A,b)\) is \(L\).
The affine hull is handled explicitly when \(P\) is not full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rational encoding bounds yield polynomial bit-length and geometric bounds needed by ellipsoid algorithms.

notation.meaning: a polynomial depending on dimension and encoding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard rational-polyhedral transfer via determinant and encoding-length bounds.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimization over Polyhedra: A Preview p. 157

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a polynomial \(p\) such that every vertex of \(P\), when it exists, has rational coordinates of binary length at most \(p(n,L)\). If \(P\) is bounded, then \(P\subseteq B(0,2^{p(n,L)})\). If \(P\) is nonempty and full-dimensional, determinant bounds also provide a point \(z\in P\) and a radius \(r\geq2^{-p(n,L)}\) with \(B(z,r)\subseteq P\). Thus rational input size supplies polynomially encoded outer and inner geometric bounds; without full dimensionality, the inner-ball assertion must be made relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial rational encoding bounds vertex bit lengths and supplies exponential-scale inner and outer radii with polynomial logarithms.

children.title: Constraint-Generation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Restricted formulations expanded through newly identified constraints.

assumptions_latex: The full problem is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in X,\ g_j(x)\leq0\ \forall j\in J\}\), with finite or implicitly represented \(J\).
A separation routine can find a violated constraint or certify that none exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination without a violated constraint returns an optimum of the full formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact constraint generation for a minimization problem with implicit constraints.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Constraint Generation for Combinatorial-Optimization Problems p. 171
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(J_0\subseteq J\). At iteration \(t\), solve the restricted master \(x^t\in\arg\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in X,\ g_j(x)\leq0\ \forall j\in J_t\}\). Apply the separation routine to \(x^t\). If it returns \(j_t\in J\) with \(g_{j_t}(x^t)>0\), set \(J_{t+1}=J_t\cup\{j_t\}\) and repeat. If it certifies \(g_j(x^t)\leq0\) for every \(j\in J\), stop and output \(x^t\). Since the restricted feasible region contains the full feasible region, this final feasible restricted-master optimum is also globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve a restricted problem, add a violated constraint found by separation, and stop when the current optimizer satisfies every constraint.

children.title: Column-Generation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Restricted formulations expanded through newly identified variables or patterns.

assumptions_latex: The master linear program is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}\lambda:A\lambda=b,\ \lambda\geq0\}\), with an implicit column set \(Q\).
Each restricted master and pricing problem is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No negative reduced-cost column certifies optimality of the restricted solution for the full linear master.

notation.meaning: dual multiplier for the master equality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear-programming column generation in equality form.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimization over Polyhedra: A Preview p. 157

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(Q_0\subseteq Q\) so the restricted master is feasible. At iteration \(t\), solve \(\min\{\sum_{q\in Q_t}c_q\lambda_q:\sum_{q\in Q_t}a_q\lambda_q=b,\ \lambda_q\geq0\}\) and obtain a dual optimum \(\pi^t\). Solve the pricing problem \(q_t\in\arg\min_{q\in Q}\{c_q-(\pi^t)^{\mathsf T}a_q\}\). If its value is negative, set \(Q_{t+1}=Q_t\cup\{q_t\}\). Otherwise stop: dual feasibility then holds for every full-master column, so the restricted primal solution and \(\pi^t\) are optimal for the full master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve an active-column master, price all implicit columns using its dual solution, and add a column exactly when its reduced cost is negative.
knowledge_statements.title: Column-Generation Interfaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pricing subproblem computes \(q^*\in\arg\min_{q\in Q}\{c_q-\pi^{\mathsf T}a_q\}\). Together with equal restricted primal and dual values, this certifies full-master optimality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-cardinality edge-exchange improvement for symmetric TSP tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer k\ge 2. Given a TSP instance (K_n,c), initialize T as any tour. Repeatedly inspect every S\subseteq E(T) with |S|=k and every tour T' satisfying E(T')\supseteq E(T)\setminus S. If c(E(T'))<c(E(T)), replace T by T' and restart the inspection. When no such improving T' exists, output T.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Improving-neighbor local search and neighborhood-relative optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General neighborhood local search for minimization, including its conditional stopping guarantee, absence of a general global-optimality guarantee, and the LP adjacency interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c(x):x\in F\}\), fix a neighborhood mapping \(N(x)\subseteq F\), start from \(x\in F\), and repeatedly replace \(x\) by a point \(y\in N(x)\) satisfying \(c(y)<c(x)\). If it is established that no such neighbor exists, then the current point is locally optimal relative to \(N\): \(c(x)\le c(y)\) for all \(y\in N(x)\). This does not generally imply global optimality or finite termination. For a linear program, vertices joined by an edge may be regarded as neighbors, and simplex pivots may accordingly be viewed as local-search moves between adjacent basic feasible solutions, subject to the usual qualifications caused by degeneracy. When the simplex method terminates with its optimality condition, its solution is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local search starts from a feasible point and repeatedly moves to a neighboring feasible point having a strictly smaller objective value. If the absence of an improving neighbor is established, the current point is at least as good as every neighbor and is locally optimal for the chosen neighborhood. It need not be globally optimal, and the procedure is not guaranteed to terminate without additional assumptions. In linear programming, edge-adjacent vertices provide a neighborhood interpretation of simplex pivots, with degeneracy requiring care; a simplex solution satisfying its termination optimality condition is globally optimal.
assumptions_latex: \text{Stopping requires establishing that no }y\in N(x)\text{ satisfies }c(y)<c(x).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\nexists y\in N(x):c(y)<c(x)\bigr)\implies \bigl(\forall y\in N(x),\ c(x)\le c(y)\bigr),\qquad x\not\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in F}c(z).

children.title: Local-Move Neighborhood Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood systems distinguished by the size and form of local changes.

children.title: Exchange Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Local move systems based on replacing selected solution components.

assumptions_latex: A current solution \(S\in\mathcal F\) and integers \(p,q\geq0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exchange neighborhood consists exactly of feasible delete-add modifications with the prescribed cardinality limits.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-system exchange neighborhood with bounded deletions and insertions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The \((p,q)\)-exchange neighborhood of \(S\) is \[N_{p,q}(S)=\{(S\setminus A)\cup B\in\mathcal F:A\subseteq S,\ B\subseteq E\setminus S,\ |A|\leq p,\ |B|\leq q,\ |A|+|B|>0\}.\] An improving exchange for an objective \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\) in a minimization problem is a member \(T\in N_{p,q}(S)\) satisfying \(f(T)<f(S)\). This definition separates the move generator from feasibility: deletions and insertions propose a candidate, while membership in \(\mathcal F\) determines whether that candidate belongs to the neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exchange move deletes up to p selected elements, inserts up to q unselected elements, and retains the result only when it is feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Exchange Neighborhoods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, and the bounded delete-add convention is internally precise. Exchange-neighborhood terminology is convention-dependent, however, and no source with an inspectable locator is supplied. The record must remain source-dependent candidate material.

children.title: Swap Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Local move systems based on paired removals and insertions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A swap replaces one selected element by one unselected element while preserving feasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-for-one set-system swap neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The swap neighborhood of \(S\) is \[N_{\mathrm{swap}}(S)=\{(S\setminus\{e\})\cup\{f\}\in\mathcal F:e\in S,\ f\in E\setminus S\}.\] Thus every neighbor has the same cardinality as \(S\) and differs from it in exactly one removed and one inserted element. For minimization of \(g:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\), the solution \(S\) is swap-locally optimal precisely when \(g(S)\leq g(T)\) for every \(T\in N_{\mathrm{swap}}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A swap neighbor removes one selected element, inserts one unselected element, and keeps only feasible results of unchanged cardinality.
knowledge_statements.title: Swap Neighborhoods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, and the one-for-one feasible swap neighborhood is mathematically precise. No cited source establishes that this is the intended convention for the taxonomy, so source support is required.

children.title: k-Opt Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Local move systems parameterized by bounded multi-component modifications.

assumptions_latex: The current solution is a Hamiltonian cycle \(H\) in a complete graph \(G=(V,E)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A k-opt neighbor is obtained by deleting k tour edges and reconnecting the resulting paths into a different Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard traveling-salesperson exact \(k\)-opt neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact \(k\)-opt neighborhood of \(H\) is \[N_k(H)=\{H'\subseteq E:H'\text{ is a Hamiltonian cycle},\ |H\setminus H'|=|H'\setminus H|=k\}.\] Equivalently, choose \(D\subseteq H\) with \(|D|=k\), delete \(D\), and insert \(I\subseteq E\setminus H\) with \(|I|=k\) so that \((H\setminus D)\cup I\) is a Hamiltonian cycle distinct from \(H\). For a minimization objective, \(H\) is exact-\(k\)-opt locally optimal when no member of \(N_k(H)\) has smaller cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-opt tour move removes exactly k tour edges and inserts exactly k other edges so the result is again a Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: k-Opt Neighborhoods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf and the record consistently defines exact k-opt rather than at-most-k-opt. Because both conventions occur in the literature and no source or locator is provided, the intended convention cannot be validated for this container.

children.title: Neighborhood Inclusion Relations
children.top_down_role: Containment and dominance relationships among local move systems.

assumptions_latex: Exchange neighborhoods use the bounded-cardinality definition given in this shard.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Increasing either exchange budget enlarges the neighborhood, and swaps form a subneighborhood of one-for-one exchanges.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion laws for the shard's bounded set-exchange conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\in\mathcal F\), if \(p\leq p'\) and \(q\leq q'\), then \(N_{p,q}(S)\subseteq N_{p',q'}(S)\). Under the one-for-one definition, \(N_{\mathrm{swap}}(S)\subseteq N_{1,1}(S)\), with equality if \(N_{1,1}(S)\) is restricted to moves making exactly one deletion and exactly one insertion. Consequently, for minimization of \(f\), local optimality with respect to a larger neighborhood implies local optimality with respect to every contained neighborhood; the converse need not hold because a larger neighborhood may contain an improving move absent from the smaller one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger deletion and insertion budgets yield larger exchange neighborhoods; local optimality for a larger neighborhood implies local optimality for each contained one.
knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood Inclusion Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the inclusion-relations leaf, and the inclusions follow from the shard's stated bounded-exchange definitions. Those underlying conventions are unsourced, and this record likewise has no citation with an inspectable locator. Source support is required before accepting the property as candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Neighborhood-Size Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search-space growth as the permitted local modification size changes.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a finite feasible set and \(N:S\to 2^S\) is a neighborhood map.
Instances are indexed by an input-size parameter \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\) is polynomial-size if \(\max_{x\in S}|N(x)|\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\), exponential-size if \(\max_{x\in S}|N(x)|=2^{\Omega(n)}\) along an infinite instance family, and implicitly searchable if an improving neighbor can be found or its absence certified in polynomial time without enumerating \(N(x)\).

notation.meaning: neighbors reachable by one allowed local move

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies neighborhoods by cardinality and by the complexity of implicit improvement search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of finite minimization instances with feasible sets \(S\), neighborhood maps \(N:S\to 2^S\), and encoded size \(n\), a neighborhood is polynomial-size when \(\max_{x\in S}|N(x)|\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\). It is exponential-size when \(\max_{x\in S}|N(x)|=2^{\Omega(n)}\) on an infinite subfamily. Independently of cardinality, it is implicitly searchable when a polynomial-time procedure, given \(x\), either returns \(y\in N(x)\) satisfying \(f(y)<f(x)\) or certifies that no such \(y\) exists. Thus a neighborhood may be exponentially large yet algorithmically searchable without explicit enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neighborhood regimes distinguish polynomial or exponential cardinality from polynomial-time implicit search for an improving move.
knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Size Regimes

children.title: Local-Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Witness structures certifying the absence of improving moves in a chosen neighborhood.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\) is minimized, and \(N:S\to 2^S\) is fixed.
A verifier can evaluate the witness predicates for every move class represented by the certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance of \(C(x)\) certifies \(f(x)\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in N(x)\), hence \(x\) is locally optimal with respect to \(N\).

notation.meaning: certificate attached to a feasible solution
objective change of a move from x to y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A neighborhood-relative certificate, not a claim of global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local-optimality certificate for \(x\in S\) is a finite witness \(C(x)\) whose verification establishes \(\Delta_x(y)=f(y)-f(x)\ge 0\) for every \(y\in N(x)\). The witness may explicitly list all move gains when \(N(x)\) is small, or encode inequalities, potentials, reduced costs, or another compact structure covering all admissible moves. If the verifier accepts \(C(x)\), then no strict improving neighbor exists and \(x\) is \(N\)-locally optimal. This conclusion need not imply global optimality unless an additional theorem identifies \(N\)-local optima with global optima for the problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verifiable witness certifies that every allowed neighboring move has nonnegative objective change, establishing neighborhood-local but not necessarily global optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Optimality Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role and neighborhood-relative conclusion are appropriate, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the certificate formulation or compact-witness examples.

children.title: Local Search Trajectory Calculus
children.top_down_role: Rules governing movement among neighboring feasible solutions.

children.title: Improvement-Path Geometry
children.top_down_role: Structural organization of improving trajectories through feasible neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Improvement-Path Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the directed graph induced by strict objective improvement and distinguishes arbitrary paths from maximal trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the directed improvement graph \(G_f=(S,A_f)\) by \(A_f=\{(x,y):y\in N(x),\ f(y)<f(x)\}\). A strict improvement trajectory \((x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_T)\) is a directed path in \(G_f\). Along it, \(f(x_0)>f(x_1)>\cdots>f(x_T)\), so no vertex repeats. Consequently, every strict improvement trajectory in the finite set \(S\) is simple and has at most \(|S|-1\) arcs. If the trajectory is maximal, meaning that it continues whenever an outgoing improvement arc exists, then its terminal vertex is a sink of \(G_f\) and hence an \(N\)-local optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict improvement trajectories are simple directed paths of at most one fewer arc than there are feasible states; a maximal such trajectory terminates at a sink representing a local optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\) is minimized, and \(N:S\to 2^S\) is a neighborhood map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every strict improvement trajectory is simple and has at most \(|S|-1\) arcs; every maximal strict improvement trajectory terminates at a sink of \(G_f\), which is an \(N\)-local optimum.

children.title: Pivot-Rule Selection
children.top_down_role: Criteria used to choose among available improving moves.

assumptions_latex: \(I(x)=\{y\in N(x):f(y)<f(x)\}\) can be generated or searched whenever it is nonempty.
A deterministic tie-breaking order is fixed whenever the selected criterion has multiple minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule produces \(x_{t+1}=r(x_t)\in I(x_t)\) while improvement is possible and stops exactly when \(I(x_t)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic first-improvement and best-improvement rules for finite minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in S\), at iteration \(t\) form or search \(I(x_t)=\{y\in N(x_t):f(y)<f(x_t)\}\). If \(I(x_t)=\varnothing\), stop and output \(x_t\). A first-improvement rule scans neighbors in the fixed order and chooses the first member of \(I(x_t)\). A best-improvement rule chooses \(r(x_t)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in I(x_t)}f(y)\), resolving ties by the fixed order. Set \(x_{t+1}=r(x_t)\) and repeat. Either rule induces a unique strict improvement trajectory once its scan and tie-breaking orders are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pivot rule repeatedly selects an improving neighbor by a fixed criterion and stops when no improving neighbor exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivot-Rule Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and deterministic tie-breaking conditions are precise and appropriate for pivot-rule selection, but no source is cited.

children.top_down_role: Dependence of path length and search behavior on pivot selection.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_r(x_0)\le |S|-1\) and the total work is at most \((T_r(x_0)+1)q(n)=O(|S|q(n))\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts pivots and per-pivot work for deterministic strict-improvement rules.

Since strict improvement prevents repeated states, \(T_r(x_0)\le |S|-1\). This bound may be exponential in encoded input size when \(|S|\) is exponential in \(n\).

children.title: Stalled-Path Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which admissible moves cease to yield useful progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Stalled-Path Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes termination boundaries for strict-improvement local search and separates them from plateau behavior under nonworsening rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A state \(x\in S\) lies on a stalled-path boundary for strict-improvement local search exactly when \(I(x)=\{y\in N(x):f(y)<f(x)\}=\varnothing\). Equivalently, \(f(x)\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in N(x)\), so \(x\) is a sink of the strict improvement graph. Equal-value neighbors in \(B(x)=\{y\in N(x):f(y)=f(x)\}\) do not prevent stalling under a strict pivot rule. If nonworsening moves are admitted, the rule may traverse or cycle on a plateau, and its termination behavior additionally depends on its pivot, memory, and revisit policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict local search stalls exactly where no neighbor improves the objective; when equal-value moves are allowed, termination also depends on how plateau moves and revisits are handled.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\) is minimized, and \(N:S\to 2^S\) is a neighborhood map.
The primary boundary condition concerns rules permitting only strict improving moves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A strict-improvement trajectory stalls at \(x\) exactly when \(I(x)=\varnothing\), equivalently when \(f(x)\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in N(x)\); this equivalence alone does not characterize termination for rules admitting equal-value moves.

children.title: Local Search Failure Boundary

children.title: Local-Optimum Traps
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood structures admitting locally optimal solutions of poor global quality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) is an \(N\)-local optimum but not a global optimum, so strict local search initialized at \(a\) cannot reach the globally optimal state \(c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal finite example separating local from global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimization on \(S=\{a,b,c\}\) with \(N(a)=\{b\}\), \(N(b)=\{a\}\), \(N(c)=\{b\}\), and objective values \(f(a)=1\), \(f(b)=2\), \(f(c)=0\). At \(a\), the only neighbor is worse, so \(f(a)<f(b)\) and \(a\) is an \(N\)-local optimum. Nevertheless, \(c\) is the unique global optimum because \(f(c)<f(a)\). A strict-improvement search initialized at \(a\) therefore stops immediately and cannot reach \(c\), demonstrating a local-optimum trap created by the chosen neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-state instance has a nonglobal local optimum whose only neighbor is worse, trapping strict local search.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Optimum Traps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit three-state counterexample is valid and fits Local-Optimum Traps, but the record contains no cited evidence or marked standard-field rationale.

children.title: Search-State Cycling
children.top_down_role: Repeated-state behavior within local improvement processes.

assumptions_latex: The pivot rule permits equal-value moves and alternates to the available neighbor without memory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated trajectory \(a,b,a,b,\ldots\) cycles indefinitely; strict improvement or a no-revisit mechanism excludes this cycle.

notation.meaning: objective function constant on the two-state plateau

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycling caused by memoryless acceptance of nonworsening plateau moves.

source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{a,b\}\), let \(N(a)=\{b\}\) and \(N(b)=\{a\}\), and set \(f(a)=f(b)=0\). A memoryless rule that accepts nonworsening moves and selects the sole neighbor generates \(a,b,a,b,\ldots\), so it never terminates despite the finite state space. The failure arises because objective monotonicity is non-strict and therefore does not exclude repeated states. Requiring \(f(x_{t+1})<f(x_t)\), forbidding revisits, or imposing a terminating tie-breaking potential eliminates this particular cycling mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing equal-value moves without memory can cycle forever even on two states; strict descent or revisit prevention restores termination.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-State Cycling

children.title: Exponential Improvement Paths
children.top_down_role: Instances whose improving trajectories may require exponentially many moves.

assumptions_latex: For each \(n\ge 1\), let \((g_0,\ldots,g_{2^n-1})\) be a binary reflected Gray-code ordering of \(\{0,1\}^n\).
Set \(N(g_i)=\{g_{i-1},g_{i+1}\}\) at interior indices, with the nonexistent endpoint neighbor omitted, and minimize \(f(g_i)=2^n-1-i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: From \(g_0\), every strict-improvement rule follows \(g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_{2^n-1}\) and performs exactly \(2^n-1\) improving pivots.

notation.meaning: the state at Gray-code position i
path neighborhood along the Gray-code ordering

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit encoded family with a unique exponential-length improving path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\), enumerate \(S_n=\{0,1\}^n\) as a binary reflected Gray code \((g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_{2^n-1})\). Give each interior \(g_i\) the path neighborhood \(N(g_i)=\{g_{i-1},g_{i+1}\}\), with the missing neighbor omitted at each endpoint, and define \(f(g_i)=2^n-1-i\). From every \(g_i\) with \(i<2^n-1\), the unique improving neighbor is \(g_{i+1}\). Hence local search started at \(g_0\) makes exactly \(2^n-1\) improving pivots before reaching \(g_{2^n-1}\), although each state and move has an \(n\)-bit description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gray-code path on n-bit states forces every improving rule to take exactly exponentially many pivots.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Improvement Paths

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gray-code construction does yield a unique exponential-length improving path, but no source supports the construction or its encoded-state and move representation claim.

children.title: Trap-Escape Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where broader moves or selection changes overcome local obstructions.

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is locally optimal for a base neighborhood \(N_1\), and \(N_1(x)\subseteq N_2(x)\).
The objective \(f\) is minimized over a finite feasible set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An enlarged-neighborhood escape exists exactly when \(\min_{y\in N_2(x)\setminus N_1(x)}f(y)<f(x)\); a perturbation escape exists exactly when some admissible \(z\) reaches a state whose strict improvement trajectory leaves the trap basin.

notation.meaning: states whose strict improvement trajectories terminate at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates neighborhood enlargement from perturbation-based escape conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be \(N_1\)-locally optimal and let \(N_1(x)\subseteq N_2(x)\). Direct escape by neighborhood enlargement is possible exactly when there exists \(y\in N_2(x)\setminus N_1(x)\) with \(f(y)<f(x)\). For a fixed strict pivot rule, define the basin \(\mathcal{B}(x)\) as the states whose induced trajectories terminate at \(x\). A perturbation mechanism escapes the trap exactly when it can produce an admissible state \(z\notin\mathcal{B}(x)\). Enlarging the neighborhood may preserve monotone descent; perturbation escape may require an intermediate worsening or equal-value move.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trap is escaped either by adding a newly improving move or by perturbing to a state outside the trapped local optimum's basin.
knowledge_statements.title: Trap-Escape Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The enlargement and fixed-rule basin conditions are coherent, but the terminology and claimed escape-regime correspondence lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Linear Relaxation Bounds
children.top_down_role: Continuous objective bounds supplied by linear relaxations.

assumptions_latex: Both minima are finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For minimization, \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min_{x\in P}c^\top x\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\min_{x\in X}c^\top x\); equality holds whenever an LP optimum belongs to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bounds for finite binary minimization through feasible-set relaxation.

source_refs.locator: Section 8. Linear Programming Interpretation and Relaxation Procedures p. 77

source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be the feasible set of a minimization problem and let \(P\subseteq[0,1]^n\) be a nonempty polyhedral relaxation with \(X\subseteq P\). For \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\min_{x\in X}c^\top x\) and \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min_{x\in P}c^\top x\). Feasible-set inclusion gives \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}\), so the LP value is a valid lower bound. If an optimal LP solution lies in \(X\), then \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=z_{\mathrm{IP}}\) and that solution is integer-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing over a superset of integer solutions yields an LP lower bound, exact whenever an LP optimum is integer feasible.

children.title: Integrality-Gap Measurement
children.top_down_role: Structural comparison between fractional and integral objective quality.

assumptions_latex: For every instance \(I\) in a class \(\mathcal{I}\), a minimization relaxation has values \(0<z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The class integrality gap is \(\operatorname{gap}(\mathcal{I})=\sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}}z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)/z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\); additive gap is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}}(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)-z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I))\).

notation.meaning: integer and relaxation optimum values on instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative and additive conventions for positive-valued minimization instances.

source_refs.locator: Section 8. Linear Programming Interpretation and Relaxation Procedures p. 77

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization instance \(I\) with \(0<z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)<\infty\), its multiplicative integrality ratio is \(\rho(I)=z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)/z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\ge 1\). For an instance class \(\mathcal{I}\), the multiplicative integrality gap is \(\operatorname{gap}(\mathcal{I})=\sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}}\rho(I)\). When zero or signed objective values make this ratio unsuitable, an additive convention is \(\operatorname{gap}_{+}(\mathcal{I})=\sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}}\bigl(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)-z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\bigr)\). The convention used must therefore be stated with the instance domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multiplicative integrality gap is the worst integer-to-LP optimum ratio; an additive difference is used when ratios are unsuitable.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Measurement

source_witnesses.locator: Section 8. Linear Programming Interpretation and Relaxation Procedures p. 77

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated multiplicative and additive conventions are mathematically precise, but the cited locators concern general linear optimization or relaxation and do not directly support the integrality-gap terminology and conventions.

children.title: Gap-to-Recovery Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between relaxation gaps and attainable discrete recovery quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap-to-Recovery Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization form relating an LP-relative rounding guarantee to the integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_I\subseteq X_R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n_{\ge 0}\), and suppose both minima are finite and positive. Define \(z_I=\min\{c^\top y:y\in X_I\}\) and \(z_R=\min\{c^\top x:x\in X_R\}\). If a recovery map \(R:X_R\to X_I\) satisfies \(c^\top R(x)\le \alpha c^\top x\) for every \(x\in X_R\), where \(\alpha\ge1\), then \[z_R\le z_I\le c^\top R(x^*)\le \alpha z_R\] for every relaxation optimum \(x^*\). Consequently, the instance integrality gap \(z_I/z_R\) is at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any rounding map whose cost is at most alpha times its fractional input bounds the minimization integrality gap by alpha.
assumptions_latex: \(c^\top R(x)\le\alpha c^\top x\) for every \(x\in X_R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_I/z_R\le\alpha\)

notation.meaning: Integral feasible set and its relaxation

children.title: Instance-Specific Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem classes distinguished by bounded, growing, or unstable relaxation gaps.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\in\mathcal G_{[a,b]}\iff a\le z_I/z_R\le b\)

notation.meaning: A discrete minimization instance with relaxation and cost
Instances in the declared family whose gaps lie between the stated endpoints
A declared family of admissible minimization instances

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-relative classification of individual minimization instances by relaxation tightness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a declared family of instances \(I=(X_I,X_R,c)\) with \(X_I\subseteq X_R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). Define \(z_I=\min\{c^\top y:y\in X_I\}\) and \(z_R=\min\{c^\top x:x\in X_R\}\). When \(0<z_R\le z_I<\infty\), the instance-specific integrality gap is \(g(I)=z_I/z_R\). For \(1\le a\le b\), define the gap regime by \[\mathcal G_{[a,b]}=\{I\in\mathcal F:a\le g(I)\le b\}.\] The tight regime is \(\mathcal G_{[1,1]}\), while the family \(\mathcal F\) has unbounded gap when \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal F}g(I)=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within a declared family, an instance belongs to a gap regime when its integral-to-relaxed optimum ratio lies in the specified interval; the family has unbounded gap when these ratios have infinite supremum.
knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Specific Gap Regimes

children.title: Rounding Method Regime Pair
children.top_down_role: High-level bridge from fractional solutions to discrete constructions.

children.title: Deterministic Rounding Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Discrete recovery based on fixed choices from fractional information.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Rounding Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic deterministic interface from a solved relaxation to an integral feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an instance \(I\), a relaxation \(X_R(I)\), an integral feasible set \(X_I(I)\subseteq X_R(I)\), and cost \(c\). Compute an optimal relaxed point \(x^*\in\arg\min_{x\in X_R(I)}c^\top x\). Apply a deterministic map \(R_I:X_R(I)\to X_I(I)\) and output \(y=R_I(x^*)\). The interface is an \(\alpha\)-rounding interface if, for every admissible instance, \[y\in X_I(I)\quad\text{and}\quad c^\top y\le\alpha c^\top x^*.\] It stops after the relaxation solver and \(R_I\) terminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the relaxation, deterministically map its optimum to an integral feasible point, and require an alpha-relative cost guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(R_I\) terminates on every admissible relaxed optimum
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_I(x^*)\in X_I(I)\) and \(c^\top R_I(x^*)\le\alpha c^\top x^*\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the deterministic-interface leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied. The record also leaves the admissible instance class, cost-vector domain, and the usual condition \(\alpha\ge1\) implicit. An authoritative deterministic-rounding locator is required before the exact interface can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Randomized Rounding Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Discrete recovery based on probability distributions derived from fractional information.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Rounding Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic randomized interface with almost-sure feasibility and expected approximation control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an instance \(I\), relaxed feasible set \(X_R(I)\), integral set \(X_I(I)\), and cost \(c\). Compute \(x^*\in\arg\min_{x\in X_R(I)}c^\top x\), sample internal randomness \(\omega\), and output \(Y=R_I(x^*,\omega)\). An \(\alpha\)-randomized rounding interface satisfies \[\Pr(Y\in X_I(I))=1\quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb E[c^\top Y]\le\alpha c^\top x^*.\] If only a success event \(S\) is guaranteed, the interface must state \(\Pr(S)\), its resampling rule, and whether the bound is conditional on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized rounding interface returns a feasible integral solution almost surely and controls its expected cost relative to the relaxed optimum.
assumptions_latex: The random map terminates almost surely
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(Y\in X_I(I))=1\) and \(\mathbb E[c^\top Y]\le\alpha c^\top x^*\)

notation.meaning: Declared success event when feasibility is not unconditional

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the randomized-interface leaf and the almost-sure feasibility/expected-cost distinction is coherent, but there is no source. The probability space or random-seed domain and \(\alpha\ge1\) are also unstated. A precise randomized-rounding source is needed to validate the selected generic interface and its success-event addendum.

children.title: Rounding-Derandomization Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between randomized constructions and deterministic counterparts.

knowledge_statements.title: Rounding-Derandomization Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-expectation conversion of sequential randomized rounding into deterministic rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a randomized rounding procedure be determined by finite choices \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\), and let \(L(B_1,\ldots,B_m)\) be an integrable loss. Suppose conditional expectations can be computed and every partial assignment has at least one next value \(b\) satisfying \[\mathbb E[L\mid B_1=b_1,\ldots,B_{k-1}=b_{k-1},B_k=b]\le \mathbb E[L\mid B_1=b_1,\ldots,B_{k-1}=b_{k-1}].\] Choosing such a value at each step produces a deterministic outcome with \(L(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\le\mathbb E[L]\). If zero loss of feasibility is encoded in \(L\), feasibility is preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix each random choice without increasing conditional expected loss; the final deterministic loss is no greater than the original expectation.
assumptions_latex: The random procedure uses finitely many sequential choices
Required conditional expectations and minimizing choices are computable
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\le\mathbb E[L(B_1,\ldots,B_m)]\)

notation.meaning: Deterministically fixed value of the kth choice
Loss or pessimistic estimator being controlled

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-expectation relation is standard and the principle kind fits the leaf, but no source is supplied. Moreover, saying that zero feasibility loss is encoded in \(L\) does not by itself imply preservation: one needs a nonnegative feasibility penalty and an initial expected-loss bound forcing the final penalty to zero. The finite choice domains and conditioning on positive-probability partial assignments also require specification.

children.title: Comparative Rounding Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions favoring deterministic or randomized recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Comparative Rounding Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of deterministic guarantees, expected guarantees, and high-probability guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a relaxed optimum \(x^*\) and nonnegative cost, deterministic \(\alpha\)-rounding requires \(c^\top y\le\alpha c^\top x^*\) for its single output. Randomized expected \(\alpha\)-rounding requires only \(\mathbb E[c^\top Y]\le\alpha c^\top x^*\), which implies that some outcome in the support has cost at most \(\alpha c^\top x^*\) but does not itself identify that outcome. A high-probability \((\alpha,\delta)\) regime requires \[\Pr(c^\top Y\le\alpha c^\top x^*)\ge1-\delta.\] Neither an expectation guarantee nor existence of a good outcome alone supplies an efficient deterministic recovery rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministic, expected, and high-probability rounding guarantees differ in quantifiers and in whether a good outcome can be efficiently found.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[c^\top Y]\le\alpha c^\top x^*\Rightarrow\exists y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y):c^\top y\le\alpha c^\top x^*\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: comparison follows from guarantee quantifiers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is suitable for comparing guarantee regimes, but no citation is supplied. For a general random output, an expectation bound guarantees an outcome of cost at most the expectation, while locating such a point in a topological support requires the support and cost regularity to be defined. The domain \(\alpha\ge1\) should also be explicit.

children.title: Iterative Relaxation Interface
children.top_down_role: High-level bridge from extreme-point structure to repeated fixing and relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Relaxation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract repeated solve–fix–relax scheme driven by extreme-point structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the residual instance \(I_0=I\) and partial integral solution \(F_0=\varnothing\). At iteration \(t\), solve the current relaxation and select an extreme optimum \(x^t\). A structural rule either fixes an integral decision from \(x^t\), updating \(F_{t+1}\), or removes or weakens a designated residual constraint, producing \(I_{t+1}\). Require every iteration to reduce a finite progress measure \(\mu(I_t)\). Stop when no variables remain, and output the completion determined by \(F_t\). Correctness requires the fixing rules to preserve extendability and the relaxation rules to account explicitly for any permitted objective or constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve an extreme-point relaxation, fix integral decisions or relax controlled constraints, and terminate when a finite progress measure reaches zero.
assumptions_latex: Each residual relaxation has an extreme optimum or reports infeasibility
Every update strictly decreases a finite measure \(\mu\)
Fixing and constraint-removal rules have declared invariants
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu(I_{t+1})<\mu(I_t)\) until a completed integral output is returned

children.title: Weak-Relaxation Failure

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Relaxation Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete graphs witness the factor-two boundary of the basic vertex-cover relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimum vertex cover on the complete graph \(K_n\), consider the relaxation \[\min\sum_{v}x_v\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_u+x_v\ge1\ \text{for every edge }uv,\quad x_v\ge0.\] The assignment \(x_v=1/2\) has value \(n/2\), and summing all edge inequalities shows it is optimal. Every integral vertex cover has at least \(n-1\) vertices. Thus the instance gap is \((n-1)/(n/2)=2-2/n\), approaching \(2\). Consequently, this relaxation cannot support a uniform recovery factor strictly below \(2\) on all complete graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic vertex-cover LP has gap approaching two on complete graphs, preventing any uniformly better LP-relative rounding guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation contains only edge-covering inequalities and nonnegativity

notation.meaning: Fractional selection variable for vertex v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical complete-graph vertex-cover gap example
